cards.why: Inactivated sodium channels reset only on repolarization, so a membrane kept depolarized runs out of ready channels.

cards.front: Electrical vs chemical synapse: what crosses between the cells, and how long is the delay?
cards.back: Electrical: ions (current) through gap junctions, almost no delay. Chemical: a neurotransmitter diffusing across a 20 nm cleft, about 0.5 ms delay.
cards.why: Current passes straight through gap junctions, but the cleft is too wide for current to jump, so a chemical must carry the signal.

cards.front: Electrical vs chemical synapse: which can excite or inhibit, and be adjusted by drugs and learning?
cards.back: The chemical synapse. An electrical synapse just follows the first cell’s voltage and can hardly be adjusted.
cards.why: At a chemical synapse the receptor protein decides the effect, and release, binding and removal can each be changed.

cards.front: What triggers neurotransmitter release from an axon terminal?
cards.back: Calcium entering through voltage-gated calcium channels, which binds sensor proteins on docked vesicles and makes them fuse.
cards.why: Calcium is about 10,000 times more concentrated outside than in the cytosol; with no calcium outside, the action potential arrives but nothing is released.

cards.front: EPSP vs IPSP: what does each do to the membrane potential and to the chance of reaching threshold?
cards.back: EPSP: depolarizes, bringing threshold closer. IPSP: hyperpolarizes or holds the membrane near rest, pushing it away from threshold.
cards.why: Both are graded potentials, so they add together at the trigger zone, the IPSPs subtracting from what the EPSPs build.

cards.front: EPSP vs IPSP: which channels and neurotransmitters typically cause each?
cards.back: EPSP: channels for sodium and potassium (net sodium in); glutamate. IPSP: chloride channels (chloride in) or potassium channels (potassium out); GABA, glycine.
cards.why: At −70 mV sodium’s inward push is far stronger than potassium’s outward push, while chloride’s equilibrium potential lies at or just below rest.

cards.front: Temporal vs spatial summation: what is the difference?
cards.back: Temporal: one input fires repeatedly in quick succession. Spatial: several inputs at different places fire at about the same time.
cards.why: Either way, each PSP arrives before the others have faded, so they stack at the trigger zone.

cards.front: Ionotropic vs metabotropic receptor protein: what is each, and how does each change the membrane potential?
cards.back: Ionotropic: a ligand-gated ion channel that opens its own pore. Metabotropic: a G-protein-coupled receptor protein that opens or closes separate channels through a G protein or second messenger.
cards.why: Only the ionotropic kind has a pore; the metabotropic kind relays the signal inside the cell.

cards.front: Ionotropic vs metabotropic: speed, duration and amplification?
cards.back: Ionotropic: under a millisecond, lasts milliseconds, no amplification. Metabotropic: tens of milliseconds or more, lasts up to minutes, amplified.
cards.why: Each step of a G protein cascade activates many copies of the next, which takes time but multiplies the signal.

cards.front: How can acetylcholine excite skeletal muscle but slow the heart?
cards.back: The receptor protein decides: ionotropic nicotinic receptor proteins let sodium in at the muscle; metabotropic receptor proteins on heart cells open potassium channels.
cards.why: A neurotransmitter is not excitatory or inhibitory in itself; its effect depends on the receptor proteins it meets.

cards.front: What are the three ways a neurotransmitter is removed from the synaptic cleft?
cards.back: Diffusion away, breakdown by enzymes (acetylcholinesterase for acetylcholine), and reuptake by transporters.
cards.why: Glutamate, GABA, glycine and the biogenic amines are removed mainly by reuptake, powered by the sodium gradient.

cards.front: Name the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the brain, the main inhibitory one of the brain, and a major inhibitory one of the spinal cord.
cards.back: Glutamate; GABA; glycine.
cards.why: Nearly all their receptor proteins in the adult brain excite (glutamate) or inhibit (GABA and glycine), whether they are channels themselves or act through a G protein.

cards.compare: Drugs and toxins at the synapse
cards.front: Botulinum toxin, organophosphates and SSRIs: which step of synaptic transmission does each change?
cards.back: Botulinum toxin: release. Organophosphates: degradation (they block acetylcholinesterase). SSRIs: reuptake of serotonin.
cards.why: Find the step and follow the chain: less release weakens the signal, and less removal makes it larger and longer.

cards.front: Divergence vs convergence in a neural circuit?
cards.back: Divergence: one neuron synapses on many. Convergence: many neurons synapse on one.
cards.why: Convergence is what spatial summation works on: a motor neuron in the spinal cord sums input from the brain, sensory neurons and interneurons.

cards.front: What does each of the five secondary brain vesicles become?
cards.back: Telencephalon: cerebrum. Diencephalon: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus. Mesencephalon: midbrain. Metencephalon: pons and cerebellum. Myelencephalon: medulla oblongata.
cards.why: The forebrain and hindbrain each split in two while the midbrain does not, turning three primary vesicles into five.

cards.compare: The cerebral lobes and their functions
cards.front: Frontal lobe: where is it, and what are its main jobs?
cards.back: In front of the central sulcus. Starting voluntary movement; planning, decisions and self-control; producing speech.
cards.why: Its motor areas send commands to the opposite side of the body, so damage causes weakness on that side or changes in judgment.

cards.compare: The cerebral lobes and their functions
cards.front: Parietal lobe: where is it, and what are its main jobs?
cards.back: Behind the central sulcus, at the top and upper side. Body sensations (touch, temperature, pain, limb position) and where things are in space.
cards.why: It receives body sensation from the opposite side, so damage causes numbness there, or ignoring one side of space.

cards.compare: The cerebral lobes and their functions
cards.front: Temporal lobe: where is it, and what are its main jobs?
cards.back: Below the lateral sulcus. Hearing; recognizing faces and objects; understanding language; forming memories of events and facts.
cards.why: Damage can cause trouble understanding speech or learning new facts.

cards.compare: The cerebral lobes and their functions
cards.front: Occipital lobe: where is it, and what is its main job?
cards.back: At the back of each hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus. Vision.
cards.why: Damage causes loss of vision in part of what you see.

cards.compare: The cerebral lobes and their functions
cards.front: Insula: where is it, and what does it do?
cards.back: Deep in the lateral sulcus, hidden by the other lobes. Taste, and sensing the state of your own body.
cards.why: It is a buried island of cortex; pull the temporal lobe down to see it.

cards.front: Damage to the cerebellum vs the motor cortex: which side of the body is affected, and how?
cards.back: Cerebellum: clumsy, poorly timed movement (ataxia) on the same side, strength normal. Motor cortex: weakness on the opposite side.
cards.why: The cerebellum corrects movements rather than starting them, and each side coordinates its own side of the body.

cards.front: What does the thalamus do, and which sense bypasses it?
cards.back: It relays and filters almost every signal reaching the cerebral cortex. Smell reaches the cortex without passing through it first.
cards.why: It adjusts how strongly each signal reaches the cortex, part of how you focus on one sound and ignore another.

cards.front: Why is crushing the medulla oblongata fatal?
cards.back: Its nuclei control the heartbeat, blood vessel diameter and the basic rhythm of breathing.
cards.why: When a swollen brain is pushed down through the foramen magnum, the medulla is compressed and breathing and circulation stop.

cards.front: Parkinson’s vs Huntington’s disease: what fails in the basal nuclei, and what movements result?
cards.back: Parkinson’s: dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra die, the brake stays on, movement is slow and hard to start. Huntington’s: striatal neurons die, the brake fails, unwanted jerky movements break through.
cards.why: The globus pallidus constantly inhibits the thalamus, and the striatum lifts that brake for chosen movements, helped by dopamine.

cards.front: Hippocampus vs amygdala: what does each do?
cards.back: Hippocampus: needed to form new memories of facts and events. Amygdala: judges emotional importance, especially threats, and drives fear.
cards.why: Both are parts of the limbic system, which links emotion, memory and the body’s responses through the hypothalamus.

cards.front: What is the reticular activating system, and what happens if it is damaged on both sides?
cards.back: Part of the brainstem’s reticular formation that keeps the cortex awake by sending signals up through the thalamus. Damage on both sides causes coma.
cards.why: Loud noise or pain boosts it, which is why an alarm clock wakes you.

cards.front: Name the three meninges from outside in.
cards.back: Dura mater (tough), arachnoid mater (web-like), pia mater (tender, on the brain surface).
cards.why: The pia follows every gyrus and sulcus; the arachnoid’s web-like strands cross the fluid-filled space between them.

cards.front: Epidural, subdural and subarachnoid spaces: which are real spaces in the skull?
cards.back: Only the subarachnoid space, which holds CSF and the large surface blood vessels. The epidural and subdural spaces are potential spaces in the skull.
cards.why: The dura is fused to the skull and the arachnoid is pressed against the dura; around the spinal cord, the epidural space is real, filled with fat and veins.

cards.compare: Epidural vs subdural vs subarachnoid bleeding
cards.front: Epidural hematoma: vessel torn, speed, and shape on a scan?
cards.back: Usually the middle meningeal artery, from a skull fracture at the side of the head; fast; lens-shaped, stopping at the sutures.
cards.why: Arterial pressure has to peel the dura off the skull, and the dura is fused most firmly at the sutures, so the clot stays compact.

cards.compare: Epidural vs subdural vs subarachnoid bleeding
cards.front: Subdural hematoma: vessel torn, speed, and shape on a scan?
cards.back: Bridging veins; often slow, over hours to weeks; crescent-shaped, crossing sutures but stopping at dural folds.
cards.why: Venous pressure is low, and nothing holds the arachnoid to the dura, so the blood spreads thinly over the brain’s surface.

cards.compare: Epidural vs subdural vs subarachnoid bleeding
cards.front: Subarachnoid hemorrhage: where is the blood, and what are the classic signs?
cards.back: In the subarachnoid space, mixed with CSF. A sudden, worst-ever headache and a stiff neck; blood in CSF from a lumbar puncture.
cards.why: Blood mixing with CSF spreads around the brain and irritates the meninges.

cards.compare: Epidural vs subdural vs subarachnoid bleeding
cards.front: Why can an older adult get a subdural hematoma from a minor fall?
cards.back: The brain shrinks with age, stretching the bridging veins, so a small jolt can tear them.
cards.why: A sudden speeding up or slowing down of the head moves the brain relative to the skull, pulling on veins that are already taut.

cards.front: How much CSF do you have at any moment, and how much do you make each day?
cards.back: About 150 mL at a time; about 500 mL made a day, so it is replaced three to four times daily.
cards.why: The choroid plexuses secrete it continuously and it drains continuously, which is why a block quickly builds pressure.

cards.front: Why is CSF not simply filtered plasma?
cards.back: Choroid plexus cells, sealed by tight junctions, secrete it by active transport, so it has almost no protein, less glucose and slightly different ions.
cards.why: Fluid cannot slip between the covering cells, so everything in CSF passes through them and they control its composition.

cards.front: Obstructive vs communicating hydrocephalus: where is the problem, and which ventricles enlarge?
cards.back: Obstructive: a block inside the ventricles, such as a closed cerebral aqueduct; only the ventricles above the block swell. Communicating: the fluid cannot get back into the blood; all four enlarge.
cards.why: CSF production barely slows as pressure rises, so fluid builds up behind wherever it is stopped.

cards.front: What actually forms the blood–brain barrier?
cards.back: The endothelial cells of brain capillaries, sealed edge to edge by continuous tight junctions, with no pores and few transport vesicles.
cards.why: Astrocyte end-feet cover the capillaries and keep the endothelium in its sealed state, but molecules could slip between the end-feet.

cards.front: Why is levodopa, not dopamine, given for Parkinson’s disease?
cards.back: Levodopa, an amino acid, rides a carrier protein across the blood–brain barrier; dopamine has no carrier and is too water-soluble to dissolve through.
cards.why: Only small lipid-soluble molecules cross freely; glucose and amino acids need carrier proteins, and most other substances are kept out.

cards.front: Where does the adult spinal cord end, and why is a lumbar puncture done at L3–L4 or L4–L5?
cards.back: At the conus medullaris, about L1–L2. Below that the dural sac holds only the cauda equina in CSF, down to about S2.
cards.why: The vertebral column grew longer than the cord after early fetal life; floating roots slide away from the needle.

cards.front: Why is the spinal cord wider at the cervical and lumbar enlargements?
cards.back: Those segments supply the limbs, which have far more muscle and skin, so they hold more motor neurons and receive more sensory axons.
cards.why: More neurons means more gray matter and a wider cord.

cards.compare: Dorsal vs ventral vs lateral horn
cards.front: Dorsal, ventral and lateral horns: what does each hold?
cards.back: Dorsal: interneurons and neurons that relay sensation up. Ventral: motor neurons to skeletal muscle. Lateral (T1 to L2 only): sympathetic motor neurons.
cards.why: Sensation enters at the back of the cord and commands leave at the front.

cards.front: Dorsal vs ventral root: which carries sensory axons in, which carries motor axons out, and which has a ganglion?
cards.back: Dorsal root: sensory, in, with the dorsal root ganglion holding their cell bodies. Ventral root: motor, out, no ganglion.
cards.why: Motor neuron cell bodies sit inside the cord in the ventral and lateral horns, so their root needs no ganglion.

cards.front: Cutting a dorsal root vs a ventral root: what is lost?
cards.back: Dorsal: sensation from the area it supplies is dulled; strength normal. Ventral: the muscles it supplies are weakened; sensation normal. (Neighboring roots overlap, so one root’s loss is partly covered.)
cards.why: Each root carries signals only one way, so cutting it removes just that direction.

cards.front: Why is white matter thickest in the cervical cord?
cards.back: Ascending axons join at every level on their way up, and descending axons leave at every level as they reach their targets, so the most axons pass through the top.
cards.why: Gray matter follows a different rule: it is largest in the enlargements, where the limbs need more neurons.

cards.front: How does a tract’s name tell you whether it is ascending or descending?
cards.back: Names give origin, then destination: “spino-” plus a brain region is ascending; a brain region plus “-spinal” is descending.
cards.why: A tract that starts in the spinal cord and ends in the brain must carry signals up.

cards.front: Why does shingles appear as a painful band of rash on one side of the body?
cards.back: The virus lies dormant in one dorsal root ganglion and travels out along that ganglion’s sensory axons, which supply a single band of skin on one side.
cards.why: Each dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies for the sensory axons of one segment on one side.

cards.front: Where are the primary somatosensory, visual and auditory cortices?
cards.back: Somatosensory: postcentral gyrus, parietal lobe. Visual: back of the occipital lobe. Auditory: top of the temporal lobe, inside the lateral sulcus.
cards.why: A primary sensory area receives the raw signal first; the association area next to it interprets it.

cards.front: Primary motor cortex vs premotor cortex: what does damage to each cause?
cards.back: Primary motor (precentral gyrus): weakness of the opposite side. Premotor: strength normal, but learned sequences such as buttoning a shirt are hard.
cards.why: The premotor and supplemental motor areas plan and sequence movements; the primary motor cortex sends the commands out.

cards.front: What happens when an association area is damaged but its primary area is intact?
cards.back: The person senses but cannot recognize: for example, sees a face clearly but cannot tell whose it is.
cards.why: The primary area still receives the signal; interpreting it is the association area’s job.

cards.front: Why are the hands, lips and tongue so large on the sensory homunculus?
cards.back: They have far more sensory receptors per square centimeter, and each one’s signal needs cortical neurons to receive it.
cards.why: That density is also why you can tell two points apart 2 to 3 mm apart on a fingertip but need about 4 cm on your back.

cards.front: Which functions does each hemisphere usually lead in?
cards.back: Left: language, in about 95% of right-handed people. Right: attending to both sides of space, recognizing faces, the emotional tone of speech.
cards.why: The corpus callosum normally shares information between them within milliseconds; the “left-brained vs right-brained people” idea is a myth.

cards.compare: Expressive vs receptive vs conduction aphasia
cards.front: Expressive vs receptive aphasia: damaged area, speech and understanding?
cards.back: Expressive (Broca’s area): slow, effortful speech, understanding mostly good. Receptive (Wernicke’s area): fluent speech with wrong or made-up words, understanding poor.
cards.why: Broca’s area builds speech plans; Wernicke’s area recognizes words and their meaning.

cards.compare: Expressive vs receptive vs conduction aphasia
cards.front: What is the telltale sign of conduction aphasia?
cards.back: Poor repetition, out of line with fluent speech and good understanding.
cards.why: The link between Wernicke’s and Broca’s areas is damaged, so a heard phrase cannot be passed forward to be spoken, though each area works.

cards.front: Declarative vs procedural memory: what does each store, and which structures form it?
cards.back: Declarative: facts and events; hippocampus and nearby temporal cortex, stored in the cortex. Procedural: skills and habits; basal nuclei and cerebellum.
cards.why: That is why Henry Molaison, without his hippocampi, could still learn a new drawing skill.

cards.front: Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia?
cards.back: Anterograde: cannot form new memories after the injury. Retrograde: loses memories formed before it, recent ones first.
cards.why: Recent memories are least consolidated; old ones, already stored in the cortex, survive best.

cards.front: What happens at a synapse during long-term potentiation?
cards.back: Strong depolarization lets calcium in through a special glutamate receptor protein, which triggers insertion of more glutamate receptor proteins; the same release now gives a larger EPSP.
cards.why: Memory is stored as changes in synaptic strength: neurons that fire together wire together.

cards.front: Order the EEG waves from fastest to slowest, with their frequencies.
cards.back: Beta (over 13 Hz), alpha (8 to 13 Hz), theta (4 to 7 Hz), delta (under 4 Hz).
cards.why: The slower and larger the waves, the more cortical neurons are working in step, as in deep sleep.

cards.front: What electrical activity does an EEG actually record?
cards.back: The summed EPSPs and IPSPs of millions of cortical neurons lined up side by side, not action potentials.
cards.why: Only when many aligned neurons receive synaptic input at once do their small currents add up to a signal big enough to reach the scalp.

cards.front: N3 vs REM sleep: EEG, muscles and dreams?
cards.back: N3: slow, large delta waves; muscles relaxed but can move; few dreams. REM: fast, small waves like waking; paralyzed except eye muscles and diaphragm; vivid dreams.
cards.why: In REM, brainstem neurons actively block the motor neurons, which stops you acting out your dreams.

cards.front: How do sleep cycles change across a night?
cards.back: Cycles of about 90 minutes repeat four to six times. Early cycles hold long N3; later ones have little N3 and longer REM, up to 30 to 60 minutes near morning.
cards.why: That is why you often wake from a dream.

cards.front: What builds sleep pressure while you are awake, and how does caffeine counter it?
cards.back: Adenosine, from ATP used by active neurons, builds up and inhibits arousal neurons through its receptor proteins. Caffeine blocks those receptor proteins.
cards.why: Sleep clears the adenosine; caffeine only hides its effect.

cards.front: What is needed for consciousness, and how does sleep differ from coma?
cards.back: The reticular activating system and the cerebral cortex on both sides, working together. A sleeper can be woken by a strong enough stimulus; a person in a coma cannot.
cards.why: Damage to one hemisphere alone does not cause coma; damage to the upper brainstem or to both hemispheres does.

cards.front: Which connective tissue layer wraps a single axon, a fascicle, and a whole nerve?
cards.back: Endoneurium around each axon, perineurium around each fascicle, epineurium around the whole nerve.
cards.why: The same pattern wraps skeletal muscle (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium). The perineurium’s tight junctions control what passes from the blood into each fascicle.

cards.front: Roots vs rami: which carry only one kind of axon, and which are mixed?
cards.back: The dorsal root is sensory only and the ventral root motor only. Both rami, dorsal and ventral, are mixed.
cards.why: The rami branch after the two roots have joined into the spinal nerve, so sensory and motor axons already run side by side in them.

cards.front: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there, by region?
cards.back: 31: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
cards.why: There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae because C1 leaves above the first vertebra and C8 below the seventh.

cards.front: Which ventral rami form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses?
cards.back: Cervical C1–C4, brachial C5–T1, lumbar L1–L4, sacral L4–S4.
cards.why: Only the dorsal rami and the thoracic ventral rami (the intercostal nerves) skip plexuses.

cards.front: Why does damage to a single nerve root weaken a limb muscle but rarely paralyze it?
cards.back: In a plexus, axons from several segments mix, so most limb muscles are supplied by two or three roots.
cards.why: Losing one root removes only part of the muscle’s motor supply; the rest still reaches it through the plexus.

cards.front: Why does an injury above C3 stop breathing, while one below C5 spares the diaphragm?
cards.back: The phrenic nerve, the diaphragm’s only motor supply, comes from C3–C5: “C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive.”
cards.why: Above C3 the commands for the diaphragm cannot reach those segments; below C5 the phrenic nerve’s segments and its commands are intact.

cards.front: A mid-shaft fracture of the humerus leaves the hand hanging. Which nerve is injured?
cards.back: The radial nerve: wrist drop.
cards.why: The radial nerve spirals around the shaft of the humerus and supplies the wrist and finger extensors.

cards.front: After hours with his legs crossed, a man’s toes drag when he walks. Which nerve is compressed?
cards.back: The common fibular nerve, where it wraps around the neck of the fibula: foot drop.
cards.why: Just below the knee it lies right under the skin, and it supplies the muscles that dorsiflex the foot.

cards.front: Numb thumb, index and middle fingers and a weak thumb: which nerve, and where is it squeezed?
cards.back: The median nerve, in the carpal tunnel at the wrist.
cards.why: The median nerve supplies most thenar muscles and the palm-side skin of the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger.

cards.front: Which dermatomes cover the nipple line, the navel, the thumb and the little toe?
cards.back: Nipple T4, navel T10, thumb C6, little toe and outer foot S1.
cards.why: On the trunk, dermatomes run as horizontal bands; on the limbs they run lengthwise because the limbs grow out from the trunk.

cards.front: Why does a shingles rash appear as a stripe on one side of the body?
cards.back: The virus reactivates in one dorsal root ganglion and travels out along its axons, so the rash fills that ganglion’s dermatome.
cards.why: Each dermatome is the skin whose sensory axons share one dorsal root, and each ganglion serves one side.

cards.front: Name the 12 cranial nerves in order.
cards.back: Olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal.
cards.why: The numbers follow the order in which they leave the underside of the brain, front (I) to back (XII).

cards.front: Which four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic axons?
cards.back: III, VII, IX and X (“1973”).
cards.why: III narrows the pupil and focuses the eye, VII drives tears and two saliva glands, IX the largest saliva gland, and X the chest and abdominal organs.

cards.front: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?
cards.back: I (olfactory), II (optic) and VIII (vestibulocochlear).
cards.why: They carry smell, vision, and hearing and balance, and have no motor axons.

cards.front: Trigeminal (V) vs facial (VII): which feels the face and which moves it?
cards.back: V feels (touch, pain, temperature) and moves the chewing muscles; VII moves the muscles of facial expression.
cards.why: A numb cheek with normal movement points to V; a slack half face that cannot close the eye points to VII.

cards.front: Trigeminal (V) vs facial (VII): what does each carry from the front two-thirds of the tongue?
cards.back: V carries touch; VII carries taste.
cards.why: The two sensations from the same patch of tongue travel in different nerves, so one can be lost without the other.

cards.front: Touching the surface of the eye makes both eyes blink. Which nerve carries the touch in, and which the blink out?
cards.back: The touch goes in on V1 (trigeminal); the blink goes out on VII (facial).
cards.why: That is why one quick test checks two cranial nerves.

cards.front: An eye turned down and out, a drooping lid and a wide pupil that ignores light: which nerve?
cards.back: The oculomotor nerve (III).
cards.why: III supplies four of six eye muscles and the lid lifter, and carries the parasympathetic axons that narrow the pupil.

cards.front: When the patient sticks out the tongue, it points to the left. Which nerve is damaged?
cards.back: The left hypoglossal nerve (XII).
cards.why: Each half of the tongue pushes its own side forward. With the left side weak, the healthy right half pushes the tip toward the left.

cards.front: About what fraction of the axons in the vagus nerve are sensory?
cards.back: Most of them, often put at about 80%.
cards.why: They carry signals from the heart, lungs and digestive organs to the brainstem: stretch of the stomach, blood pressure, lung inflation.

cards.front: Dorsal column pathway vs spinothalamic tract: what does each carry?
cards.back: Dorsal column: fine touch, two-point discrimination, vibration, conscious proprioception. Spinothalamic: pain, temperature, itch, crude touch.
cards.why: That is why a clinician tests vibration and position for one pathway and pinprick and temperature for the other.

cards.front: Dorsal column pathway vs spinothalamic tract: where does each cross the midline?
cards.back: Dorsal column: in the medulla oblongata. Spinothalamic: in the spinal cord, within a segment or two of entry.
cards.why: In both, it is the second-order axon that crosses; the difference is where the first-order neuron ends.

cards.front: Dorsal column pathway vs spinothalamic tract: on which side of the spinal cord does each climb, relative to the body part?
cards.back: Dorsal column: the same side. Spinothalamic: the opposite side.
cards.why: The dorsal column axon climbs uncrossed to the medulla; the spinothalamic axon has already crossed near its entry level.

cards.front: Dorsal column pathway vs spinothalamic tract: where does the first-order neuron end?
cards.back: Dorsal column: nucleus gracilis or cuneatus in the medulla. Spinothalamic: the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
cards.why: The dorsal column axon climbs the whole cord without synapsing; the pain axon synapses almost at once.

cards.front: The right half of the cord is cut at T10. Where is vibration lost, and where is pain lost?
cards.back: Vibration is lost on the right from T10 down; pain and temperature on the left, from a segment or two below.
cards.why: The right dorsal column carries the right side, uncrossed. The right spinothalamic tract carries signals that crossed from the left.

cards.front: Where are the cell bodies of the first-, second- and third-order neurons of a pathway to conscious touch?
cards.back: First: dorsal root ganglion (or cranial nerve ganglion). Second: spinal cord or brainstem. Third: thalamus.
cards.why: The second-order axon crosses and climbs to the thalamus; the third-order neuron runs from the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex.

cards.front: Tonic vs phasic sensory receptors: which keeps firing during a steady stimulus?
cards.back: Tonic (slowly adapting) sensory receptors keep firing; phasic (rapidly adapting) ones fire at the start and end, then fall silent.
cards.why: Nociceptors and proprioceptors are tonic so injuries and body position stay reported; lamellated corpuscles are phasic, so they signal change.

cards.front: Action potentials are all-or-none. How is a stronger stimulus coded, then?
cards.back: By a higher firing frequency in each sensory neuron, and by more sensory neurons firing.
cards.why: A larger depolarization of the sensory ending holds the trigger zone further above threshold, so the next action potential fires sooner after each refractory period.

cards.front: Why does a blow to the eye make you “see stars”?
cards.back: The labeled line principle: the brain reads the modality from which neurons fire, and the vision pathway is firing.
cards.why: Action potentials look the same in every sensory neuron; only the pathway they travel on tells the brain what kind of sensation it is.

cards.front: Why is heart pain often felt in the inner left arm?
cards.back: Heart pain axons enter the cord at about T1–T4 and converge on the same dorsal horn neurons as axons from the chest and inner arm skin.
cards.why: Those second-order neurons usually report skin, so the brain places the pain in the matching dermatomes: referred pain.

cards.front: Stub your toe: why do you feel a sharp jolt first, then a throbbing ache?
cards.back: Sharp pain travels on thin myelinated axons; slow, aching pain on thinner unmyelinated axons, which conduct far more slowly.
cards.why: The same injury fires both kinds of axon, but the signals arrive at different times.

cards.compare: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
cards.front: Upper vs lower motor neuron damage: what happens to muscle tone?
cards.back: Upper: raised tone, spasticity (after an early floppy phase). Lower: low tone, flaccidity.
cards.why: Cutting the lower motor neuron removes the steady firing that makes tone. Upper motor neuron damage releases spinal circuits from the brain’s restraint.

cards.compare: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
cards.front: Upper vs lower motor neuron damage: what happens to the tendon jerks and the plantar response?
cards.back: Upper: brisk jerks (hyperreflexia), sometimes clonus, and a Babinski sign. Lower: weak or absent jerks, toes down or no response.
cards.why: After upper damage the reflex circuit is intact but undamped; after lower damage its way out to the muscle is gone.

cards.compare: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
cards.front: Upper vs lower motor neuron damage: which causes marked wasting and fasciculations?
cards.back: Lower motor neuron damage.
cards.why: Muscle fibers that lose their nerve supply waste within weeks, and a sick lower motor neuron fires on its own, twitching its whole motor unit.

cards.compare: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
cards.front: Upper vs lower motor neuron damage: what pattern of weakness does each give?
cards.back: Upper: whole movements over a region, such as one side of the body. Lower: only the muscles supplied by that segment, root or nerve.
cards.why: Upper motor neurons command movements; each lower motor neuron supplies particular muscle fibers.

cards.compare: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
cards.front: Give two causes of upper and two of lower motor neuron damage.
cards.back: Upper: loss of blood flow to the motor cortex or internal capsule; multiple sclerosis. Lower: polio; a cut or compressed nerve; Bell’s palsy.
cards.why: Upper motor neurons live in the brain and descending tracts; lower motor neurons in the ventral horn, cranial nerve nuclei and the nerves themselves.

cards.front: Where does most of the corticospinal tract cross, and what does that mean for the side of weakness?
cards.back: At the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. Damage above it weakens the opposite side; damage in the cord weakens the same side.
cards.why: About 85–90% of the axons cross there and descend in the lateral corticospinal tract.

cards.front: Why does a stroke in the motor cortex droop the opposite lower face but spare the forehead?
cards.back: The forehead part of the facial nucleus receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres; the lower-face part mainly from the opposite one.
cards.why: Bell’s palsy, a lower motor neuron lesion, weakens the whole half face, forehead included, because there is no second route.

cards.front: What is the Babinski sign, and what does it mean in an adult?
cards.back: Stroking the outer sole makes the big toe extend upward, often with the toes fanning. In an adult it means corticospinal tract damage.
cards.why: The normal adult plantar reflex curls the toes down. Infants show the upward toe normally, because their corticospinal axons are not yet fully myelinated.

cards.front: Parkinson’s vs Huntington’s disease: what fails in the basal nuclei loop, and what is the result?
cards.back: Parkinson’s: dopamine neurons die, the brake stays on, movement is slow and stiff. Huntington’s: indirect-pathway neurons die, the brake lifts, unwanted movements break through.
cards.why: The globus pallidus output is a constant brake on the thalamus; dopamine favors the “go” pathway that releases it.

cards.front: Which side of the body shows the signs of damage to one cerebellar hemisphere, and what are they?
cards.back: The same side: dysmetria, intention tremor, clumsy rapid alternating movements, with normal strength.
cards.why: The cerebellum’s output crosses and the corticospinal tract crosses back, so the two crossings cancel.

cards.front: Somatic vs visceral reflexes: what is the effector of each?
cards.back: Somatic: skeletal muscle. Visceral (autonomic): smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands.
cards.why: Reflexes are sorted by their effector, matching the two parts of the motor division.

cards.front: Somatic vs visceral reflexes: how many motor neurons run from the CNS to the effector?
cards.back: Somatic: one, myelinated all the way. Visceral: two, synapsing in a ganglion outside the CNS; the second axon is unmyelinated.
cards.why: That is why visceral reflexes are slower than somatic ones.

cards.front: Somatic vs visceral reflexes: can each one inhibit its effector?
cards.back: A somatic reflex always excites (contracts) its muscle. A visceral reflex can excite or inhibit.
cards.why: A motor neuron to skeletal muscle only ever causes contraction; autonomic transmitters can speed or slow their targets.

cards.front: Give an example of a somatic and of a visceral reflex.
cards.back: Somatic: the knee jerk, or pulling your foot off a tack. Visceral: the pupils narrowing in bright light, or saliva flowing when you eat.
cards.why: The first two act on skeletal muscle; the second two on smooth muscle and glands.

cards.front: Name the five parts of a reflex arc in order.
cards.back: Sensory receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector.
cards.why: A missing reflex can come from a break in any of the five, which the rest of the exam must sort out.

cards.compare: Muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ
cards.front: Muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ: what does each detect?
cards.back: Spindle: muscle length and how fast it changes. Tendon organ: muscle tension (force).
cards.why: Spindles lie parallel to the muscle fibers and stretch with them; tendon organs lie in series with them and are squeezed when the muscle pulls.

cards.compare: Muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ
cards.front: Muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ: what does each one’s reflex do to its own muscle?
cards.back: The stretch reflex (spindle) excites it, monosynaptically. The tendon reflex (tendon organ) inhibits it, through interneurons.
cards.why: Each reflex does the opposite to the antagonist: the stretch reflex inhibits it, the tendon reflex excites it.

cards.front: Where is the sensor of a “deep tendon reflex”?
cards.back: In the muscle: the muscle spindles. Every deep tendon reflex is a stretch reflex.
cards.why: The tap stretches the muscle through its tendon, and the spindles respond.

cards.front: Which spinal segments does each deep tendon reflex test: biceps, triceps, knee, ankle?
cards.back: Biceps C5–C6, triceps C7, knee L3–L4, ankle S1.
cards.why: “One, two, buckle my shoe; three, four, kick the door; five, six, pick up sticks; seven, eight, lay them straight.”

cards.front: Stretch reflex vs withdrawal reflex: which is monosynaptic, and which involves the opposite limb?
cards.back: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic and one-sided. The withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic and comes with the crossed-extensor reflex in the other limb.
cards.why: Interneurons let the withdrawal signal spread over many segments and across the cord.

cards.front: On the 0 to 4+ scale, what do 0, 2+ and 4+ mean?
cards.back: 0: absent even with reinforcement. 2+: normal. 4+: very brisk, with clonus.
cards.why: Always compare with the same reflex on the other side: symmetry matters more than the number.

cards.front: Name the five parts of the neurological exam and what each tests.
cards.back: Mental status (cerebrum), cranial nerves (brainstem and its nerves), sensory (ascending pathways), motor with reflexes (descending pathways, lower motor neurons, muscles), coordination and gait (cerebellum).
cards.why: Each part checks a known region, so the pattern of findings points to where the problem is.

cards.front: What are the GCS ranges for mild, moderate and severe impairment?
cards.back: Mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe 8 or less. The total runs from 3 to 15.
cards.why: Eye opening (1–4), verbal (1–5) and motor (1–6) are added; always report the parts too.

cards.front: A person is steady with eyes open but sways with eyes closed. What is lost?
cards.back: Position sense from the legs (a positive Romberg test): the dorsal columns or large sensory nerve axons.
cards.why: Vision was making up for the missing position sense. Cerebellar damage makes a person unsteady even with eyes open.

cards.front: Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke: cause, share of strokes, and why a scan is needed before treatment.
cards.back: Ischemic: a blocked artery, about 85–87%. Hemorrhagic: a burst artery, about 13–15%. Clot-dissolving drugs help one and worsen the other.
cards.why: The signs alone cannot tell them apart, so a brain scan comes before any clot-dissolving drug.

cards.front: What does BE FAST stand for?
cards.back: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time.
cards.why: Sudden loss of balance or vision, a drooping face, a weak arm or strange speech means a possible stroke: note when the person was last well and call for help at once.

cards.front: Tetraplegia vs paraplegia: level of injury and limbs affected?
cards.back: Tetraplegia: cervical cord, all four limbs and the trunk. Paraplegia: thoracic, lumbar or sacral cord, both legs and the trunk below the level; hands normal.
cards.why: The arms’ motor neurons sit in the cervical enlargement, which runs down to T1; the hand’s small muscles come from C8 and T1. An injury below T1 leaves the hands normal, while a cervical injury weakens them.

cards.front: Whole-face weakness on the right, with weak, brisk-reflexed left limbs. Where is the lesion?
cards.back: The right side of the pons.
cards.why: The right facial nucleus (a lower motor neuron) sits beside corticospinal axons that have not yet crossed. Findings on opposite sides of face and body mark a brainstem lesion.

cards.front: Pinprick is lost below the navel on both sides, with stiff, weak legs. Where is the damage?
cards.back: The spinal cord at about T10.
cards.why: A sensory level, a line below which sensation is lost, points to the cord at that dermatome, and the umbilicus is T10.

cards.front: Which taste qualities work through ion channels, and which through G protein–coupled receptor proteins?
cards.back: Ion channels: salty (Na+) and sour (H+). G protein–coupled receptor proteins: sweet, umami and bitter.
cards.why: Salty and sour ions flow straight in and depolarize the cell; the other three need a second messenger cascade.

cards.front: Is sweet sensed only at the tip of the tongue?
cards.back: No. Every region with taste buds detects all five qualities; the “tongue map” is a myth.
cards.why: The map came from a misreading of small differences in sensitivity. A single taste bud usually holds cells for several qualities.

cards.front: Which cranial nerves carry taste, and from where?
cards.back: VII (facial) from the front two-thirds of the tongue, IX (glossopharyngeal) from the back third, X (vagus) from the throat and epiglottis.
cards.why: All three deliver taste to one nucleus in the medulla oblongata, which relays through the thalamus to the insula.

cards.front: Taste cells vs olfactory sensory neurons: which are neurons?
cards.back: Olfactory sensory neurons are neurons (bipolar) with their own axons. Taste cells are epithelial cells that pass the signal to a sensory neuron.
cards.why: Both are replaced from basal stem cells throughout life.

cards.front: What is unusual about the route smell takes to the cortex?
cards.back: It reaches the olfactory cortex without first relaying in the thalamus, and it links directly with the limbic system.
cards.why: That tight link to the amygdala and hippocampal areas is why a smell can bring back a memory so vividly.

cards.front: Why does food taste flat when a cold blocks your nose?
cards.back: Most flavor is smell. Odorants cannot reach the olfactory epithelium, but the taste buds still work.
cards.why: People with a blocked nose can still tell sweet from salty; they have lost the smell part of flavor.

cards.front: Rods vs cones: which works in dim light, and which gives color?
cards.back: Rods work in dim light (night vision, no color). Cones need bright light and give color and fine detail.
cards.why: Rods have one pigment, rhodopsin; cones have three kinds of pigment, one per cone type.

cards.front: Rods vs cones: where on the retina is each concentrated?
cards.back: Cones in the fovea (which has only cones); rods outside it, densest in a ring about 20 degrees out.
cards.why: That is why you see a faint star better by looking slightly to one side of it.

cards.front: Rods vs cones: why are rods more sensitive but give less detail?
cards.back: Many rods converge on one ganglion cell, so their small signals add up; a foveal cone has its own bipolar and ganglion cell.
cards.why: Pooled rod signals can fire a ganglion cell in faint light, but the brain cannot tell which rod caught the light.

cards.front: Rods vs cones: roughly how many of each are in one retina?
cards.back: About 90 million rods and about 4.5 million cones.
cards.why: Older texts give 120 million and 6 million; the ratio, about 20 rods per cone, is the same.

cards.front: Myopia: cause, what blurs, and the correcting lens?
cards.back: Eyeball too long (or cornea too curved); distant objects blur; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.
cards.why: Distant light focuses in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads the rays so the focus moves back onto the retina.

cards.front: Hyperopia: cause, what blurs, and the correcting lens?
cards.back: Eyeball too short (or cornea too flat); near objects blur first; corrected with a convex (converging) lens.
cards.why: Light would focus behind the retina. A young person can accommodate to make up for it, which strains the eyes.

cards.front: Presbyopia: cause, when it starts, and the correcting lens?
cards.back: The lens stiffens and cannot round up; from the mid-40s; convex lenses for near work only.
cards.why: Distant vision is unaffected because far focus needs no rounding up.

cards.front: For near vision, what do the ciliary muscle, the zonule fibers and the lens each do?
cards.back: The ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule fibers go slack, and the lens rounds up.
cards.why: The ciliary muscle is a ring: contracting shrinks it toward the lens, releasing the tension that held the lens flat.

cards.front: Which does most of the eye’s bending of light, and which can change its bending?
cards.back: The cornea does about two thirds, at a fixed power; the lens does the rest and is the only part that can change.
cards.why: The jump from air into the cornea is the largest change in the light’s path.

cards.front: Where is the damage in bitemporal hemianopia, and in a homonymous hemianopia?
cards.back: Bitemporal: the middle of the optic chiasm (often a pituitary tumor). Homonymous: one optic tract, optic radiation or visual cortex.
cards.why: The chiasm’s crossing fibers carry both outer fields; everything behind the chiasm carries the opposite half of the field from both eyes.

cards.front: In the dark, is a rod depolarized or hyperpolarized, and what does light do?
cards.back: Depolarized (about −40 mV) by the dark current, releasing glutamate steadily. Light hyperpolarizes it and cuts glutamate release.
cards.why: Light activates transducin, which lowers cGMP, so the cGMP-held cation channels close.

cards.front: Light in either eye narrows only the left pupil; the right stays wide. Afferent or efferent damage, and where?
cards.back: Efferent: the right oculomotor nerve.
cards.why: The signal gets in from both eyes and the midbrain drives both sides, but the right pupil’s command cannot get out.

cards.front: Cochlea vs vestibular apparatus: what does each sense?
cards.back: Cochlea: hearing. Vestibular apparatus: tilt and straight-line movement (utricle and saccule) and turning (semicircular canals).
cards.why: Both use hair cells and send signals in cranial nerve VIII, the cochlear and vestibular branches.

cards.front: Cochlea vs vestibular apparatus: what do the stereocilia touch, and what bends them?
cards.back: Cochlea: the tectorial membrane (only the outer hair cells' tallest stereocilia are embedded; the inner hair cells' are bent by fluid), bent by basilar membrane vibration. Maculae: the otolithic membrane, bent by gravity and lagging gel. Canals: the cupula, bent by lagging endolymph.
cards.why: The otoliths make the maculae’s gel heavy, so gravity pulls it; the cupula has no crystals, so it senses only turning.

cards.front: Cochlea vs vestibular apparatus: where is the first brain relay for each?
cards.back: Cochlea: the cochlear nuclei. Vestibular apparatus: the vestibular nuclei. Both are in the brainstem.
cards.why: Vestibular signals then go to the cerebellum, the spinal cord, the eye movement nuclei and the cortex.

cards.front: Which end of the basilar membrane responds to high notes, and why?
cards.back: The base, near the oval window, where the membrane is narrow and stiff. The wide, floppy apex responds to low notes.
cards.why: Each sound’s traveling wave peaks at the place tuned to its frequency; which hair cells fire tells the brain the pitch.

cards.front: Conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss: where is the problem in each?
cards.back: Conductive: the external or middle ear (wax, fluid, a torn eardrum, a fused stapes). Sensorineural: the cochlea (usually hair cells) or the cochlear nerve.
cards.why: Conductive loss blocks delivery of sound; sensorineural loss blocks conversion or transmission.

cards.front: Conductive vs sensorineural loss in the left ear: where is the Weber fork heard, and what does the left Rinne test show?
cards.back: Conductive: Weber louder on the left; Rinne bone better than air. Sensorineural: Weber louder on the right; Rinne air better than bone, both faint.
cards.why: Bone conduction bypasses the external and middle ear, so it stays normal in a conductive loss but falls with a damaged cochlea or nerve.

cards.front: Why does opening channels in a hair cell’s stereocilia let K+ flow in, not out?
cards.back: The stereocilia stand in endolymph, which is K+-rich and about 80 mV positive, so both gradients push K+ into the cell.
cards.why: What matters is the gradient across that membrane, not the ion’s usual direction.

cards.front: How does the middle ear raise the pressure of sound about 20-fold?
cards.back: The eardrum is about 17–20 times the area of the stapes footplate, and the ossicles add a little lever force.
cards.why: Pressure is force divided by area, so concentrating the eardrum’s force on the small oval window raises the pressure.

cards.front: Why do words stay clear when you shake your head, but blur when you shake the page?
cards.back: The vestibulo-ocular reflex: the semicircular canals signal the head’s turn, and the eyes turn the same amount the opposite way within about 10 ms.
cards.why: When the page moves instead, there is no head movement to drive the reflex.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic: where do the preganglionic neurons sit?
cards.back: Sympathetic: lateral horn of T1–L2 (thoracolumbar). Parasympathetic: brainstem nuclei (with nerves III, VII, IX, X) and sacral cord S2–S4 (craniosacral).
cards.why: Sympathetic fibers reach every level through the chain, but they leave the CNS only from T1–L2.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic: where are the ganglia, and which fiber is long?
cards.back: Sympathetic: chain and collateral ganglia near the cord; short preganglionic, long postganglionic. Parasympathetic: terminal and intramural ganglia at the organ; long preganglionic, short postganglionic.
cards.why: Where the ganglion sits decides which fiber has to cover the distance to the organ.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic: why is sympathetic output widespread and parasympathetic output local?
cards.back: Each sympathetic preganglionic neuron diverges to many postganglionic neurons, and the adrenal medulla adds a hormone; each parasympathetic one reaches only a few, near one organ.
cards.why: So a single sympathetic burst reaches many organs at once, while the stomach can be stimulated without the pupils narrowing.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic: which reaches the skin, the limbs and most blood vessels?
cards.back: Only the sympathetic division, through the gray rami and the spinal nerves.
cards.why: Parasympathetic fibers have no chain and do not travel in the gray rami, so they supply only the head and the organs of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

cards.front: Somatic vs autonomic motor pathways: how many neurons, and which effectors?
cards.back: Somatic: one neuron to skeletal muscle. Autonomic: two neurons, meeting in a ganglion, to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
cards.why: Every autonomic signal changes neurons in a ganglion outside the CNS.

cards.front: Somatic vs autonomic motor pathways: what happens to the effector if its nerve is cut?
cards.back: Somatic: the skeletal muscle is paralyzed and wastes away. Autonomic: the effector keeps working on its own; the heart keeps beating and the gut keeps moving.
cards.why: Autonomic nerves adjust effectors that have their own activity; skeletal muscle contracts only on command.

cards.front: Somatic vs autonomic motor pathways: how does each axon end on its effector?
cards.back: Somatic: one neuromuscular junction per muscle fiber. Autonomic: varicosities strung along the axon, releasing transmitter onto many cells.
cards.why: Transmitter from a varicosity spreads to many nearby smooth muscle cells.

cards.front: White vs gray rami communicantes: what fibers does each carry, and at which levels?
cards.back: White: myelinated preganglionic fibers into the chain, only at T1–L2. Gray: unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back to the spinal nerve, at every level.
cards.why: The colors come from myelin: white rami look white because their fibers are myelinated.

cards.front: What are the three routes a preganglionic fiber can take through the sympathetic chain?
cards.back: Synapse at its own level; climb or descend and synapse at another level; or pass through without synapsing, in a splanchnic nerve, to a collateral ganglion.
cards.why: Climbing the chain is how the head and neck get sympathetic supply from T1 and below.

cards.front: Why does the adrenal medulla count as part of the sympathetic division?
cards.back: Its chromaffin cells are stimulated directly by preganglionic fibers and come from the same tissue as postganglionic neurons, but release epinephrine into the blood.
cards.why: It behaves like a sympathetic ganglion whose “postganglionic” cells have no axons.

cards.front: Nicotinic vs muscarinic receptor proteins: where is each in the autonomic system?
cards.back: Nicotinic: on all postganglionic neurons of both divisions and on adrenal chromaffin cells. Muscarinic: on all parasympathetic targets and on eccrine sweat glands.
cards.why: Every preganglionic neuron releases ACh onto nicotinic receptor proteins; parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release it onto muscarinic ones.

cards.front: Nicotinic vs muscarinic receptor proteins: which is ionotropic, and which can inhibit?
cards.back: Nicotinic: ionotropic, fast and always excitatory. Muscarinic: metabotropic (G protein–coupled), slower, excitatory or inhibitory by subtype.
cards.why: A ligand-gated channel can only open; a G protein can open or close channels and change second messengers.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What does alpha-1 activation usually do? Give examples.
cards.back: Smooth muscle contracts: small arteries of skin, gut and kidneys constrict, the pupil widens (dilator contracts), sphincters tighten, hair stands up.
cards.why: Alpha-1 receptor proteins raise calcium inside smooth muscle cells.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What does beta-1 activation do?
cards.back: The heart: faster rate and stronger contractions.
cards.why: Beta-1 raises cyclic AMP; in pacemaker tissue that brings threshold sooner, and in heart muscle it lets more calcium in.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What does beta-2 activation do, and what mainly activates it?
cards.back: Smooth muscle relaxes (small airways widen) and the liver releases glucose. Mainly circulating epinephrine, since NE binds beta-2 weakly.
cards.why: Most beta-2 receptor proteins are not reached by sympathetic varicosities.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What do alpha-2 receptor proteins on an adrenergic varicosity do?
cards.back: NE binding them cuts further NE release: local negative feedback.
cards.why: Alpha-2 receptor proteins lower cyclic AMP; in the brainstem they reduce sympathetic output as a whole, which is how clonidine lowers blood pressure.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: How do sympathetic nerves and circulating epinephrine each act on small arteries in resting skeletal muscle?
cards.back: Sympathetic nerves constrict them (NE on alpha-1); low levels of circulating epinephrine dilate them (beta-2).
cards.why: Alpha-1 and beta-2 pull in opposite directions; which wins depends on whether NE or epinephrine is binding. In working muscle, chemicals released by the muscle itself override the constriction.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What transmitter and receptor protein drive eccrine sweat glands?
cards.back: ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins, released by sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
cards.why: Sweating is the famous exception: a sympathetic response carried by a cholinergic neuron, which is why atropine dries the skin.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: What does each division do to the bladder wall and its outlet, and through which receptor proteins?
cards.back: Sympathetic: the wall relaxes (mainly beta-3) and the outlet tightens (alpha-1). Parasympathetic: the wall contracts (muscarinic) and the outlet relaxes (mainly nitric oxide).
cards.why: So parasympathetic activity empties the bladder and sympathetic activity puts emptying off.

cards.compare: Autonomic receptor proteins and their effects
cards.front: How do the two divisions each change saliva?
cards.back: Parasympathetic: a large volume of watery saliva (muscarinic). Sympathetic: a small volume of thick, protein-rich saliva (mainly beta-1).
cards.why: Both increase secretion, which is why a nervous mouth feels dry and sticky rather than simply dry.

cards.front: Norepinephrine vs epinephrine: source, how each acts, and how each signal ends?
cards.back: NE: sympathetic varicosities, a neurotransmitter, ended by reuptake in about a second. Epinephrine: the adrenal medulla, a hormone, cleared from the blood over minutes.
cards.why: That is why the effects of a fright outlast the nerve activity.

cards.front: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. What are its main effects?
cards.back: Faster heart rate, wide pupils, dry mouth, dry skin, slowed gut and difficulty emptying the bladder.
cards.why: Every one is a parasympathetic (or sweat gland) effect removed. It leaves skeletal muscle alone, because the neuromuscular junction uses nicotinic receptor proteins.

cards.front: Agonist vs antagonist?
cards.back: An agonist binds and activates a receptor protein; an antagonist binds without activating it, blocking the natural transmitter.
cards.why: The response belongs to the receptor protein, so a drug that binds one class reproduces or blocks one slice of autonomic control.

cards.front: Vagal tone vs sympathetic tone: the best example of each, and what happens if it is removed?
cards.back: Vagal tone holds the resting heart rate 20–40 beats below its own rate; removing it (atropine, transplant) raises the rate. Sympathetic tone keeps most vessels partly constricted; removing it widens them and blood pressure falls.
cards.why: Because some tone is always present, one division can turn an effector both up and down.

cards.front: Which effectors receive only sympathetic fibers, and how are they turned down?
cards.back: Most blood vessels, sweat glands, arrector pili muscles and the adrenal medulla. They are turned down by reducing sympathetic tone.
cards.why: With no opposing division, less firing lets the effector relax below its resting level.

cards.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic activation: heart, airways, pupils, gut?
cards.back: Sympathetic: heart faster and stronger, airways wider, pupils wider, gut slower. Parasympathetic: heart slower, airways narrower, pupils narrower, gut faster.
cards.why: The two divisions usually act in opposite directions on the same organs: dual innervation.

cards.front: During exercise, sympathetic output constricts vessels in the skin and gut. Why do vessels in working muscle widen instead?
cards.back: Chemicals released by the working muscle override the sympathetic constriction, with some help from circulating epinephrine on beta-2.
cards.why: Sympathetic nerves themselves constrict skeletal muscle vessels through alpha-1; the local chemicals win in active muscle, shifting blood toward it.

cards.front: How does heat widen skin vessels on the palms compared with most other skin?
cards.back: Palms, soles and lips: mainly by withdrawing sympathetic tone. Most other (hairy) skin: mainly by an active route, sympathetic cholinergic fibers releasing vasodilating signals.
cards.why: Human studies show the active route provides most of the rise in blood flow in hairy skin; many textbooks describe only withdrawal of tone.

cards.front: Why do your heart and hands keep racing and shaking for minutes after a fright has passed?
cards.back: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla keeps circulating for a few minutes after sympathetic firing has fallen back to its resting tone.
cards.why: Nerve signals end within seconds; a hormone in the blood lasts until it is cleared.

cards.front: Which levels of the CNS control the autonomic system, from lowest to highest?
cards.back: Spinal cord (simple visceral reflexes), brainstem (main reflex centers), hypothalamus (master integrator), limbic system and cortex (emotions and thoughts).
cards.why: Higher levels act through lower ones, so fear, embarrassment or the sight of blood can change heart rate and vessels.

cards.front: You stand up quickly and arterial pressure dips. What does the medulla oblongata change?
cards.back: It reduces vagal output and increases sympathetic output: the heart speeds up and strengthens, and vessels constrict.
cards.why: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the large arteries fire less when the pressure falls, and the reflex restores it by negative feedback.

cards.front: A tube of blood is spun in a centrifuge. What are the three layers, from bottom to top?
cards.back: Packed red blood cells (about 45%), a thin buffy coat of white blood cells and platelets (under 1%), and plasma (about 55%).
cards.why: Spinning presses the densest material to the bottom, and red cells are the densest part of blood.

cards.front: Why are the cells of blood called formed elements rather than blood cells?
cards.back: Because platelets are not whole cells: they are fragments of megakaryocytes. Formed elements are red cells, white cells and platelets.
cards.why: The word covers everything in blood that is a cell or a piece of one.

cards.front: What is the hematocrit, and what are its usual ranges?
cards.back: The percentage of blood volume made up of red cells (packed cell volume): about 37–47% in women and 42–52% in men.
cards.why: It is read from the packed red column after spinning, so it is a ratio of heights.

cards.front: Two things can raise a hematocrit. What are they?
cards.back: More red cells, or less plasma (for example dehydration).
cards.why: The hematocrit is red cell volume divided by blood volume, so either the top or the bottom of the fraction can move.

cards.front: Why is the hematocrit unchanged right after a sudden bleed?
cards.back: Cells and plasma are lost together, in their usual proportion. It falls over the following hours as fluid from the tissues dilutes the remaining cells.
cards.why: A ratio cannot show the loss of whole blood until one part of it changes.

cards.front: Give blood’s volume, pH and viscosity in an adult.
cards.back: About 5 L (70 mL/kg, 7–8% of body weight); arterial pH 7.35–7.45; four to five times as viscous as water.
cards.why: Buffers in plasma and red cells hold the pH; red cells supply most of the viscosity.

cards.front: What is plasma made of?
cards.back: About 92% water and 7% proteins, with under 1% each of electrolytes, nutrients, wastes, gases and hormones.
cards.why: The water is the solvent that carries everything else, and heat.

cards.front: What makes albumin, and what are its two main jobs?
cards.back: The liver. It holds water in the blood with its osmotic pull, and it carries poorly soluble substances such as fatty acids, some hormones, calcium and drugs.
cards.why: Albumin cannot cross capillary walls, so it is a solute the barrier holds back, and water follows it.

cards.front: Where do alpha, beta and gamma globulins come from, and what do they do?
cards.back: Alpha and beta: mostly the liver; transport proteins. Gamma: white blood cells; immune proteins that bind specific foreign molecules.
cards.why: Gamma globulins are the one plasma protein group not made by the liver.

cards.front: What is fibrinogen, and is it in serum?
cards.back: A clotting protein made by the liver (4–7% of plasma protein), converted to the threads of a clot. It is not in serum.
cards.why: Fibrinogen is used up when blood clots, so the fluid squeezed from a clot lacks it.

cards.front: A failing liver makes too little albumin. What happens to the tissues?
cards.back: They swell with extra fluid.
cards.why: Less albumin means less osmotic pull holding water in the blood, so more water stays in the tissues.

cards.front: How is serum different from plasma?
cards.back: Serum is plasma without its clotting proteins. Plasma comes from blood kept from clotting; serum is squeezed from blood allowed to clot.
cards.why: Fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins are consumed in building the clot.

cards.front: Which sample is used for clotting tests, and which for many chemistry tests?
cards.back: Plasma for clotting tests; serum for many chemistry and immune tests.
cards.why: Serum has already clotted and lost its clotting proteins, so it cannot be used to measure clotting.

cards.compare: Red cells vs white cells vs platelets
cards.front: How many red cells, white cells and platelets are in each µL of blood?
cards.back: Red cells about 4–6 million; white cells about 4,500–11,000; platelets about 150,000–450,000.
cards.why: There are roughly 500 to 1,000 red cells for every white cell, which is why the buffy coat is so thin.

cards.compare: Red cells vs white cells vs platelets
cards.front: How long do red cells, white cells and platelets usually last in circulation?
cards.back: Red cells about 120 days; white cells hours to years depending on type; platelets about 7–10 days.
cards.why: None of them divides in the blood, so the marrow must replace them all the time.

cards.front: Where does hematopoiesis happen in an adult?
cards.back: In the red bone marrow of flat bones and the ends of some long bones: skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, hip bones, and upper femur and humerus.
cards.why: Much of the marrow of the long bones turns to fatty yellow marrow with age.

cards.front: What do myeloid and lymphoid stem cells give rise to?
cards.back: Myeloid: red cells, megakaryocytes (platelets) and most white cells. Lymphoid: one family of white cells, the ones at the heart of the immune system.
cards.why: Both descend from the hematopoietic stem cell, which divides so that one daughter stays a stem cell.

cards.front: Which growth factor drives each line: red cells, platelets, white cells?
cards.back: Erythropoietin (kidneys) for red cells; thrombopoietin (mainly liver) for platelets; colony-stimulating factors and interleukins for white cells.
cards.why: Each binds receptor proteins on particular stem and blast cells and makes them divide and mature.

cards.front: How does a red cell’s shape and content suit it to carrying oxygen?
cards.back: A thin biconcave disc with no nucleus or organelles, packed with hemoglobin, with a flexible spectrin skeleton.
cards.why: No point is far from the membrane, so oxygen diffuses fast; no organelles leaves room for hemoglobin; flexibility lets it squeeze through capillaries.

cards.front: Why does a red cell not use up the oxygen it carries?
cards.back: It has no mitochondria, so it makes its ATP by glycolysis, which does not use oxygen.
cards.why: The mitochondria are broken down as the cell matures, to make room for hemoglobin.

cards.front: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin carry, and why?
cards.back: Four: one on the iron ion at the center of each of its four heme groups.
cards.why: Adult hemoglobin has two alpha and two beta globin chains, each holding one heme.

cards.front: What does the reticulocyte count tell you?
cards.back: How fast the marrow is working. Normally about 1%; it rises when the marrow speeds up and stays low when it cannot respond.
cards.why: Each new red cell spends about a day in the blood as a reticulocyte.

cards.front: What does the marrow need to make red cells?
cards.back: Iron for heme, vitamin B12 and folate for DNA, amino acids for globin, and energy.
cards.why: Erythroblasts divide fast, so they are among the first cells to suffer when B12 or folate runs short.

cards.front: What does the erythropoietin loop actually sense?
cards.back: The oxygen reaching the kidney tissue, not the number of red cells.
cards.why: So anything that lowers oxygen delivery (anemia, altitude, lung disease) raises EPO, and failing kidneys lower it.

cards.front: At high altitude, when does EPO peak and when do red cells rise?
cards.back: EPO peaks within one to two days and then eases back; reticulocytes rise after 3–5 days and the red cell count climbs over weeks.
cards.why: As more red cells restore oxygen delivery to the kidneys, EPO release falls: negative feedback.

cards.front: When a macrophage breaks down hemoglobin, what happens to globin, iron and heme?
cards.back: Globin becomes amino acids for reuse; iron is carried by transferrin to the marrow or storage; heme becomes biliverdin, then bilirubin.
cards.why: The heme ring cannot be reused once its iron is removed, so it is turned into a waste pigment.

cards.front: Transferrin, ferritin, hemosiderin: what does each do?
cards.back: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores it in a quickly released form inside cells; hemosiderin is a long-term store of clumped ferritin.
cards.why: Free iron is toxic, so iron is almost always bound to a protein.

cards.front: What does a low plasma ferritin mean?
cards.back: Empty iron stores.
cards.why: A little ferritin leaks into plasma in proportion to the store inside cells.

cards.front: Where does most of the iron for new red cells come from each day?
cards.back: Recycled from old red cells: about 20–25 mg a day, against only 1–2 mg absorbed from food.
cards.why: Iron is recycled far more than it is replaced, and the body has no way to excrete extra iron.

cards.compare: Jaundice before, in and after the liver
cards.front: In which kind of jaundice are the urine dark and the feces pale?
cards.back: After the liver: bile cannot drain, so conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood and urine, and none reaches the intestine.
cards.why: Only conjugated bilirubin dissolves in water and can enter urine; stercobilin forms only from bilirubin that reaches the gut.

cards.compare: Jaundice before, in and after the liver
cards.front: Why is the urine normally colored in jaundice from red cell destruction?
cards.back: The extra bilirubin is unconjugated, rides on albumin and does not dissolve in water, so it cannot enter urine.
cards.why: Destruction overwhelms the liver before conjugation, so the unconjugated form builds up.

cards.front: Why is jaundice common in newborns?
cards.back: A newborn breaks down its short-lived fetal red cells while its liver’s conjugating enzyme is still immature.
cards.why: Bilirubin peaks around days 3–5; blue-light phototherapy turns it into forms excreted without conjugation.

cards.front: Which anemias have a high reticulocyte count, and which a low one?
cards.back: High: blood loss (after 3–5 days) and hemolytic anemias. Low: iron deficiency, pernicious anemia, aplastic anemia and kidney failure.
cards.why: A healthy marrow facing loss or destruction speeds up; a marrow short of iron, B12 or EPO, or one that has failed, cannot.

cards.front: Why are red cells small in iron deficiency but large in B12 deficiency?
cards.back: Without iron, erythroblasts keep dividing but cannot fill with hemoglobin. Without B12 or folate, DNA synthesis stalls, so cells grow but divide too few times.
cards.why: Cell size points to the missing ingredient.

cards.front: What causes pernicious anemia, and how is it treated?
cards.back: Too little B12 is absorbed because the stomach lining no longer makes the protein needed to absorb it. B12 injections, or very high oral doses.
cards.why: Injections bypass absorption; a small fraction of a large swallowed dose is absorbed without the carrier protein.

cards.front: What is aplastic anemia, and what else falls with the red cells?
cards.back: The marrow stops making blood cells (drugs, toxins, radiation, immune attack). White cells and platelets fall too.
cards.why: All three lines come from the same marrow stem cells.

cards.front: Why do failing kidneys cause anemia, and what do the red cells look like?
cards.back: The kidneys make too little EPO. The cells are normal in size, and reticulocytes are low.
cards.why: The marrow has what it needs to build each cell but too little signal to make enough.

cards.front: In hemorrhagic anemia from slow bleeding, why do the cells eventually become small and pale?
cards.back: Each lost red cell takes its iron with it, so slow bleeding eventually empties the iron stores.
cards.why: Once iron runs out, it becomes an iron-deficiency anemia.

cards.front: What is thalassemia?
cards.back: An inherited anemia in which too little alpha or beta globin chain is made; cells are small and pale, and many are destroyed early.
cards.why: Without enough of one chain, the cell cannot fill with working hemoglobin.

cards.front: Why does anemia speed breathing mainly on exertion, not at rest?
cards.back: On exertion, muscles short of oxygen lean on glycolysis and release acid, which drives breathing. The blood’s oxygen sensors respond to dissolved oxygen, which stays normal in anemia.
cards.why: Anemia lowers the oxygen carried on hemoglobin, not the pressure of dissolved oxygen.

cards.front: What single change causes sickle cell disease, and what does it do?
cards.back: Valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta chain. Deoxygenated HbS sticks into stiff fibers that bend red cells into sickles, which jam small vessels and are destroyed early.
cards.why: One amino acid changes the protein’s surface, and shape sets function.

cards.front: Why is the sickle gene common where malaria was widespread?
cards.back: One copy (sickle cell trait) usually causes no symptoms and gives partial protection against severe malaria.
cards.why: Carriers survived malaria more often and passed the gene on.

cards.compare: Primary vs secondary vs relative polycythemia
cards.front: Primary, secondary and relative polycythemia: what raises the hematocrit in each?
cards.back: Primary: marrow stem cells make red cells without EPO (EPO low). Secondary: raised EPO, as at altitude. Relative: plasma loss, with normal red cell mass.
cards.why: The EPO level and the plasma volume tell them apart.

cards.front: Rank the five leukocytes from most to least common in blood.
cards.back: Neutrophils (50–70%), lymphocytes (20–40%), monocytes (2–8%), eosinophils (1–4%), basophils (0.5–1%).
cards.why: A memory aid: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas.

cards.front: Neutrophil: nucleus, granules, job, and when it rises?
cards.back: 3–5 lobes; small, faint lilac granules; engulfs and kills bacteria; rises in bacterial infections.
cards.why: Its granules are lysosomes full of enzymes, and it makes toxic oxygen compounds to kill what it swallows.

cards.front: Eosinophil: nucleus, granules, job, and when it rises?
cards.back: 2 lobes; large red-orange granules; attacks parasitic worms and modulates allergic reactions; rises in worm infections and allergies.
cards.why: Worms are too big to engulf, so eosinophils release toxic granule proteins onto them.

cards.front: Basophil: nucleus, granules, job?
cards.back: 2 lobes hidden by large dark blue-purple granules; releases histamine in allergic and inflammatory reactions.
cards.why: Histamine widens vessels and makes them leaky, so fluid and leukocytes move into the tissue.

cards.front: Lymphocyte: appearance, job, and when it rises?
cards.back: Round cell almost filled by a large dark nucleus with a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm; specific immune defense; rises in viral infections.
cards.why: Most lymphocytes live in lymphoid tissue and pass back and forth through the blood.

cards.front: Monocyte: appearance, job, and when it rises?
cards.back: The largest leukocyte, with a kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus; leaves the blood to become a macrophage; rises in long-lasting infections.
cards.why: Macrophages arrive after neutrophils and survive for months, so they dominate once an infection lasts.

cards.front: Which leukocytes are granulocytes and which are agranulocytes?
cards.back: Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes: lymphocytes, monocytes.
cards.why: The groups are sorted by granules visible on a stained smear; agranulocytes have only tiny lysosomes too small to see.

cards.front: What is pus made of?
cards.back: Mostly dead neutrophils, dead bacteria and debris.
cards.why: Neutrophils are the first to arrive at a bacterial infection and survive only a day or two in the tissues.

cards.front: What are band cells, and why do they rise?
cards.back: Young neutrophils with a curved, unsegmented nucleus, released early from the marrow in a serious bacterial infection.
cards.why: The marrow empties its reserve before the nucleus has finished lobing.

cards.front: What is the difference between an antigen and an antibody?
cards.back: An antigen is a molecule the immune system recognizes as a target. An antibody is a Y-shaped gamma globulin whose arm tips fit one antigen’s shape.
cards.why: Each antibody has two or more binding sites, so it can coat a microbe or link neighboring cells into clumps.

cards.front: A differential shows lymphocytes 10% of a white count of 16,000/µL. Are lymphocytes low?
cards.back: No: 16,000 × 0.10 = 1,600/µL, within the normal range. The percentage fell because neutrophils rose.
cards.why: Always check absolute counts before calling a type high or low.

cards.front: Define leukocytosis and leukopenia.
cards.back: Leukocytosis: a white count above about 11,000/µL. Leukopenia: below about 4,500/µL.
cards.why: The dangerous part of leukopenia is a low neutrophil count, the first defense against bacteria.

cards.front: Leukemia vs lymphoma: where does each grow, and how does it first show?
cards.back: Leukemia: blood-forming cells in the marrow and blood; fatigue, bruising, infections, abnormal count. Lymphoma: lymphocytes in lymph nodes; painless swollen nodes.
cards.why: Leukemic cells crowd out normal marrow, so red cells and platelets fall even as the white count rises.

cards.front: How are platelets made?
cards.back: Thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes, which push arms of cytoplasm into marrow vessels; the flowing blood breaks them into thousands of platelets.
cards.why: A megakaryocyte copies its DNA many times without dividing, so it grows huge.

cards.front: A platelet has no nucleus. What can and cannot it do?
