cards.back: It cannot divide or make new RNA, but it can make a few proteins from RNA left by its megakaryocyte. It cannot renew itself and lasts about 7–10 days.
cards.why: That leftover RNA runs out, so a platelet is replaced rather than repaired.

cards.front: What do a platelet’s granules release when it is activated?
cards.back: ADP, serotonin and calcium (to recruit platelets and help clotting), clotting proteins including fibrinogen, and growth factors for repair.
cards.why: Granule release is how one activated platelet recruits the next.

cards.front: What are petechiae, and what causes them?
cards.back: Tiny red-purple pinpoint spots in the skin where single capillaries have bled: a sign of too few platelets.
cards.why: Platelets seal the small breaks that happen every day in small vessels.

cards.front: What are the three overlapping steps of hemostasis?
cards.back: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation and coagulation.
cards.why: All three are set off by the same injury within seconds; clotting is only the third.

cards.front: What causes vascular spasm?
cards.back: Direct injury to the smooth muscle, chemicals such as thromboxane A2 and serotonin, and local nerve reflexes from pain fibers.
cards.why: A narrower vessel leaks less, and slower flow lets platelets and clotting proteins build up.

cards.front: What does von Willebrand factor do?
cards.back: It sticks to exposed collagen and catches platelets, even in fast arterial flow; it also carries and protects factor VIII.
cards.why: That is why von Willebrand disease causes both poor adhesion and low factor VIII.

cards.front: Why is platelet plug formation positive feedback, and what keeps it local?
cards.back: Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2, which activate more platelets. The healthy lining nearby releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin and destroys ADP.
cards.why: The response strengthens the stimulus, so something outside the loop must confine it.

cards.front: What is the end point of coagulation?
cards.back: Thrombin cuts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin threads, which factor XIIIa cross-links into a mesh.
cards.why: Everything else in coagulation is about making a large burst of thrombin in the right place.

cards.front: Name factors I, II, III and IV.
cards.back: I fibrinogen, II prothrombin, III tissue factor, IV calcium ions.
cards.why: Factors are numbered in the order they were discovered, not the order they act.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: What are the three phases of the cell-based model, and where does each happen?
cards.back: Initiation on tissue factor cells, amplification on platelets, propagation on the activated platelet surface.
cards.why: A trickle of thrombin made on tissue factor cells primes platelets, whose surface then makes the burst.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: In your body, what starts clotting, and when?
cards.back: Tissue factor with factor VIIa, exposed by the tear itself, at the same time platelets start to stick.
cards.why: Tissue factor sits on cells in the vessel wall that blood never touches while the lining is intact.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: Which pathways do the PT and the aPTT test?
cards.back: PT (reported as INR): extrinsic and common. aPTT: intrinsic and common.
cards.why: The PT adds tissue factor; the aPTT adds a contact activator. Both add phospholipid and calcium.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: List the lab model’s intrinsic, extrinsic and common pathways.
cards.back: Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX (+VIII) → X. Extrinsic: tissue factor + VIIa → X. Common: Xa (+Va) turns prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin turns fibrinogen to fibrin, XIIIa cross-links.
cards.why: For your exam, this is the picture most courses expect, and it is how clotting tests are read.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: People without factor XII have a very long aPTT but do not bleed. What does that show?
cards.back: Factor XII is not needed to stop bleeding in the body; tissue factor starts clotting there.
cards.why: The lab model cannot explain this; the cell-based model can.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: Why does the lab model fail to explain bleeding in hemophilia?
cards.back: It says the extrinsic pathway alone should be enough. In the body, tissue factor–VIIa is switched off within seconds, and the burst on platelets needs IXa with VIIIa.
cards.why: The cell-based model explains why missing VIII or IX leaves a trickle but no burst.

cards.compare: Intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway (the lab model) vs the cell-based model
cards.front: What role do platelets play in the lab model and in the cell-based model?
cards.back: Lab model: none (phospholipid is added instead). Cell-based model: central; their surface hosts the thrombin burst.
cards.why: Clotting factors work fast only when held on a membrane surface by calcium.

cards.front: What stops a clot from spreading beyond the injury?
cards.back: Flow dilutes activated factors; the healthy lining releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin and carries thrombomodulin (thrombin then activates protein C); antithrombin inactivates thrombin and Xa.
cards.why: Clotting is fast where tissue factor and activated platelets are and stopped where there is healthy lining.

cards.front: Which factors need vitamin K, and what does it do for them?
cards.back: II, VII, IX and X (and protein C). The liver uses it to add acid groups that bind calcium, letting the factors attach to phospholipid surfaces.
cards.why: Without it the proteins are made but do not work.

cards.front: Why are newborns given a vitamin K injection?
cards.back: Little vitamin K reaches the fetus, breast milk holds little, and the newborn gut is only beginning to gain bacteria, so stores are very low.
cards.why: One injection prevents a rare but serious bleeding disease of newborns.

cards.front: What is clot retraction?
cards.back: Within 30–60 minutes, platelets use actin and myosin to pull on fibrin, tightening the clot, squeezing out serum and drawing the vessel edges together.
cards.why: The fluid squeezed out is serum, because the clotting proteins stay in the clot.

cards.front: Why is plasmin made on the clot and not throughout the blood?
cards.back: Both plasminogen and tPA bind fibrin, so tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin right on the clot.
cards.why: That confines the breakdown of fibrin to where fibrin is.

cards.front: Heparin vs warfarin: how each works and how each is monitored.
cards.back: Heparin speeds antithrombin, acts in minutes, is monitored by aPTT and reversed by protamine. Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, acts over 3–5 days, is monitored by PT/INR and reversed by vitamin K.
cards.why: Warfarin is slow because working factors already in the blood must be used up first.

cards.front: Does heparin or warfarin dissolve a clot?
cards.back: Neither. They stop a clot growing and new ones forming, while fibrinolysis clears the old one.
cards.why: They act on making thrombin, not on breaking down fibrin.

cards.front: Is heparin one of the plasma’s natural anticoagulants?
cards.back: Not normally: heparin is stored in mast cell and basophil granules. Heparin-like molecules on the vessel lining speed antithrombin. (Many exams list heparin from mast cells and basophils as a natural anticoagulant.)
cards.why: Heparin is not normally found in plasma; its natural role is packing granule contents.

cards.front: Why is aspirin often stopped a week before surgery?
cards.back: It permanently blocks the platelet enzyme that makes thromboxane A2, and a platelet, with no nucleus, can make almost no new enzyme, so the effect lasts for the platelet’s 7–10 day life.
cards.why: Only new platelets, made after the last dose, work normally.

cards.front: How does the bleeding pattern tell a platelet problem from a clotting factor problem?
cards.back: Platelet problems: petechiae, bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding. Factor problems: deep bleeding into joints and muscles, and bleeding that restarts hours later.
cards.why: With a factor problem the plug forms but no fibrin reinforces it.

cards.front: Which factors are missing in hemophilia A and B, and why are most patients male?
cards.back: A: factor VIII. B: factor IX. Both genes lie on the X chromosome; males have one X, so one faulty copy causes disease.
cards.why: Females have two X chromosomes and are usually carriers without symptoms.

cards.front: Thrombus vs embolus?
cards.back: A thrombus is a clot attached to the wall of an unbroken vessel. An embolus is a mass carried in the blood until it lodges and blocks a vessel.
cards.why: A piece of a deep leg vein thrombus can break off and lodge in the lungs as an embolus.

cards.front: What three conditions make a thrombus likely?
cards.back: Slow or stagnant flow, damage to the vessel lining, and blood that clots more readily than normal (Virchow’s triad).
cards.why: Slow flow lets activated factors build up; damaged lining loses its anticlotting defenses.

cards.front: What antigens and plasma antibodies go with types A, B, AB and O?
cards.back: A: A antigen, anti-B. B: B antigen, anti-A. AB: both antigens, no anti-A or anti-B. O: neither antigen, both antibodies.
cards.why: The plasma has antibodies against the ABO antigens its own red cells lack.

cards.front: Why does everyone have anti-A or anti-B without ever receiving blood?
cards.back: Bacteria in the gut and food carry sugar chains that look like A and B antigens, and the immune system makes antibodies against those its own cells lack.
cards.why: That is why a first ABO-mismatched transfusion reacts at once.

cards.front: How does the Rh group differ from ABO in its antibodies?
cards.back: Anti-D forms only after exposure to Rh-positive cells, over weeks; anti-A and anti-B are present from infancy without exposure.
cards.why: So a first Rh mismatch usually causes no reaction but sensitizes the person.

cards.front: Which type is the universal red cell donor, and which the universal recipient?
cards.back: O negative is the universal donor; AB positive the universal recipient.
cards.why: O-negative cells carry no A, B or D antigen; AB-positive plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D. When there is time, hospitals still give type-specific, crossmatched blood.

cards.front: For plasma transfusions, which ABO type can be given to anyone?
cards.back: AB plasma, because it holds no anti-A or anti-B.
cards.why: For plasma the logic reverses: it is the donor’s antibodies that matter, not the donor’s red cell antigens.

cards.front: Can two type A parents have a type O child? Can two type O parents have a type A child?
cards.back: Yes, if each parent carries one O copy. No: an O copy makes no working enzyme, so two O parents can only pass on O.
cards.why: A and B copies make their antigen whenever present; O shows only when both copies are O.

cards.front: Blood clumps with anti-A and anti-D but not anti-B. What is the type?
cards.back: A positive.
cards.why: Clumping in a well means the red cells carry the antigen that well’s antibody binds.

cards.front: Agglutination vs coagulation?
cards.back: Agglutination: antibodies clump cells by their surface antigens. Coagulation: fibrin threads form a clot.
cards.why: Both can happen in a transfusion reaction, but they are different processes.

cards.front: What is a crossmatch?
cards.back: Mixing the patient’s plasma with red cells from the actual donor unit and checking for agglutination before the unit is issued.
cards.why: ABO and Rh are only two of many blood groups, so a crossmatch catches other antibodies.

cards.front: What is the first thing to do when a transfusion reaction is suspected, and why?
cards.back: Stop the transfusion at once.
cards.why: Every extra milliliter of incompatible cells adds to the agglutination, hemolysis and falling blood pressure.

cards.front: Why is the first Rh-positive baby of an Rh-negative mother usually unharmed?
cards.back: Fetal cells enter her blood mostly at delivery, and she makes anti-D over the following weeks, after that baby is born.
cards.why: The harm comes in later Rh-positive pregnancies, when her anti-D crosses to the fetus.

cards.front: How is Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn prevented?
cards.back: Anti-D immune globulin for the Rh-negative mother at about 28 weeks, within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive baby, and after any event that may mix the bloods.
cards.why: The injected anti-D clears fetal Rh-positive cells before her own immune system responds, so she never makes her own.

cards.front: Why do ABO differences between mother and fetus usually cause only mild disease?
cards.back: Most anti-A and anti-B cannot reach the fetus, and fetal red cells carry A and B antigens only weakly.
cards.why: A type O mother has some anti-A and anti-B of the crossing kind, so her type A or B baby can be mildly affected even in a first pregnancy.

cards.front: Steroid vs peptide hormones: what is each built from, and does each dissolve in water or lipid?
cards.back: Peptide and protein hormones: amino acids; water-soluble. Steroid hormones: cholesterol; lipid-soluble.
cards.why: What a hormone is built from decides whether it dissolves in the watery plasma or in the lipid bilayer, and that sets how it travels and acts.

cards.front: Steroid vs peptide hormones: how does the gland store and release each?
cards.back: Peptide: made ahead, stored in vesicles, released by exocytosis. Steroid: not stored; made on demand and diffuses out as soon as it is made.
cards.why: A lipid-soluble steroid would leak straight through a vesicle membrane, so it cannot be stored that way.

cards.front: Steroid vs peptide hormones: how does each travel in the blood, and which lasts longer?
cards.back: Peptide: mostly free in the plasma; half-life of minutes. Steroid: mostly bound to carrier proteins; half-life of hours.
cards.why: Binding to carrier proteins shields a hormone from the liver’s enzymes and from filtering by the kidneys, so bound hormones last longer.

cards.front: Steroid vs peptide hormones: where is each one’s receptor protein, and what does it change?
cards.back: Peptide: receptor protein in the plasma membrane; switches existing proteins on or off. Steroid: receptor protein inside the cell; changes which genes are transcribed.
cards.why: A water-soluble hormone cannot cross the bilayer, so it must act from outside through a second messenger. A steroid crosses and acts on DNA.

cards.front: Steroid vs peptide hormones: which acts faster, and which can be taken as a tablet?
cards.back: Peptide: seconds to minutes; usually not a tablet, because it is digested like any protein. Steroid: hours to days; yes, absorbed intact.
cards.why: Changing existing proteins is fast; making new proteins through transcription and translation takes hours.

cards.front: Which form of a lipid-soluble hormone is active: bound or free?
cards.back: Only free hormone. It alone can leave the capillaries and bind receptor proteins.
cards.why: The bound form is a reservoir. A small change in binding can double the free hormone, even when the total barely changes.

cards.front: A hormone’s half-life is 10 minutes. Its gland stops at a level of 80 units. What is the level 30 minutes later?
cards.back: 10 units: three half-lives, 80 → 40 → 20 → 10, one eighth of the start.
cards.why: Each half-life removes half of what is left, so after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)<sup>n</sup>.

cards.front: Put the cAMP pathway in order, from hormone to response.
cards.back: Hormone binds receptor protein → G protein → adenylyl cyclase → ATP to cAMP → protein kinase A → proteins phosphorylated → response.
cards.why: Each step switches on the next, and each multiplies the signal, which is why a tiny hormone concentration can change a whole organ.

cards.front: What three things end a cAMP signal?
cards.back: Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down to AMP, phosphatases remove the added phosphates, and the G protein switches itself off.
cards.why: A signal that could not be stopped would be useless; blocking phosphodiesterase (theophylline) makes cAMP last longer.

cards.front: Name the three kinds of stimulus for hormone release, with an example of each.
cards.back: Humoral: a change in a blood ion or nutrient (high glucose, low calcium). Hormonal: another hormone (a pituitary hormone driving the thyroid gland). Neural: nerve fibers (sympathetic fibers on the adrenal medulla).
cards.why: Whatever starts release, negative feedback usually stops it, because the hormone’s effect removes the stimulus.

cards.front: Permissive, synergistic, antagonistic: define each with an example.
cards.back: Permissive: A lets B work fully (the thyroid gland’s hormones and epinephrine). Synergistic: together more than the sum (epinephrine and a glucose-raising pancreatic hormone). Antagonistic: opposite effects on one variable (the two pancreatic hormones that lower and raise glucose in the blood).
cards.why: Permissive effects often work by raising the number of the other hormone’s receptor proteins.

cards.front: Anterior vs posterior pituitary: other name, tissue and embryonic origin?
cards.back: Anterior: adenohypophysis; glandular epithelium; an upgrowth from the roof of the mouth. Posterior: neurohypophysis; nervous tissue (hypothalamic axons and glia); a downgrowth of the hypothalamus.
cards.why: Two glands with different origins explain why the hypothalamus controls them in two different ways.

cards.front: Anterior vs posterior pituitary: how does the hypothalamus control each?
cards.back: Anterior: by releasing and inhibiting hormones carried in the hypophyseal portal system. Posterior: by nerve impulses in the same neurons that make its hormones.
cards.why: The anterior lobe has no nerve link to the brain, so the signal must travel in blood; the posterior lobe is made of the neurons’ axons.

cards.front: Anterior vs posterior pituitary: which hormones does each release, and which makes its own?
cards.back: Anterior: makes and releases GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin (FLAT PiG). Posterior: makes none; stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
cards.why: The four in FLAT are tropic hormones that drive other endocrine glands.

cards.front: Why does the hypothalamus reach the anterior pituitary through a portal system rather than the general circulation?
cards.back: The portal veins carry its hormones straight from the first capillary network to the second, undiluted.
cards.why: Tiny amounts reach high concentrations at the pituitary, and almost none reaches the rest of the body.

cards.front: The infundibulum is cut. Which anterior pituitary hormone rises, and why?
cards.back: Prolactin, because dopamine, its inhibiting hormone, can no longer reach the anterior pituitary.
cards.why: Prolactin is held back more than it is pushed; the other anterior hormones depend on releasing hormones and fall.

cards.front: How does growth hormone make long bones grow?
cards.back: Mostly through IGF-1 from the liver and other tissues, which makes chondrocytes in the epiphyseal plates divide.
cards.why: GH also acts directly on fuel use: it breaks down fat and raises the glucose in the blood.

cards.front: Gigantism vs acromegaly: what decides which one too much GH causes?
cards.back: Whether the epiphyseal plates are still open. Open (childhood): gigantism, very tall. Closed (adult): acromegaly, thick hands, feet, jaw and face, no change in height.
cards.why: Only open plates can lengthen long bones; closed bones can still thicken.

cards.front: Low final hormone with high tropic hormone points to which level of an axis? And low with low?
cards.back: Low with high: the target gland has failed. Low with low: the pituitary or hypothalamus has failed.
cards.why: Long-loop feedback: when the target gland fails, the brake comes off and the healthy pituitary releases more tropic hormone.

cards.front: What is ADH’s main trigger, and what else raises or lowers it?
cards.back: Main: a rise in plasma osmolarity sensed by osmoreceptors. Also raised by a large fall in blood volume or pressure (about 5 to 10% or more), nausea and pain; lowered by alcohol.
cards.why: Osmoreceptors respond to a rise of only 1–2%, so osmolarity is by far the most sensitive signal.

cards.front: Diabetes insipidus vs SIADH: urine volume, urine concentration and plasma sodium?
cards.back: Diabetes insipidus: very large volume of very dilute urine; plasma sodium high or high-normal. SIADH: small volume of concentrated urine; plasma sodium low.
cards.why: Too little ADH action means water is not kept; too much means too much water is kept and the plasma is diluted.

cards.front: What does oxytocin do in labor, and is labor impossible without it?
cards.back: It strengthens uterine contractions through positive feedback. Labor can still start and progress without it; hospitals give it when contractions are weak.
cards.why: Mice lacking oxytocin or its receptor protein give birth normally. (For your exam: oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions through positive feedback.)

cards.front: Hypothyroid vs hyperthyroid: most common cause of each, and the TSH level?
cards.back: Hypothyroidism: Hashimoto thyroiditis (worldwide, iodine deficiency); TSH high when the gland itself fails. Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease; TSH very low.
cards.why: In Graves disease an immune protein switches on the TSH receptor protein, and feedback drives TSH down.

cards.front: Hypothyroid vs hyperthyroid: temperature, weight and heart rate?
cards.back: Hypothyroid: feels cold, gains a little weight despite a poor appetite, slow heart rate. Hyperthyroid: feels hot, loses weight despite a big appetite, fast heart rate at rest.
cards.why: Thyroid hormones set how many pumps and mitochondria cells make, and how many beta-1 receptor proteins the heart has.

cards.front: Hypothyroid vs hyperthyroid: nervous system, skin and gut?
cards.back: Hypothyroid: slowed thinking, tiredness, slow reflexes; dry, thick skin; slow bowel. Hyperthyroid: anxiety, fine tremor, brisk reflexes; warm, moist skin; frequent bowel movements.
cards.why: Almost every sign follows from more or less oxygen use, heat and sympathetic sensitivity in every tissue.

cards.front: Why can a goiter come with too little thyroid hormone or with too much?
cards.back: Iodine deficiency: low hormone, TSH high, TSH makes the gland grow. Graves disease: a stimulating immune protein makes it grow and overproduce.
cards.why: Both drive the TSH receptor protein, so a goiter alone does not tell you the hormone level.

cards.front: T4 vs T3: which does the gland mostly release, and which is active?
cards.back: The gland releases mostly T4 (about 90%). T3 is the active form, binding the receptor protein about ten times more tightly; most T3 is made from T4 in target tissues.
cards.why: T4 works as a long-lasting reserve that tissues activate as they need it.

cards.front: A patient starts levothyroxine. Why is TSH rechecked after about six weeks, not after a few days?
cards.back: T4’s half-life is about a week, so its blood level keeps climbing for about five to six weeks before it levels off.
cards.why: A level takes about five half-lives to reach a steady state; testing sooner would catch it still rising.

cards.front: Why is TSH usually the first blood test for a thyroid problem?
cards.back: The pituitary is very sensitive to feedback: a small fall in free T4 produces a large rise in TSH.
cards.why: TSH moves a lot for a small change in the thyroid gland’s output, so it flags a problem early.

cards.front: How does a follicular cell get iodide from the blood?
cards.back: A cotransporter carries iodide in together with sodium, concentrating it 20 to 40 times: secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient.
cards.why: The gland takes up radioactive iodine the same way, which is how that treatment targets it.

cards.front: After the whole thyroid gland is removed (parathyroid glands intact), does blood calcium change?
cards.back: No: it stays normal, although calcitonin is lost.
cards.why: In adults, PTH and calcitriol are the main regulators; calcitonin’s effect is small. (For your exam: calcitonin is the hormone that lowers blood calcium, by inhibiting osteoclasts.)

cards.front: What does PTH do at bone, at the kidneys, and through calcitriol?
cards.back: Bone: binds osteoblasts, which make osteoclasts form and dissolve bone. Kidneys: keep calcium, lose phosphate. Calcitriol: switches on its making, so the intestine absorbs more calcium.
cards.why: Net effect: higher blood calcium and lower blood phosphate.

cards.front: Hyperparathyroidism vs hypoparathyroidism: calcium, phosphate and nerve and muscle excitability?
cards.back: Hyper: calcium high, phosphate low, nerves and muscles less excitable (weakness, slow gut). Hypo: calcium low, phosphate high, overexcitable (tingling, cramps, tetany).
cards.why: Low extracellular calcium lets voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily.

cards.front: Osteomalacia vs osteoporosis: what is wrong with the bone?
cards.back: Osteomalacia: matrix is laid down but not mineralized, so bone is soft (too little vitamin D). Osteoporosis: too little bone, but what there is is normally mineralized.
cards.why: Without calcitriol, too little calcium and phosphate reach the osteoid.

cards.front: Insulin vs glucagon: which cells make each, and what is the main stimulus?
cards.back: Insulin: beta cells; high blood glucose (also amino acids, gut hormones, the vagus nerve). Glucagon: alpha cells; low blood glucose (also amino acids, sympathetic activity and epinephrine).
cards.why: Both are islet cells that sense glucose directly, so the loop needs no nerve.

cards.front: Insulin vs glucagon: effect on glycogen and gluconeogenesis in the liver?
cards.back: Insulin: glycogenesis on; glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis off. Glucagon: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis on; glycogenesis off.
cards.why: The two are antagonistic: the glucose level at any moment reflects the balance between them.

cards.front: Insulin vs glucagon: main targets, and the effect on glucose uptake by muscle and fat?
cards.back: Insulin: liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; uptake up, by moving GLUT4 to the membrane. Glucagon: mainly the liver; no direct effect on uptake.
cards.why: Skeletal muscle has almost no glucagon receptor proteins, so its glycogen stays in the muscle.

cards.front: Insulin vs glucagon: chemical class and how each signals inside the cell?
cards.back: Insulin: a small protein; its receptor protein is itself an enzyme that phosphorylates proteins. Glucagon: a peptide; G protein–coupled receptor protein, cAMP and protein kinase A.
cards.why: Both are water-soluble, so both act from the plasma membrane.

cards.front: How does a beta cell sense a rise in glucose?
cards.back: Glucose enters and is broken down, ATP rises, ATP closes potassium channels, the cell depolarizes, calcium channels open, and calcium triggers insulin exocytosis.
cards.why: The beta cell is its own sensor and control center; sulfonylurea drugs close the same potassium channels directly.

cards.front: Does the brain need insulin to take up glucose?
cards.back: No. Neurons take glucose in through carriers that are always in the membrane, but they depend entirely on how much glucose is in the blood.
cards.why: Neurons store almost no glycogen and burn almost no fatty acids, so a low blood glucose affects the brain within minutes.

cards.front: Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes: main defect and insulin level?
cards.back: Type 1: beta cells destroyed by the immune system; insulin very low or absent. Type 2: insulin resistance, then beta cells that cannot keep up; insulin normal or high early, falling later.
cards.why: In type 2, beta cells release extra insulin for years before glucose rises.

cards.front: Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes: share of cases, usual onset and treatment?
cards.back: Type 1: about 5–10%; often childhood but any age, sudden over weeks; insulin always. Type 2: about 90–95%; usually adults, gradual over years; activity, diet, weight loss and drugs such as metformin, insulin if needed.
cards.why: For your exam: “juvenile-onset” and “adult-onset” are outdated names for type 1 and type 2.

cards.front: Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes: which carries the high risk of acid blood from fat breakdown, and why?
cards.back: Type 1. With no insulin, nothing blocks fat breakdown, and glucagon is high, so the liver pours out acids made from fat.
cards.why: In type 2, even a little insulin holds back fat breakdown.

cards.front: Why does untreated diabetes cause polyuria and polydipsia?
cards.back: Above about 180 mg/dL the kidney’s glucose carriers are saturated; glucose left in the urine holds water by osmosis, so urine volume rises, the plasma concentrates, and thirst rises.
cards.why: Water follows the glucose that the kidneys cannot take back.

cards.front: What results diagnose diabetes (each confirmed on a second test)?
cards.back: Fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more; 200 or more two hours after a glucose drink; A1C 6.5% or more; or a random 200 or more with the classic symptoms.
cards.why: A1C reflects the average glucose over the past two to three months.

cards.front: Convert a glucose of 7.0 mmol/L to mg/dL.
cards.why: Glucose weighs 180 g per mole, and a liter is 10 dL, so 1 mmol/L = 18 mg/dL.

cards.front: In what order does the body defend against a falling blood glucose?
cards.back: About 80 mg/dL: beta cells cut insulin. About 65–70: alpha cells raise glucagon and the adrenal medulla raises epinephrine. Lower: warning symptoms, then brain symptoms.
cards.why: Only insulin lowers glucose, but several hormones raise it; the first defenses act on the liver.

cards.front: How is hypoglycemia treated in a conscious and in an unconscious person?
cards.back: Conscious: about 15 g of fast sugar, recheck after 15 minutes. Unconscious: nothing by mouth; glucagon by injection or nasal spray, or glucose into a vein.
cards.why: Glucagon works by making the liver release glucose; anything by mouth could be inhaled.

cards.front: Name the three zones of the adrenal cortex, from outside in, and the main hormone of each.
cards.back: Zona glomerulosa: aldosterone. Zona fasciculata: cortisol. Zona reticularis: adrenal androgens such as DHEA.
cards.why: Memory hook: salt, sugar, sex. All three are steroids made from cholesterol.

cards.front: Aldosterone vs cortisol vs epinephrine: source and chemical class?
cards.back: Aldosterone: zona glomerulosa; steroid (mineralocorticoid). Cortisol: zona fasciculata; steroid (glucocorticoid). Epinephrine: chromaffin cells of the medulla; amine (catecholamine).
cards.why: Cortex and medulla are two glands in one, with different origins and different kinds of hormone.

cards.front: Aldosterone vs cortisol vs epinephrine: main stimulus for each?
cards.back: Aldosterone: high plasma potassium and angiotensin II. Cortisol: ACTH (stress, daily rhythm). Epinephrine: sympathetic preganglionic fibers releasing acetylcholine.
cards.why: That is why a pituitary failure lowers cortisol but mostly spares aldosterone.

cards.front: Aldosterone vs cortisol vs epinephrine: mechanism and speed?
cards.back: Aldosterone and cortisol: lipid-soluble, intracellular receptor protein, new proteins; act over hours and last a day or more. Epinephrine: water-soluble, membrane receptor proteins and second messengers; acts in seconds, lasts minutes.
cards.why: Making new proteins takes hours; switching existing proteins on takes seconds.

cards.front: Aldosterone vs cortisol vs epinephrine: what happens with too little of each?
cards.back: Aldosterone: low sodium, high potassium, low blood volume. Cortisol: weakness, low blood glucose, low blood pressure. Epinephrine: usually no disease, because sympathetic nerves cover.
cards.why: The sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine directly onto most of epinephrine’s targets.

cards.front: Put the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system in order.
cards.back: Low pressure in the kidney → renin → angiotensinogen (from the liver) cut to angiotensin I → ACE (mostly in the lungs) makes angiotensin II → aldosterone, vasoconstriction, ADH and thirst.
cards.why: Every product travels in the blood, so four organs can take part without sitting near one another.

cards.front: Why does a person taking an ACE inhibitor tend to keep more potassium?
cards.back: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, and aldosterone is what makes the kidney secrete potassium.
cards.why: Aldosterone makes the last stretch of the kidney’s tubules keep sodium and lose potassium.

cards.front: Name cortisol’s four groups of effects.
cards.back: Raises blood glucose (gluconeogenesis, protein breakdown, insulin resistance); damps inflammation and immunity; permissive for vessel responses to sympathetic signals; slows bone building and affects mood and sleep.
cards.why: The same actions, in excess, explain the signs of Cushing syndrome.

cards.front: Addison disease vs Cushing syndrome: cortisol, ACTH, blood pressure and blood glucose?
cards.back: Addison: cortisol low, ACTH high, blood pressure low, glucose low. Cushing: cortisol high, ACTH low with medication or an adrenal tumor (high with a pituitary tumor), blood pressure high, glucose high.
cards.why: ACTH follows feedback: it rises when the cortex fails and falls when cortisol comes from elsewhere.

cards.front: Why does the skin darken in Addison disease but not when the pituitary fails?
cards.back: In Addison disease ACTH is very high, and ACTH and a related hormone cut from the same precursor stimulate melanocytes. When the pituitary fails, ACTH is low.
cards.why: Low cortisol takes the brake off a healthy pituitary.

cards.front: Why must a glucocorticoid drug taken for months be tapered, not stopped suddenly?
cards.back: The drug suppressed CRH and ACTH, and the zona fasciculata shrank. After stopping, ACTH stays low for weeks, so there is little cortisol from either source and an adrenal crisis can follow.
cards.why: Tapering gives the hypothalamus, pituitary and cortex time to restart.

cards.front: What happens in the stage of exhaustion of the stress response?
cards.back: Prolonged exposure to the stress hormones does damage: muscle wasting, high blood glucose, raised blood pressure, weaker immune defenses. The adrenal glands do not run out.
cards.why: Long-term stress usually keeps cortisol normal or high. (For your exam: resources are depleted and resistance fails.)

cards.front: Alarm reaction vs stage of resistance: which hormones carry each?
cards.back: Alarm (seconds to minutes): sympathetic nerves and epinephrine. Resistance (hours to weeks): cortisol, with angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH holding salt and water.
cards.why: Nerve and amine signals act in seconds; steroids act over hours through new proteins.

cards.front: What controls melatonin release?
cards.back: Light, through melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, the suprachiasmatic nucleus and sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion. At night, as timed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the pathway drives release; light shuts it off within minutes.
cards.why: Melatonin is a timing signal telling the body’s clocks what time of night it is, more than a sleeping pill.

cards.front: Where is the master clock, and what resets it each day?
cards.back: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm; morning light resets it.
cards.why: Left without time cues, most people drift to a cycle of about 24.2 hours.

cards.front: What releases ANP, and what does it do?
cards.back: Stretch of the heart’s upper chambers. The kidneys excrete more sodium and water, renin, aldosterone and ADH fall, and vessels dilate.
cards.why: ANP is the counterweight to the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

cards.front: What makes the kidneys release erythropoietin, and what does it do?
cards.back: Hypoxia in the kidney tissue. EPO makes the red bone marrow produce more red blood cells, raising oxygen delivery over weeks.
cards.why: The kidney receives a lot of blood but extracts little oxygen, so its tissue oxygen tracks what the blood can deliver.

cards.front: Hypoxia vs hypoxemia: what does each mean, and can one occur without the other?
cards.back: Hypoxemia: too little oxygen in the arterial blood. Hypoxia: too little oxygen reaching the tissues. After a large bleed, tissues are hypoxic without hypoxemia.
cards.why: With too few red cells and too little flow, each milliliter of blood can carry normal oxygen yet deliver too little.

cards.front: Why does giving leptin do little for most people with obesity?
cards.back: Most have high leptin already; their brains respond to it weakly (leptin resistance).
cards.why: Only the rare children born unable to make leptin are helped by injections.

cards.front: Which hormone closes the epiphyseal plates in both sexes?
cards.back: Estrogen. In males, much of it is made from testosterone by aromatase.
cards.why: Men without working aromatase or estrogen receptor protein keep growing into their twenties and thirties.

cards.front: Why do anabolic steroids shrink the testes?
cards.back: High androgen feeds back to suppress GnRH, LH and FSH, so the testes lose their drive and sperm production falls.
cards.why: The same negative feedback can leave the user with low testosterone for months after stopping.

cards.front: About how much fluid enters lymph each day, and how much reaches the veins through the lymphatic ducts?
cards.back: About 8 L enters lymph in the tissues; lymph nodes return up to half straight to the blood, so about 3 to 4 L reaches the veins through the ducts. The classic exam answer for lymph returned to the blood is about 3 L a day.
cards.why: Capillaries filter along almost their whole length and reabsorb little; without lymphatic return, blood volume would fall and tissues would swell.

cards.front: Why can fluid enter a lymphatic capillary but not leak back out?
cards.back: Overlapping endothelial cells act as one-way flaps: higher pressure outside pushes them in; higher pressure inside presses them shut.
cards.why: Anchoring filaments pull the vessel open as the tissue swells, so drainage speeds up just when there is more fluid to remove.

cards.front: Lymph has no heart. What moves it toward the veins?
cards.back: Smooth muscle in each valved segment of the collecting vessels, the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump and the pulse of nearby arteries.
cards.why: One-way valves turn every squeeze into forward flow, which is why lymph flow in a still limb nearly stops.

cards.front: Thoracic duct vs right lymphatic duct: what does each drain, and where does it empty?
cards.back: Thoracic duct: both legs, abdomen, pelvis and the left side of the chest, arm, head and neck (about three quarters of the body), into the left internal jugular–subclavian junction. Right lymphatic duct: right arm, right chest, right head and neck, into the right junction.
cards.why: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli, which receives the lumbar and intestinal trunks.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary lymphoid organs: examples, and what happens in each?
cards.back: Primary (red bone marrow, thymus): lymphocytes are made and mature, with no foreign antigen needed. Secondary (lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, Peyer’s patches, other MALT): mature lymphocytes gather and meet antigens.
cards.why: Maturing happens before a lymphocyte meets anything foreign; responding needs antigen brought in by lymph, blood or across a mucous membrane.

cards.front: Why does lymph slow down inside a lymph node, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Several afferent vessels feed one or two efferent vessels, and the maze of sinuses has a wide total cross section.
cards.why: Slow lymph lingers beside the macrophages lining the sinuses, giving them time to engulf bacteria, debris and cancer cells.

cards.front: In a lymph node, which lymphocytes gather in the nodules of the cortex, and which in the paracortex?
cards.back: Cortex nodules (follicles): the line of lymphocytes that can become antibody-releasing cells; a germinal center forms when they meet their antigen. Paracortex (deep cortex): mostly the thymus-matured line.
cards.why: Lymphocytes enter from the blood in the paracortex, through high endothelial venules.

cards.front: White pulp vs red pulp of the spleen: what fills each and what does it do?
cards.back: White pulp: lymphocytes around central arteries, where lymphocytes meet antigens carried in the blood. Red pulp (about three quarters): blood in cords and venous sinuses, where macrophages remove old red cells, platelets and bacteria.
cards.why: Blood must squeeze through narrow slits into the sinuses; stiff old or sickled red cells get stuck and are engulfed.

cards.front: Is the spleen a large lymph node?
cards.back: No. It has no afferent lymphatic vessels, so no lymph reaches it: it filters blood, not lymph.
cards.why: That is why losing the spleen raises the risk of bloodstream infection while the lymph nodes go on filtering lymph as before.

cards.front: Name three lasting effects of losing the spleen.
cards.back: More old and misshapen red cells in circulation; a higher platelet count; a lifelong higher risk of overwhelming infection with sugar-coated bacteria.
cards.why: The spleen held about a third of the platelets and was the main filter for bacteria that are hard to engulf elsewhere, so patients get extra vaccines.

cards.compare: Edema from high capillary pressure vs lymphedema
cards.front: Edema from high capillary pressure vs lymphedema: what fails, protein content, and pitting?
cards.back: High capillary pressure: filtration outruns normal drainage; fluid low in protein; pits easily, often both legs. Lymphedema: drainage fails at normal filtration; fluid rich in protein; pits early, then turns firm and non-pitting, usually one limb.
cards.why: Stagnant, protein-rich fluid draws in lymphocytes whose signals make fibroblasts lay down collagen, and fat builds up.

cards.front: Why do surgeons examine the first lymph node draining a tumor?
cards.back: Cancer cells that break off a tumor travel in lymph and are caught first in that node.
cards.why: A hard, painless, growing node may hold cancer cells dividing there, unlike the tender swelling of a node fighting an infection.

cards.front: Innate vs adaptive immunity: how fast does each act?
cards.back: Innate: ready at birth, acts within minutes to hours. Adaptive: about a week to build on first exposure, peaking in one to two weeks.
cards.why: Adaptive responses start from the few lymphocytes that fit, which must multiply first.

cards.front: Innate vs adaptive immunity: what does each recognize?
cards.back: Innate: molecular patterns shared by whole groups of microbes, and signs of damage. Adaptive: one specific antigen per lymphocyte.
cards.why: Innate cells use inherited pattern recognition receptor proteins; each lymphocyte’s receptor protein fits one antigen.

cards.front: Innate vs adaptive immunity: which improves with repeat exposure?
cards.back: Adaptive: faster and stronger the next time, through memory. Innate: essentially the same response each time.
cards.why: Memory lymphocytes left from the first response are more numerous and switch on more easily.

cards.front: Innate vs adaptive immunity: main cells and molecules?
cards.back: Innate: neutrophils, macrophages, eosinophils, mast cells, NK cells; complement, interferons, antimicrobial proteins, cytokines. Adaptive: the two main lines of lymphocytes; antibodies, and receptor proteins on lymphocytes that fit one antigen.
cards.why: The two work together: innate cells alert lymphocytes, and adaptive immunity points innate killers at its targets.

cards.front: What do pattern recognition receptor proteins (such as Toll-like receptor proteins) bind?
cards.back: Molecules microbes make and you do not, and cannot easily change: bacterial wall molecules, flagellar protein, viral double-stranded RNA. Some also bind molecules from your own damaged cells.
cards.why: Binding damage signals is why a sterile injury, with no microbe present, still inflames.

cards.front: Link each sign of inflammation to its cause: redness and heat, swelling, pain.
cards.back: Redness and heat: arterioles dilate. Swelling: capillaries and venules leak plasma. Pain: prostaglandins act on pain-sensing endings, plus pressure from swelling.
cards.why: Histamine and prostaglandins drive both vessel changes; the leak also delivers complement, antibodies and clotting proteins.

cards.front: In what order do leukocytes leave the blood at an inflamed site?
cards.back: Rolling, sticking, diapedesis (squeezing between endothelial cells), then chemotaxis toward the attractants.
cards.why: Cytokines make the venule wall sticky; the leukocyte must be held against the wall before it can squeeze through.

cards.front: Acute vs chronic inflammation: duration, main cells, outcome?
cards.back: Acute: hours to days; neutrophils; usually full resolution. Chronic: weeks to years; macrophages and lymphocytes; ongoing damage and fibrosis.
cards.why: Chronic inflammation persists when a microbe, foreign material or trigger cannot be cleared, as in atherosclerosis or inhaled silica.

cards.front: Why does a phagocyte’s oxygen use jump when it kills?
cards.back: The oxidative burst: an enzyme in the vesicle membrane makes superoxide from oxygen, which becomes hydrogen peroxide and, in neutrophils, hypochlorous acid.
cards.why: The oxygen is used to make weapons, not ATP. In chronic granulomatous disease this enzyme is faulty and phagocytes cannot kill many bacteria.

cards.front: How does an NK cell decide to kill a cell?
cards.back: It weighs “kill me” stress proteins against the “leave me alone” self-identity protein. Too little self-identity protein or many stress proteins tip it to kill.
cards.why: Many viruses and cancers switch off the self-identity protein to hide from lymphocytes, which exposes them to NK cells.

cards.front: What three things does complement do once C3 is split?
cards.back: Opsonization (C3b coats microbes for phagocytes), inflammation (C3a and C5a trigger mast cells; C5a attracts neutrophils), and the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9 punch a pore).
cards.why: All three pathways, classical, lectin and alternative, converge on splitting C3. Opsonization is the most important of the three.

cards.front: How do type I interferons slow a virus’s spread?
cards.back: An infected cell releases them; they bind neighboring cells and switch on genes for antiviral proteins that block viral protein synthesis and break down viral RNA.
cards.why: The infected cell usually cannot save itself, but paracrine warning makes its neighbors resist infection.

cards.front: What causes the chills at the start of a fever?
cards.back: Pyrogens make prostaglandin E2 raise the hypothalamic set point, so normal body temperature is now below it; the hypothalamus runs heat-gain responses: skin vasoconstriction and shivering.
cards.why: Fever is negative feedback around a higher set point; when the set point falls again, you flush and sweat.

cards.front: Fever vs overheating from hard exercise in the heat: set point, and do fever-reducing drugs help?
cards.back: Fever: set point raised by pyrogens; body temperature rises to meet it; drugs that block prostaglandin synthesis lower it. Overheating: set point normal; temperature is above it; those drugs do nothing, cooling is needed.
cards.why: The drugs work by lowering the set point, which is only raised in a fever.

cards.front: What is an epitope?
cards.back: The small part of an antigen, about 5 to 20 amino acids or a few sugars, that one antigen receptor protein or antibody binds.
cards.why: A protein has many epitopes and a bacterium hundreds of proteins, so many different lymphocytes respond at once: a polyclonal response.

cards.front: B cell vs T cell: where does each mature and what does its antigen receptor protein bind?
cards.back: B cell: red bone marrow; binds epitopes on intact antigens, free or on surfaces. T cell: thymus; binds short peptides held on MHC proteins on another cell.
cards.why: A B cell needs no presenting cell; a T cell sees nothing unless a cell displays the antigen on MHC.

cards.compare: MHC class I vs class II
cards.front: MHC class I vs class II: which cells carry it, and where do its peptides come from?
cards.back: Class I: nearly all nucleated cells; peptides from proteins made inside the cell, loaded in the ER. Class II: mainly antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); peptides from material taken in from outside, loaded in vesicles fused with lysosomes.
cards.why: Class I says “this cell is infected or abnormal”; class II says “this is what I found in the tissues”.

cards.front: Why do dendritic cells start almost every new T cell response?
cards.back: They sample the skin and mucous membranes, engulf microbes, then carry processed antigen through afferent lymph to a lymph node’s paracortex, where naïve T cells pass through.
cards.why: Naïve T cells circulate between blood and lymph nodes and never wander into a small cut, so the antigen must be brought to them.

cards.front: With about 20,000 genes, how do you make millions of different antigen receptor proteins?
cards.back: Each maturing lymphocyte cuts and joins gene pieces at random, adding or removing a few DNA letters at each join.
cards.why: The receptor proteins exist before any antigen arrives; the antigen selects cells that already fit rather than shaping them.

cards.front: Positive vs negative selection in the thymus: what does each test, and where?
cards.back: Positive (cortex): can the receptor protein bind self MHC at least weakly? If not, the cell dies of neglect. Negative (mostly medulla): does it bind self peptide on self MHC too strongly? If so, it is killed (clonal deletion).
cards.why: About 98 percent of thymocytes fail. The survivors see foreign peptides on self MHC without reacting strongly to self.

cards.front: What happens to a T cell that binds its self peptide on a resting dendritic cell?
cards.back: It becomes unresponsive for a long time: clonal anergy.
cards.why: A resting dendritic cell has detected no danger and gives no confirming second signal. This is part of peripheral tolerance.

cards.front: Why does a first response to a new antigen take about a week?
cards.back: Only about 1 in 100,000 to 1 in a million naïve lymphocytes fits any one epitope; the antigen selects them, and they must divide every 6 to 8 hours for several days to build clones of tens of thousands or more.
cards.why: Clonal expansion is also why the lymph nodes draining an infection swell.

cards.front: Why is a second encounter with the same microbe met faster?
cards.back: Memory cells left from clonal expansion are 100 to 1,000 times more numerous than the original naïve cells, live for years or decades and switch on faster with less stimulation.
cards.why: The response starts within 1 to 3 days, so the microbe is usually cleared before illness. Vaccines work this way.

cards.front: Why are brothers and sisters checked first as bone marrow donors?
cards.back: They have a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting the same two sets of MHC genes.
cards.why: MHC genes are the most variable in the population, so an unrelated donor almost never matches.

cards.front: Which MHC class does CD4 bind, and which does CD8 bind?
cards.back: CD4 binds MHC class II; CD8 binds MHC class I. (4 × 2 = 8 and 8 × 1 = 8.)
cards.why: The coreceptor clamps onto the MHC beside the T cell receptor protein, so it decides which cells a T cell can respond to.

cards.compare: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells
cards.front: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells: surface marker and MHC class recognized?
cards.back: Helper: CD4, class II. Cytotoxic: CD8, class I. Regulatory: CD4 (with FOXP3 inside), class II.
cards.why: Class I is on nearly every cell, so the killer answers it; class II is on presenting cells, so the coordinators answer it.

cards.compare: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells
cards.front: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells: main action and main tools?
cards.back: Helper: directs other cells (cytokines such as interferon gamma, IL-2, IL-4, and contact). Cytotoxic: kills infected and abnormal cells (perforin, granzymes, Fas ligand). Regulatory: suppresses other lymphocytes (IL-10, TGF-beta, IL-2 uptake).
cards.why: Regulatory T cells also strip B7 from dendritic cells, so other T cells cannot get costimulation.

cards.compare: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells
cards.front: Helper vs cytotoxic vs regulatory T cells: what happens if each type is lost?
cards.back: Helper: most adaptive responses fail, antibody and cytotoxic. Cytotoxic: viral infections and some cancers spread. Regulatory: T cells attack the body’s own tissues (as in IPEX, from a broken FOXP3 gene).
cards.why: Helper T cells sit at the hub: B cells and cytotoxic T cells both depend on their signals.

cards.front: What three signals does a naïve T cell need to switch on?
cards.back: Signal 1: its T cell receptor protein binds peptide on MHC. Signal 2: costimulation, CD28 binding B7. Signal 3: cytokines that steer what it becomes.
cards.why: A dendritic cell makes plenty of B7 only after sensing a microbe, so signal 1 without signal 2 leads to anergy instead.

cards.front: How does IL-2 drive clonal expansion of an activated T cell?
cards.back: The activated T cell makes both IL-2 and the receptor protein for it, so it stimulates its own division (autocrine signaling).
cards.why: Drugs such as tacrolimus block IL-2 production, which is how they prevent transplant rejection.

cards.front: Th1 vs Th2 cells: main cytokines and what each is best against?
cards.back: Th1: interferon gamma and IL-2; arm macrophages and cytotoxic T cells against viruses and bacteria living inside cells. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; direct eosinophils, mast cells and mucus against parasitic worms.
cards.why: Each holds the other back: interferon gamma blocks Th2 development and IL-4 blocks Th1. Th2 gone wrong gives allergy.

cards.front: Why does a cytotoxic T cell kill by apoptosis instead of bursting the target?
cards.back: Apoptosis breaks the cell into tidy fragments that macrophages engulf, destroying virus still being assembled inside, with little inflammation.
cards.why: Perforin makes pores and granzymes enter to switch on the target’s own caspases; Fas ligand binding Fas does the same.

cards.compare: Cytotoxic T cell vs natural killer cell
cards.front: Cytotoxic T cell vs NK cell: what does each recognize, and which leaves memory?
cards.back: Cytotoxic T cell: one specific peptide in MHC class I; needs about a week of activation first; leaves memory cells. NK cell: stress signals and missing MHC class I; acts within hours; mostly no memory.
cards.why: Both kill the same way, with perforin, granzymes and Fas ligand, ending in apoptosis.

cards.compare: Hyperacute vs acute vs chronic rejection
cards.front: Hyperacute vs acute vs chronic rejection: timing and main cause?
cards.back: Hyperacute: minutes to hours, antibodies already present against ABO or HLA on the donor’s vessels. Acute: days to months, recipient T cells attacking donor HLA. Chronic: months to years, slow T cell and antibody damage.
cards.why: Hyperacute is prevented by ABO matching and crossmatching; acute by drugs that suppress T cells; chronic is the main long-term cause of graft loss.

cards.front: Why is transplant rejection so vigorous?
cards.back: Between 1 and 10% of all your T cells react to any one foreign HLA type, compared with far fewer than 1 in 10,000 for a typical microbial peptide.
cards.why: Donor HLA with its own peptides looks to your T cells like self MHC holding a foreign peptide.

cards.front: What is graft-versus-host disease?
cards.back: Mature T cells in a donor bone marrow graft recognize the recipient’s HLA as foreign and attack the recipient’s skin, liver and gut.
cards.why: The recipient’s own immune system has been wiped out, so nothing stops the donor cells. The same cells can attack leftover leukemia cells.

cards.front: Humoral vs cell-mediated immunity: main cells and weapon?
cards.back: Humoral: B cells and plasma cells; antibodies released into body fluids. Cell-mediated: T cells; the T cell itself, acting by contact and cytokines.
cards.why: Helper T cells link the two arms: they help B cells as well as cytotoxic T cells.

cards.front: Humoral vs cell-mediated immunity: what does each recognize and what is it best against?
cards.back: Humoral: whole antigens in their natural shape; toxins, and bacteria and viruses outside cells. Cell-mediated: short peptides held in MHC; viruses and bacteria inside cells, and abnormal cells.
cards.why: Antibodies cannot reach a virus once it is inside a cell, so only cells that detect peptides on MHC can find it there.

cards.front: Describe the structure of an antibody.
cards.back: Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds into a Y. The variable regions at the arm tips form two identical antigen-binding sites; the Fc stem is heavy chain constant region only.
cards.why: The variable end decides what it binds; the constant end, which sets the class, decides what happens next.

cards.front: IgG: shape, share of serum antibody, main jobs?
cards.back: Monomer; about 75–80%; neutralizes, coats microbes for phagocytes, activates complement; the main antibody of a second exposure.
cards.why: It is the only class actively carried across to the fetus, giving a newborn months of protection copied from the mother.

cards.front: IgA: shape and where it works?
cards.back: Monomer in blood, dimer in secretions; guards mucus, tears, saliva, breast milk and the gut lining, blocking microbes before they get in.
cards.why: You make more IgA than every other class combined, but most leaves the blood for secretions, so it ranks second in serum.

cards.front: IgM: shape and main jobs?
cards.back: Pentamer when released (monomer on B cells); the first antibody of a first exposure; best at agglutination and at activating complement.
cards.why: Ten binding sites let it grab and clump microbes even when each site fits loosely. It is too large to cross to the fetus.

cards.front: IgE: where it sits and what it does?
cards.back: Bound by its Fc region to mast cells and basophils; triggers them against worms, and causes allergy symptoms. The scarcest class in serum.
cards.why: An antigen linking two IgE molecules makes the mast cell release histamine.

cards.front: IgD: where it is found?
cards.back: On the surface of naïve B cells, as a B cell receptor protein alongside IgM. Its role is unclear; under 1% of serum antibody.
cards.why: The memory aid GAMED lists all five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD.

cards.front: Which antibody class crosses from mother to fetus, and what follows from that?
cards.back: Only IgG. So anti-D (an IgG) can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn, while anti-A and anti-B, mostly IgM, usually do not harm an ABO-mismatched fetus.
cards.why: IgG is small and actively carried across in late pregnancy; IgM is a large pentamer.

cards.front: What is class switching, and what decides the new class?
cards.back: A B cell changes from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE, keeping the same variable region, by cutting out DNA. Helper T cell contact (CD40 ligand–CD40) is needed; IL-4 steers to IgE, TGF-beta to IgA, interferon gamma to IgG.
cards.why: The new antibody binds exactly the same antigen but its stem, and so its job, differs. The switch cannot be reversed.

cards.front: Which antibody actions depend on the variable region, and which on the Fc region?
cards.back: Variable region: neutralization and agglutination. Fc region: opsonization, complement activation and directing killer cells.
cards.why: An antibody kills nothing itself; it binds, blocks and flags, and other cells and proteins do the destruction.

cards.front: Primary vs secondary antibody response: lag, peak and main class?
cards.back: Primary: lag of about 5–10 days, peaking in one to two weeks; low peak; IgM first, then IgG. Secondary: lag of about 1–3 days; peak often 10 to 100 times higher; mostly IgG, better fitting and lasting months or years.
cards.why: Memory B cells are more numerous, need less stimulation and already make switched, well-fitting antibody.

cards.front: A patient has IgM against a virus. What does that suggest, compared with IgG alone?
cards.back: IgM points to a current or recent infection; IgG alone points to an older infection or a vaccine.
cards.why: Every B cell makes IgM first; switching to IgG takes days, and IgM falls away within weeks.

cards.front: What is the window period of an infection?
cards.back: The time before seroconversion, when antibody is not yet detectable, so an antibody test is negative even though the person is infected.
cards.why: A primary response needs days to weeks for clonal selection and expansion before antibody appears.

cards.front: Active vs passive immunity: who makes the antibodies, how fast, how long, memory?
cards.back: Active: you do; a week or more; years to a lifetime; memory cells form. Passive: someone else (a person, an animal or a lab); at once; days to a few months; no memory cells.
cards.why: Borrowed antibody is broken down and does not activate your own B cells.

cards.front: Give a natural and an artificial example of active and of passive immunity.
cards.back: Active: recovering from chickenpox; a vaccine. Passive: IgG crossing to the fetus or IgA in breast milk; antivenom, tetanus immune globulin, anti-D injections.
cards.why: The deciding question is who made the antibodies, not whether a needle was involved.

cards.front: Why are vaccines against capsule bacteria made as conjugate vaccines?
cards.back: Capsule sugars are T cell-independent antigens: mostly IgM, little memory, and poor responses under about age 2. Attaching the sugar to a protein lets helper T cells that recognize the protein help the B cells that recognize the sugar.
cards.why: With helper T cell help, B cells can switch class, improve their fit and form memory cells.

cards.front: Why is a plasma cell packed with rough ER?
cards.back: It makes and exports antibody, about 2,000 molecules per second.
cards.why: Some plasma cells move to the bone marrow and keep releasing antibody for years, which is why antibody can stay up long after a vaccine.

cards.front: What are the three kinds of immune disorder?
cards.back: Too much against something harmless (hypersensitivity), aimed at yourself (autoimmune disease), and too little (immunodeficiency).
cards.why: The same weapons that protect you do damage when aimed at the wrong target, or when they are missing.

cards.front: Type I hypersensitivity: what does the damage, timing, examples?
cards.back: IgE on mast cells and basophils releasing histamine and other mediators; minutes after re-exposure; hay fever, hives, food allergy, anaphylaxis.
cards.why: The allergen cross-links two IgE molecules on a mast cell, which degranulates within seconds.

cards.front: Type II hypersensitivity: what does the damage, examples?
cards.back: IgG or IgM bound to an antigen fixed on a cell surface or its receptor proteins; transfusion reaction, hemolytic disease of the newborn, Graves disease, myasthenia gravis.
cards.why: Bound antibody activates complement, coats the cell for phagocytes, directs NK cells, or blocks or switches on a receptor protein.

cards.front: Type III hypersensitivity: what does the damage, examples?
cards.back: Antibody–antigen immune complexes formed in the blood that lodge in small vessel walls, joints and the kidneys’ filters; lupus, kidney inflammation after strep throat.
cards.why: The lodged complexes activate complement, which calls in neutrophils whose enzymes damage the tissue.

cards.front: Type IV hypersensitivity: what does the damage, timing, examples?
cards.back: Th1 cells, macrophages and cytotoxic T cells; 24 to 72 hours; poison ivy, nickel allergy, the tuberculin skin test, type 1 diabetes.
cards.why: It is delayed because memory T cells take time to gather at the site. Types I to III are caused by antibodies; type IV by T cells.

cards.front: Why does no one have an allergic reaction on the immune system’s very first meeting with an allergen?
cards.back: The first contact only sensitizes: it makes IgE or memory T cells against the allergen. A later exposure causes the reaction.
cards.why: Someone who reacts badly to a “first” bee sting was usually sensitized by an earlier sting they never noticed.

cards.front: Why does MAP fall in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Both terms of MAP = CO × TPR fall: vasodilation lowers TPR, and pooling plus plasma leak lower venous return and so cardiac output.
cards.why: It is distributive shock with a hypovolemic part from the leak; the falling MAP reduces baroreceptor firing and the heart rate climbs.

cards.front: How does epinephrine reverse each part of anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Alpha-1: vessels constrict, TPR and venous return rise, leak falls. Beta-1: heart rate and contractility rise. Beta-2: airways widen, and mast cells release less.
cards.why: It is the only drug that works against every part of anaphylaxis at once.

cards.front: How is epinephrine given for anaphylaxis, and at what dose?
cards.back: Into the outer thigh muscle: 0.01 mg per kg from a vial, up to 0.5 mg in an adult and 0.3 mg in a child; auto-injectors give 0.3 mg (adults and larger children) or 0.15 mg (small children). Repeat after 5 to 15 minutes if needed.
cards.why: Lay the person flat with legs raised: standing up can leave too little venous return to fill the heart.

cards.front: Why is an antihistamine not a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis?
cards.back: It blocks only histamine, not leukotrienes, acts slowly, and does nothing for low blood pressure or narrowed airways; it relieves itching and hives.
cards.why: Epinephrine reverses vasodilation, leak, weak cardiac output and airway narrowing through its adrenergic receptor proteins.

cards.front: Name four things that can tip self-tolerance into autoimmune disease.
cards.back: Genes (certain HLA types), molecular mimicry (a microbe antigen resembling self, as in rheumatic fever), sex (about four in five patients are women), and tissue damage or infection putting B7 on dendritic cells.
cards.why: Self-reactive cells that escaped negative selection are normally held back by anergy and regulatory T cells.

cards.front: Rheumatoid arthritis vs lupus: main target and main damage?
cards.back: RA: synovial membranes of small joints on both sides; T and B cells and TNF erode cartilage and bone; rheumatoid factor. Lupus: antibodies against nuclear contents, including DNA; immune complexes lodge in vessels, joints, kidneys, skin and serous membranes.
cards.why: Kidney damage is the most dangerous part of lupus; drugs that block TNF now prevent most joint damage in RA.

cards.front: Why is the weakness of myasthenia gravis worse with repeated effort?
cards.back: Antibodies remove acetylcholine receptor proteins, so each end plate potential is smaller; as acetylcholine release falls with repeated firing, more end plate potentials drop below threshold.
cards.why: Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, lets acetylcholine bind more of the remaining receptor proteins.

cards.front: Why do babies with SCID seem well for a few months?
cards.back: Their mother’s IgG, carried across in late pregnancy, protects them until it is broken down.
cards.why: SCID leaves no working T cells and no useful antibody; a bone marrow transplant, or in some forms gene therapy, can cure it.

cards.front: Which cells does HIV infect, and why those?
cards.back: Cells carrying CD4: helper T cells, and also macrophages and dendritic cells. Its envelope protein binds CD4, then a chemokine receptor protein.
cards.why: Losing helper T cells makes both antibody and cytotoxic responses fail.

cards.front: After the acute phase of HIV, what brings the virus down to a steady level?
cards.back: Mainly CD8 cytotoxic T cells killing infected cells. Antibodies appear but the virus mutates around them.
cards.why: Cytotoxic T cells never clear HIV, because silent virus hides in some long-lived memory T cells.

cards.front: When is AIDS diagnosed?
cards.back: When the CD4 count falls below 200 per microliter, or a defining illness appears, such as Pneumocystis lung infection or Kaposi sarcoma. The normal count is about 500 to 1,500.
cards.why: Untreated, the chronic phase lasts about ten years on average. Treatment that keeps the virus undetectable prevents sexual transmission.

cards.front: Name three ways a cancer escapes the immune system.
cards.back: Losing MHC class I (hiding from cytotoxic T cells), putting PD-L1 on its surface to switch T cells off, and drawing in regulatory T cells and releasing suppressive cytokines.
cards.why: Checkpoint inhibitors block PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 to release those brakes; their side effects are T cell attacks on healthy organs.

cards.front: Gastrin vs secretin vs CCK: where is each made, and what releases it?
cards.back: Gastrin: lower stomach lining, released by protein fragments, stretch and the vagus. Secretin: first part of the small intestine, released by acid. CCK: first parts of the small intestine, released by fats and protein fragments.
cards.why: Each hormone is made where its stimulus arrives: gastrin where food sits in the stomach, secretin and CCK where the stomach’s output enters the intestine.

cards.front: Gastrin vs secretin vs CCK: main effect of each?
cards.back: Gastrin: more stomach acid. Secretin: bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and the ducts that carry bile. CCK: gallbladder contracts and the pancreas releases enzymes.
cards.why: Gastrin pushes the stomach’s own work forward; secretin neutralizes the acid that released it; CCK brings in bile and enzymes for the fat and protein that released it.

cards.front: Which of gastrin, secretin and CCK slow stomach emptying?
cards.back: Secretin and CCK slow it; gastrin has little effect on it.
cards.why: Secretin and CCK come from the intestine and hold the stomach back until the intestine has dealt with what it already has.

cards.front: Gastrin vs secretin vs CCK: what switches each off?
cards.back: Gastrin: strong acid in the stomach. Secretin: the acid being neutralized. CCK: fats and proteins being digested and absorbed.
cards.why: Each is negative feedback: the hormone’s own effect removes the stimulus that released it.

cards.front: Mechanical vs chemical digestion: what changes in each?
cards.back: Mechanical: only the size of the pieces; the molecules stay the same. Chemical: the molecules themselves, as enzymes break bonds by hydrolysis.
cards.why: Chewing and churning break food apart physically; only enzymes split the bonds that make starch, protein and fat into absorbable monomers.

cards.front: Mechanical digestion makes nothing absorbable. Why does it still matter?
cards.back: Smaller pieces have more surface, and enzymes can only act on a particle’s surface.
cards.why: The same meat swallowed whole digests far more slowly than when it is chewed well, because the enzymes reach less of it.

cards.front: Peristalsis vs segmentation: job and net movement?
cards.back: Peristalsis: propulsion, moving contents forward, often a long way. Segmentation: mixing, with very little net movement.
cards.why: Peristalsis is a contraction that travels along the tube; segmentation is rings that contract in place and then alternate.

cards.front: What two things must happen at once for peristalsis to push food forward?
cards.back: Behind the food, circular muscle contracts (acetylcholine); ahead of it, circular muscle relaxes (nitric oxide).
cards.why: Without the relaxation ahead, the food would be squeezed against a closed tube. Enteric motor neurons produce both halves as a short reflex.

cards.front: The four layers of the GI wall, from the lumen outward?
cards.back: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa (adventitia where there is no peritoneum, as around the esophagus in the chest).
cards.why: Every part of the tube keeps this plan; each organ changes the details, such as the stomach’s extra oblique muscle layer.

cards.front: Myenteric vs submucosal plexus: where is each, and what does it control?
cards.back: Myenteric: between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers; controls motility. Submucosal: in the submucosa; controls secretion and local blood flow in the lining.
cards.why: Each plexus sits next to what it controls: the muscle layers or the glands and vessels of the lining.

cards.front: Does the brain run peristalsis?
cards.back: No. The enteric nervous system runs it by short reflexes; the autonomic nerves only turn it up (parasympathetic) or down (sympathetic).
cards.why: A length of intestine removed from the body, kept warm and oxygenated, still pushes a ball along by peristalsis.

cards.front: Short vs long GI reflex?
cards.back: Short: stays inside the gut wall, through the enteric plexuses. Long: travels to the brainstem or spinal cord and back through autonomic nerves.
cards.why: Long reflexes let the gut respond to things outside it, such as the smell of food or fear; stretch of the stomach increasing acid through the vagus is a long, vagovagal reflex.

cards.front: Name digestive organs that are retroperitoneal.
cards.back: The pancreas, most of the first part of the small intestine, and the parts of the large intestine running up the right side and down the left side.
cards.why: They lie against the back wall behind the peritoneum, covered only in front, so they are held fixed instead of hanging on a mesentery.

cards.compare: Incisors vs canines vs premolars vs molars
cards.front: Incisors vs canines vs premolars vs molars: shape and job?
cards.back: Incisors: chisel blade, cut. Canines: single point, tear. Premolars: two cusps, crush and grind. Molars: broad, four or five cusps, grind.
cards.why: Each crown’s shape matches its job, from cutting at the front to grinding at the back.

cards.compare: Incisors vs canines vs premolars vs molars
cards.front: How many teeth in the adult and deciduous sets, and which kinds does the deciduous set lack?
cards.back: Adult: 32 (8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars). Deciduous: 20, with no premolars and no third molars.
cards.why: Each quarter of an adult mouth holds two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars: 8 × 4 = 32.

cards.front: Why can a cavity in enamel never grow back?
cards.back: Enamel has no living cells once the tooth has come in, so nothing can rebuild it.
cards.why: Minerals from saliva, helped by fluoride, can reharden an early weak spot, but a hole once formed stays.

cards.front: Parotid vs submandibular vs sublingual gland: where, and what kind of saliva?
cards.back: Parotid: in front of and below the ear; watery, rich in enzyme. Submandibular: under the mandible; mixed, most saliva at rest. Sublingual: floor of the mouth; mostly mucus.
cards.why: The parotid is the largest, the sublingual the smallest; all three reach the mouth through ducts, as exocrine glands do.

cards.front: What does saliva contain besides water?
cards.back: Mucus, salivary amylase, a trace of lingual lipase, lysozyme, defensins, IgA, and bicarbonate and phosphate, which buffer acids.
cards.why: Mucus binds and lubricates the bolus, amylase starts starch digestion, the defenses damage bacteria, and the buffers protect enamel.

cards.front: Which enzyme does the fat digestion that happens before the small intestine in adults?
cards.back: Gastric lipase, from the chief cells of the stomach. Lingual lipase is only a trace in humans.
cards.why: Lingual lipase matters in rats and mice, but in humans there is only a trace of it, so pre-duodenal fat digestion is done by gastric lipase.

cards.front: Why does anxiety leave your mouth dry and sticky?
cards.back: Sympathetic activity makes the salivary glands release only a small volume of thick saliva; the large watery flow needs parasympathetic signals.
cards.why: Salivation is controlled almost entirely by autonomic nerves, not hormones, and both divisions increase secretion, in different amounts.

cards.front: The three phases of swallowing, and which one you control?
cards.back: Voluntary (tongue pushes the bolus into the oropharynx), pharyngeal (a brainstem reflex seals the nose and airway), esophageal (peristalsis to the stomach). Only the voluntary phase.
cards.why: Once the bolus touches the oropharynx, the swallowing center fires a fixed sequence you cannot stop.

cards.front: In a swallow, what closes the airway first?
cards.back: The vocal folds close, at or before the start of the larynx’s rise; then the larynx rises and the epiglottis tips over its opening.
cards.why: Sealing from inside comes first, so the airway is already closed before the bolus is squeezed past it.

cards.front: Upper vs lower esophageal sphincter: muscle type, and what closure prevents?
cards.back: Upper: skeletal muscle; stops air entering the esophagus as you breathe in. Lower: smooth muscle helped by the diaphragm; stops stomach contents flowing back up.
cards.why: Both are closed at rest. The upper opens when its motor neurons stop and the larynx pulls it open; the lower relaxes when enteric neurons release nitric oxide.

cards.front: What kind of muscle is in the wall of the esophagus?
cards.back: Skeletal in the upper third, a mixture in the middle third, smooth in the lower third.
cards.why: The top is driven directly by brainstem motor neurons; the lower part also relies on the enteric nervous system.

cards.front: What causes reflux in most people with GERD?
cards.back: Brief relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter not linked to swallowing, set off by stretch of the upper stomach after a meal.
cards.why: A constantly weak sphincter and a hiatal hernia make it worse, but transient relaxations are the main cause.

cards.front: What do parietal cells secrete?
cards.back: Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
cards.why: Acid denatures protein, kills microbes and activates pepsin; intrinsic factor lets you absorb vitamin B12.

cards.front: What do chief cells secrete?
cards.back: Pepsinogen and gastric lipase.
cards.why: Pepsinogen becomes pepsin in acid and starts protein digestion; gastric lipase starts fat digestion.

cards.front: G cells vs ECL cells vs D cells: what does each release?
cards.back: G cells: gastrin into the blood. ECL cells: histamine onto the parietal cells. D cells: somatostatin, which restrains the others.
cards.why: These enteroendocrine cells release their products toward the blood or neighboring cells, not into the lumen.

cards.front: Why does an H<sub>2</sub> blocker cut acid strongly, though it blocks only one of three signals?
cards.back: Acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine together produce far more acid than the sum of each alone, and gastrin acts mostly through histamine.
cards.why: Remove histamine and both its own effect and most of gastrin’s are lost. A proton pump inhibitor goes further, blocking the pump itself.

cards.front: What is the alkaline tide?
cards.back: During a meal, blood leaving the stomach is slightly alkaline, because every H<sup>+</sup> secreted leaves a bicarbonate ion that enters the blood.
