cards.why: Carbonic anhydrase makes H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> together; the H<sup>+</sup> goes to the lumen and the bicarbonate to the blood, until pancreatic bicarbonate secretion balances it.

cards.front: Why do chief cells make pepsinogen instead of pepsin?
cards.back: Pepsinogen is an inactive zymogen, so it can be stored without digesting the cell’s own proteins.
cards.why: It becomes pepsin only in acid below about pH 5, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen: positive feedback.

cards.front: Which secretion of the stomach can you not live without?
cards.back: Intrinsic factor.
cards.why: Without it you absorb almost no vitamin B12. A person without a stomach digests food well with small meals but needs B12 replacement for life.

cards.compare: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase
cards.front: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase: where is the stimulus?
cards.back: Cephalic: head (sight, smell, taste, thought, chewing). Gastric: stomach (stretch, protein, rising pH). Intestinal: first part of the small intestine (acid, fat, stretch).
cards.why: The phases are named for where the stimulus is, not where the secretion happens.

cards.compare: Cephalic vs gastric vs intestinal phase
cards.front: Which phase of gastric secretion supplies most of the acid, and which mostly inhibits?
cards.back: The gastric phase supplies about half or more; the cephalic about a third. The intestinal phase mostly inhibits.
cards.why: In the intestinal phase, the enterogastric reflex, secretin and CCK act as the brake on the stomach.

cards.front: Rank carbohydrate, protein and fat by how fast they leave the stomach.
cards.back: Carbohydrate fastest, protein slower, fat slowest.
cards.why: Fat releases the most CCK, and CCK weakens the antrum’s waves and tightens the pylorus.

cards.front: What makes up the gastric mucosal barrier?
cards.back: Alkaline mucus with bicarbonate, tight junctions, renewal of the surface cells every 3 to 5 days, mucosal blood flow, and prostaglandins.
cards.why: Together they keep the cell surface near pH 7 while the lumen, less than a millimeter away, is near pH 1 to 2.

cards.front: What causes most peptic ulcers?
cards.back: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAIDs, both of which weaken the mucosal barrier.
cards.why: Ulcers usually form because the barrier fails, not because acid secretion is high. Stress and spicy food are not causes.

cards.front: In vomiting, what supplies the force?
cards.back: The diaphragm and abdominal muscles contracting together; the stomach and lower esophageal sphincter are relaxed.
cards.why: The relaxed stomach is squeezed between them. Repeated vomiting loses H<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> and leads to alkalosis and low potassium.

cards.front: Jejunum vs ileum: how do their walls and folds differ?
cards.back: Jejunum: thicker, wider, redder, with tall close circular folds, tall villi and few Peyer’s patches. Ileum: thinner, paler, with low sparse folds, shorter villi and many Peyer’s patches.
cards.why: The jejunum does most nutrient absorption, so its surface is largest; the ileum’s many lymphoid nodules guard the approach to the bacteria-rich large intestine.

cards.front: Which jobs belong to the ileum alone?
cards.back: Absorbing vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor, and reclaiming about 95% of the salts in bile for reuse.
cards.why: The carriers and receptor proteins for both are found only in the terminal ileum, so no other part can take over.

cards.front: How long is the small intestine in a living adult?
cards.back: About 3 to 5 meters. After death, when its muscle loses tone, it measures about 6 meters.
cards.why: Living muscle keeps some tone and shortens the tube. Exams may still give the older 6 m (20 ft) figure.

cards.front: How large is the absorptive surface of the small intestine, and how much do folds, villi and microvilli multiply it?
cards.back: About 30 m², roughly 100- to 200-fold a smooth tube. The textbook estimate is 3 × 10 × 20 = 600-fold, or 200 to 300 m².
cards.why: Direct measurements in the living intestine found smaller multipliers than the old estimates; exams may still expect the tennis-court figure.

cards.front: What carries absorbed nutrients away inside a villus?
cards.back: Blood capillaries take sugars, amino acids and water; a central lacteal takes absorbed fat.
cards.why: Fat is packaged into droplets too large for blood capillaries, so it enters the lymphatic lacteal instead.

cards.front: Why does cancer chemotherapy so often damage the gut?
cards.back: Stem cells in the intestinal glands divide constantly to replace the lining every 3 to 5 days, and chemotherapy kills dividing cells.
cards.why: The intestinal lining is one of the fastest-renewing tissues in the body.

cards.front: Is intestinal juice rich in digestive enzymes?
cards.back: No. It is 1 to 2 L a day of watery, slightly alkaline fluid with mucus and very little enzyme.
cards.why: Its job is to keep chyme fluid. The last digestive cuts are made by brush border enzymes fixed in the microvillus membrane.

cards.front: Lactase, sucrase, maltase: substrate and products?
cards.back: Lactase: lactose to glucose and galactose. Sucrase: sucrose to glucose and fructose. Maltase: maltose to two glucose.
cards.why: Each is named for its substrate, and each sits in the microvillus membrane beside the carriers that absorb its products.

cards.front: When the villi are damaged, which brush border enzyme is usually the first to fall?
cards.back: Lactase.
cards.why: It is the least abundant of them, so losing cells shows first as lactase shortage; it recovers when the lining heals.

cards.front: Segmentation vs migrating motor complex: when, trigger, and job?
cards.back: Segmentation: during and after a meal, driven by chyme stretching the wall; mixes. Migrating motor complex: between meals, every 90 to 120 minutes, driven by motilin; sweeps residue and bacteria into the large intestine.
cards.why: Eating stops the migrating motor complex at once, and segmentation takes over again.

cards.front: What share of the liver’s blood comes from the hepatic portal vein, and what share from the hepatic artery?
cards.back: About three quarters from the hepatic portal vein, about a quarter from the hepatic artery.
cards.why: Portal blood is rich in absorbed nutrients but partly deoxygenated; the artery supplies oxygenated blood.

cards.front: In a liver lobule, which way do blood and bile flow?
cards.back: Blood flows inward, from the portal triads through the sinusoids to the central vein. Bile flows outward, through the canaliculi to the bile ducts in the triads.
cards.why: The two run in opposite directions in separate channels and never mix.

cards.front: Does bile digest fat?
cards.back: No. Bile has no enzymes. Its bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets, multiplying the surface pancreatic lipase can act on.
cards.why: A bile salt has a hydrophobic face in the fat and a hydrophilic face in the water, which stops droplets merging again.

cards.front: Does the gallbladder make bile?
cards.back: No. It stores and concentrates it, up to about tenfold, by absorbing sodium and letting water follow.
cards.why: Between meals the closed hepatopancreatic sphincter backs bile up the cystic duct into the gallbladder; CCK empties it after a meal.

cards.front: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct. Name three signs.
cards.back: Jaundice with dark urine, pale feces, and fat in the feces.
cards.why: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and urine instead of reaching the gut, and without bile salts fat is digested more slowly and much of it is not absorbed.

cards.compare: Secretin vs CCK on the pancreas
cards.front: Secretin vs CCK: which pancreatic cells does each target, and what juice results?
cards.back: Secretin: duct cells; a large volume rich in bicarbonate, with few enzymes. CCK: acinar cells; a small volume rich in enzymes.
cards.why: Each hormone calls for what removes its own stimulus: bicarbonate for acid, enzymes for fat and protein.

cards.compare: Secretin vs CCK on the pancreas
cards.front: Secretin vs CCK: effect on the gallbladder and the hepatopancreatic sphincter?
cards.back: CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter. Secretin has little direct effect on either.
cards.why: Bile is needed for fat, and fat is CCK’s stimulus, not secretin’s.

cards.front: Why is the pancreas not digested by its own trypsin?
cards.back: It makes trypsinogen, an inactive zymogen, which is switched on only by enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border.
cards.why: The acinar cells also make a trypsin inhibitor, and their secretions keep flowing out of the gland. In acute pancreatitis, trypsin is activated inside the gland.

cards.front: How is making pancreatic bicarbonate the mirror image of making stomach acid?
cards.back: Pancreatic duct cells put bicarbonate into the duct and H<sup>+</sup> into the blood; parietal cells put H<sup>+</sup> into the stomach and bicarbonate into the blood.
cards.why: So blood leaving the stomach after a meal is slightly alkaline (the alkaline tide), and blood leaving the pancreas slightly acidic.

cards.front: Hepatitis vs cirrhosis: what is each?
cards.back: Hepatitis: inflammation of the liver, acute or long-lasting. Cirrhosis: scarring that replaces normal lobules with scar bands and nodules, after years of injury.
cards.why: Long-lasting hepatitis from any cause can end in cirrhosis.

cards.front: Can cirrhosis get better?
cards.back: Partly. Scarring can regress once the cause is removed, as when hepatitis C is cured, but the liver seldom returns fully to normal.
cards.why: Cirrhosis that has already caused complications regresses least; hepatitis often recovers fully once its cause is gone.

cards.front: Which cells lay down the scar in cirrhosis?
cards.back: Hepatic stellate cells, star-shaped cells just outside the sinusoid lining, once activated by repeated injury.
cards.why: They are not the macrophages of the sinusoids; activated, they make collagen.

cards.front: Why does cirrhosis cause bleeding veins at the lower esophagus?
cards.back: Scar squeezes the sinusoids, pressure in the hepatic portal vein rises, and blood backs up into veins linking the portal system to the systemic veins, which swell and can rupture.
cards.why: Portal vein pressure is raised in cirrhosis but usually normal in hepatitis.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: surface of the lining and goblet cells?
cards.back: Small: circular folds, villi and microvilli; goblet cells present. Large: no circular folds or villi, a flat surface with deep glands; very many goblet cells.
cards.why: Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, which needs the surface; the colon needs mucus to lubricate drying feces and keep bacteria off its cells.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: outer longitudinal muscle and main movements?
cards.back: Small: a continuous layer; segmentation after meals and the migrating motor complex between them. Large: three teniae coli that gather it into haustra; slow haustral contractions and a few mass movements a day.
cards.why: The teniae coli are shorter than the colon wall, so their tone bunches it into pouches.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: how much water does each absorb a day?
cards.back: Small intestine: about 7 to 8 L. Large intestine: about 1.3 L, around 90% of what reaches it.
cards.why: The colon’s share is small, but it is the last chance, so any change in it shows in the stool.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: length, width, and time contents spend there?
cards.back: Small: about 3 to 5 m in life, 2.5 cm wide, 3 to 5 hours. Large: about 1.5 m, 6 to 7 cm wide, 12 to 48 hours or longer.
cards.why: “Small” and “large” refer to width, not length.

cards.front: Small vs large intestine: enzymes and bacteria?
cards.back: Small: brush border enzymes plus pancreatic juice and bile; relatively few bacteria. Large: no digestive enzymes of its own; trillions of bacteria do the breaking down.
cards.why: Stomach acid and fast flow keep bacteria sparse higher up; the slow, oxygen-poor, fiber-rich colon lets them thrive.

cards.front: Do bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one?
cards.back: No: roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells, about one to one.
cards.why: A careful recount in 2016 replaced the old ten-to-one estimate, though some exams still expect it.

cards.front: What do colon bacteria make from fiber, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) and gases. Butyrate is the main fuel of the colon’s epithelial cells.
cards.why: You have no enzymes for most fiber, so bacterial fermentation recovers some of its energy, roughly 5 to 10% of your daily energy.

cards.front: How does the colon absorb water, with no water pump?
cards.back: It absorbs sodium through apical channels, pumps it out with sodium–potassium pumps, chloride follows, and water follows by osmosis.
cards.why: Aldosterone adds channels and pumps, so the colon saves more sodium and water when your body is low on them.

cards.front: Internal vs external anal sphincter: muscle, control and nerves?
cards.back: Internal: smooth muscle, involuntary, autonomic and enteric nerves; relaxes by reflex when the rectum stretches. External: skeletal muscle, voluntary, somatic motor neurons from the sacral cord.
cards.why: The reflex opens the internal sphincter; the external one stays closed until you decide to relax it.

cards.front: A spinal cord injury above the sacral segments: what happens to defecation?
cards.back: The reflex still works, but the person no longer feels the urge or controls the external anal sphincter.
cards.why: The reflex arc runs through the sacral cord (S2–S4); the injury cuts only the path to and from the brain.

cards.front: Diarrhea vs constipation: time in the colon and water absorbed?
cards.back: Diarrhea: time usually shortened, less water absorbed. Constipation: time usually lengthened, more water absorbed.
cards.why: The colon keeps absorbing water for as long as contents stay, so time decides how hard the stool is.

cards.front: Diarrhea vs constipation: main danger?
cards.back: Diarrhea: loss of water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate. Constipation: discomfort and, rarely, a blockage of hard stool.
cards.why: Stool water carries potassium, which the colon secretes, and bicarbonate, so severe diarrhea lowers blood volume and potassium and makes the blood more acidic.

cards.front: Secretory vs osmotic diarrhea: mechanism and example?
cards.back: Secretory: a toxin makes the lining secrete chloride, and sodium and water follow (cholera). Osmotic: an unabsorbed solute holds water in the lumen (magnesium laxatives, sorbitol).
cards.why: Either way, more water stays in the lumen than the colon can take back.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Salivary and pancreatic amylase: substrate and products?
cards.back: Starch and glycogen, split into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins.
cards.why: Amylase cannot cut the bond at a branch point, so α-dextrins keep their branches until brush border α-dextrinase splits them.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Pepsin vs trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase: source and products?
cards.back: Pepsin: stomach chief cells; large polypeptides. Trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase: pancreas; shorter peptides.
cards.why: Each cuts inside the chain, at bonds next to particular amino acids; peptidases then finish the pieces.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Carboxypeptidase vs aminopeptidase: source, and which end does each trim?
cards.back: Carboxypeptidase: pancreas; removes amino acids from the carboxyl end. Aminopeptidase: brush border; removes them from the amino end.
cards.why: Trimming from both ends, with dipeptidase splitting dipeptides, leaves single amino acids and short peptides.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: Gastric vs pancreatic lipase: products and share of fat digestion?
cards.back: Gastric: fatty acids and diglycerides, a small share (roughly 10 to 30% in adults). Pancreatic: fatty acids and monoglycerides, most of it.
cards.why: Pancreatic lipase works on bile-emulsified droplets, anchored to their surface by colipase.

cards.compare: Digestive enzymes by source, substrate and product
cards.front: How are DNA and RNA from food digested?
cards.back: Pancreatic ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease cut them into nucleotides; brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases split those into pentose sugars, nitrogenous bases and phosphate.
cards.why: Every cell you eat contains nucleic acids, and only these small parts can be absorbed.

cards.front: SGLT1 uses no ATP. Why does stopping the sodium–potassium pumps stop glucose absorption?
cards.back: The pumps keep sodium low inside the cell; SGLT1 is powered by sodium running down that gradient. Without the pumps, the gradient collapses.
cards.why: This is secondary active transport: the energy comes from the ATP the pumps spent, one step removed.

cards.front: How do glucose, galactose and fructose enter and leave an absorptive cell?
cards.back: Glucose and galactose enter with sodium through SGLT1; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. All three leave through GLUT2.
cards.why: Each membrane has its own carriers, and that difference makes absorption run one way.

cards.front: Are dietary proteins absorbed only as single amino acids?
cards.back: No: much crosses the brush border as dipeptides and tripeptides, carried with hydrogen ions and split inside the cell. Almost all reaches the blood as amino acids.
cards.why: Many textbooks and exams still say "absorbed as amino acids", which is true of what enters the blood.

cards.front: Micelle vs chylomicron: where does each form, and what is its job?
cards.back: Micelle: in the lumen; carries digested lipids to the brush border. Chylomicron: inside the absorptive cell; carries absorbed lipids out of the cell.
cards.why: Micelles need bile salts and release their lipids at the membrane; chylomicrons are rebuilt triglycerides packaged for export.

cards.front: Where do chylomicrons go, and why not into the blood capillaries?
cards.back: Into the lacteal, then the lymph, the thoracic duct and the veins where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.
cards.why: They are tens to hundreds of times wider than a micelle, too large for blood capillaries, so absorbed fat reaches the blood without passing the liver first.

cards.front: Name four organs vitamin B12 absorption depends on.
cards.back: Stomach (acid, pepsin, intrinsic factor), pancreas (proteases that free it from haptocorrin), terminal ileum (receptor proteins), and liver (stores 3 to 5 years’ worth).
cards.why: A break anywhere causes deficiency, but only years later because of the liver’s store. High oral doses let a small fraction cross without intrinsic factor.

cards.front: About how much water passes through the gut each day, and how much leaves in the feces?
cards.back: About 9 L in (about 2 L from food and drink, 7 L from secretions); about 150 mL leaves in the feces, so about 98% is absorbed.
cards.why: Water in = water absorbed + water in the feces. Gastric juice alone is about 2 L a day.

cards.front: Why does an oral rehydration solution need glucose as well as salt?
cards.back: Cholera toxin does not stop SGLT1, so glucose carries sodium into the cells, and water follows, even while secretion continues.
cards.why: Salt alone is absorbed poorly when the gut is secreting; coupling sodium to glucose opens a route the toxin leaves intact.

cards.front: Lactose intolerance vs milk allergy: cause and molecule?
cards.back: Intolerance: too little lactase to digest lactose, a sugar; no immune response. Allergy: an immune response, often IgE-mediated, to milk proteins such as casein.
cards.why: Intolerance depends on the dose and small amounts are usually tolerated; in an allergy even tiny amounts can trigger a reaction.

cards.front: Why does undigested lactose cause gas and diarrhea?
cards.back: It holds water in the lumen by osmosis, and colon bacteria ferment it into hydrogen, carbon dioxide and fatty acids.
cards.why: The gas causes bloating and flatus; the water and extra solutes cause osmotic diarrhea. The absorbed hydrogen is what the breath test detects.

cards.front: Where does the thoracic duct return absorbed fat to the blood?
cards.back: At the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins meet.
cards.why: Chyle climbs from the cisterna chyli through the thoracic duct, so absorbed long-chain fat bypasses the liver on its first pass.

cards.front: Fat-soluble vs water-soluble vitamins: which vitamins are in each group?
cards.back: Fat-soluble: A, D, E and K. Water-soluble: the eight B vitamins and vitamin C.
cards.why: Whether a vitamin dissolves in fat or in water decides how it is absorbed, carried, stored and how easily it builds up to a harmful level.

cards.front: Fat-soluble vs water-soluble vitamins: how is each group absorbed?
cards.back: Fat-soluble: with dietary fat, in micelles and then chylomicrons into the lymph, so they need bile and pancreatic lipase. Water-soluble: by carriers across the intestinal lining straight into the blood (B12 also needs intrinsic factor).
cards.why: Fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in the fat droplets, so they follow fat through every step of its absorption; water-soluble ones dissolve in the gut fluid and cross like other small solutes.

cards.front: Fat-soluble vs water-soluble vitamins: which group is stored, and which is more likely to reach a toxic level?
cards.back: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and fat tissue, mostly for months, so they can build up (especially A and D). Water-soluble vitamins are stored little and the extra leaves in urine.
cards.why: A molecule that dissolves in fat stays in fat and liver cells; one that dissolves in water stays in the plasma, where the kidneys can remove the excess. Water-soluble is still not harmless: high doses of B6 damage nerves.

cards.front: A gallstone blocks the bile duct for weeks. Which vitamins run short, and which lack shows first?
cards.back: The fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Vitamin K runs short first, so bleeding is often the first sign.
cards.why: Without bile, fat and the vitamins dissolved in it are poorly absorbed. Vitamin K stores last only days to weeks, while the other fat-soluble vitamins are stored for months.

cards.front: Why can B12 deficiency appear years after a person stops eating animal foods, when a lack of vitamin C shows within months?
cards.back: The liver holds a B12 store that lasts three to five years; the vitamin C store lasts only one to three months.
cards.why: B12 is the exception among water-soluble vitamins: it is stored in large amounts, so symptoms wait until the store is used up.

cards.front: Macronutrients vs micronutrients: which are which, and which supply energy?
cards.back: Macronutrients (grams a day): carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and water; the first three supply energy. Micronutrients (milligrams or micrograms a day): vitamins and minerals, which supply no energy.
cards.why: Micronutrients let enzymes and other proteins work, for example as coenzymes, but they are not broken down for fuel.

cards.front: How many kilocalories does your body get from 1 g of carbohydrate, protein, fat and alcohol?
cards.back: About 4, 4, 9 and 7 kcal per gram.
cards.why: Fat is mostly carbon–hydrogen bonds with few oxygen atoms, so each carbon can release more energy as it is oxidized. Alcohol supplies energy but is not a nutrient.

cards.front: A sandwich has 40 g carbohydrate, 25 g protein and 12 g fat. Why is fat 29% of its energy but only 16% of its grams?
cards.back: Fat gives 12 × 9 = 108 kcal of the 368 kcal total, because each gram of fat gives more than twice the energy of a gram of carbohydrate or protein.
cards.why: Energy share depends on grams times kcal per gram, so always compare energy, not weight.

cards.front: What makes a nutrient essential?
cards.back: Your body cannot make it, or cannot make it fast enough, so it must come from food.
cards.why: Glucose is not essential because the liver can make it from amino acids; lysine is, because no human cell can build it.

cards.front: Why does a diet missing one essential amino acid stop protein building, even if the other amino acids are plentiful?
cards.back: Ribosomes stall where the missing amino acid is needed, so the protein is not finished, and the other amino acids are broken down for fuel.
cards.why: A protein needs every amino acid in its sequence at the moment it is added, and the body has no store of amino acids to wait with.

cards.front: Why do grains and beans eaten on the same day make a complete protein supply?
cards.back: Grains are low in lysine and beans are low in methionine, so each supplies what the other lacks.
cards.why: A complete protein supply needs all 9 essential amino acids in useful amounts; complementary proteins cover each other’s gaps.

cards.front: Which two fatty acids are essential, and why can your cells not make them?
cards.back: Linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3). Your cells cannot put a double bond near the tail end of a fatty acid chain.
cards.why: Both have a double bond 6 or 3 carbons from the tail end, a position human enzymes cannot make, so they must come from plant oils, nuts and seeds.

cards.front: Does a B vitamin tablet give you energy?
cards.back: No. It contains 0 kcal. B vitamins are parts of coenzymes that help release energy from fuel, but they are not fuel themselves.
cards.why: Like a key that starts a car, a coenzyme lets the reaction run but adds nothing to the fuel supply.

cards.front: Why is poor vision in dim light the first sign of vitamin A lack?
cards.back: Retinal, made from vitamin A, is the light-absorbing part of rhodopsin, and rods run short of rhodopsin first.
cards.why: Some retinal is lost each time a rod responds to light and must be replaced from the blood; with too little vitamin A, rods, which work in dim light, fail first.

cards.front: How does vitamin K let blood clot, and how does warfarin interfere?
cards.back: An enzyme that needs vitamin K adds carboxyl groups to clotting factors II, VII, IX and X so they can bind calcium. Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so these factors stay unfinished.
cards.why: Unfinished factors cannot gather on platelet surfaces, so clotting slows.

cards.front: Why is folic acid advised for anyone who could become pregnant, not only after a pregnancy is known?
cards.back: The neural tube closes about four weeks after a pregnancy begins, often before it is known, and folate is needed to make DNA for its fast-dividing cells.
cards.why: A lack of folate at that time raises the risk of neural tube defects; adding folic acid to flour has cut them sharply.

cards.front: Why does a lack of vitamin C make gums bleed and old wounds reopen?
cards.back: Vitamin C keeps the iron in the enzymes that strengthen new collagen in its active form. Without it, new collagen is weak and is broken down, so vessel walls, gums and scars weaken.
cards.why: Collagen is always being replaced, so tissues that depend on it fail within one to three months of the vitamin running out, and recover within days once it returns.

cards.front: Why is iron-deficiency anemia more common in people who eat no meat, and how does vitamin C help?
cards.back: Heme iron from meat is absorbed well; iron from plants is absorbed poorly. Vitamin C eaten at the same meal keeps plant iron in the form the intestine takes up best.
cards.why: Absorption can matter as much as intake: the same milligrams of iron are not equally available.

cards.front: Major vs trace minerals: how are they told apart? Give two examples of each.
cards.back: Major minerals are needed at more than 100 mg a day (calcium, potassium, sodium, magnesium); trace minerals at less than 100 mg a day (iron, iodine, zinc, selenium).
cards.why: The grouping is by the amount needed, not by importance: a lack of a trace mineral such as iodine can be as serious as a lack of calcium.

cards.compare: Energy-consuming vs energy-yielding phase of glycolysis
cards.front: Energy-consuming vs energy-yielding phase of glycolysis: ATP and NADH in each?
cards.back: Energy-consuming phase (steps 1 to 5): 2 ATP spent, no NADH. Energy-yielding phase (steps 6 to 10): 4 ATP and 2 NADH made. Net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate per glucose.
cards.why: The first phase spends ATP to add phosphates and split the sugar; each three-carbon half then pays back more than was spent.

cards.front: Why does hexokinase adding a phosphate to glucose keep glucose flowing into the cell?
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphate is charged and the membrane glucose carriers do not carry it, so it is trapped, and free glucose inside the cell stays low.
cards.why: Low free glucose inside keeps the concentration gradient pointing inward, so facilitated diffusion keeps bringing glucose in.

cards.front: What speeds up and what slows down phosphofructokinase, the main control step of glycolysis?
cards.back: High ATP and citrate slow it; AMP speeds it up.
cards.why: AMP builds up when ATP is spent faster than it is made, so a working muscle speeds glycolysis within seconds; a cell full of ATP slows it.

cards.front: What does the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA make per glucose, and can it run backward?
cards.back: 2 acetyl CoA, 2 CO<sub>2</sub> and 2 NADH. It cannot run backward.
cards.why: Because the carbon cannot return to pyruvate, carbon that has become acetyl CoA can never be made into glucose.

cards.front: Why does thiamine (B1) deficiency starve brain cells of ATP?
cards.back: Thiamine is a coenzyme for the enzyme complex that turns pyruvate into acetyl CoA. Without it pyruvate piles up and is turned into lactate.
cards.why: The brain depends on glucose broken down fully in its mitochondria; if pyruvate cannot enter the citric acid cycle, only glycolysis’s 2 ATP per glucose remain.

cards.front: What does one turn of the citric acid cycle make?
cards.back: 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, 3 NADH, 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 1 ATP (by way of GTP). Two turns per glucose.
cards.why: The cycle’s main product is loaded electron carriers, not ATP; their electrons make most of the ATP later, at the electron transport chain.

cards.front: The citric acid cycle uses no oxygen. Why does it stop within seconds without oxygen?
cards.back: It needs a supply of NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD, and only the electron transport chain, which needs oxygen, turns NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> back into them.
cards.why: With the chain stopped, the carriers stay loaded, NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD run out in the matrix, and the cycle’s oxidation steps cannot run.

cards.compare: Electron transport chain vs ATP synthase
cards.front: Electron transport chain vs ATP synthase: what does each do to the H<sup>+</sup> gradient?
cards.back: The electron transport chain builds it, pumping H<sup>+</sup> out of the matrix. ATP synthase spends it, letting H<sup>+</sup> back in and using that flow to make ATP.
cards.why: The two are coupled: electrons flow only as fast as ATP synthase lets H<sup>+</sup> back in, so oxygen use rises with ATP use.

cards.compare: Electron transport chain vs ATP synthase
cards.front: Electron transport chain vs ATP synthase: which one uses oxygen?
cards.back: The electron transport chain, at complex IV. ATP synthase uses none.
cards.why: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor: it takes electrons from the end of the chain and becomes water, so the carriers upstream can keep passing electrons along.

cards.front: Why does one NADH yield about 2.5 ATP but one FADH<sub>2</sub> only about 1.5?
cards.back: NADH gives its electrons to complex I, so they pass three pumping complexes; FADH<sub>2</sub> gives them to complex II, which pumps no H<sup>+</sup>, so they pass only two.
cards.why: About 10 H<sup>+</sup> are pumped per NADH against about 6 per FADH<sub>2</sub>, and ATP synthase needs about 4 H<sup>+</sup> per ATP.

cards.front: How many ATP does one glucose yield when fully broken down with oxygen, and why do some exams say 36 to 38?
cards.back: About 30 to 32. Older counts used whole numbers of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>, which give 36 to 38.
cards.why: The current values of about 2.5 and 1.5 come from measuring the H<sup>+</sup> pumped per carrier and used per ATP, including the cost of moving ATP out of the mitochondrion. Give 36–38 if your exam expects it.

cards.front: Substrate-level vs oxidative phosphorylation: how many of the ATP from one glucose does each make?
cards.back: Substrate-level: 4 (2 in glycolysis, 2 in the citric acid cycle). Oxidative: the other 26 to 28, about 88%.
cards.why: Substrate-level phosphorylation moves a phosphate straight from a fuel molecule onto ADP; oxidative phosphorylation needs the electron transport chain and oxygen.

cards.front: Cyanide blocks complex IV. Why does venous blood look unusually red?
cards.back: Oxygen is still delivered but the cells cannot use it, so blood leaving the tissues keeps much of its oxygen.
cards.why: With complex IV blocked, no electrons pass to oxygen, so oxygen use stops even though supply is normal.

cards.front: A drug lets H<sup>+</sup> leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing through ATP synthase. What happens to fuel use, ATP and heat?
cards.back: Fuel and oxygen use rise, ATP made falls, and heat rises.
cards.why: The chain runs flat out trying to rebuild the gradient, but the energy leaves as heat instead of ATP. Dinitrophenol killed users this way; brown fat does the same through its own channel protein when norepinephrine switches it on.

cards.front: Liver vs skeletal muscle: why can only the liver release glucose from its glycogen into the blood?
cards.back: Liver cells have glucose-6-phosphatase, which removes the phosphate so free glucose can leave. Muscle lacks it, so its glucose-6-phosphate stays trapped and goes into glycolysis in that muscle.
cards.why: Charged glucose-6-phosphate cannot cross the plasma membrane; only free glucose can leave by the glucose carriers.

cards.front: Why does glucose from muscle glycogen give 3 ATP by glycolysis instead of 2?
cards.back: Glycogen phosphorylase breaks each bond with phosphate (phosphorolysis), so the glucose comes off already phosphorylated and skips the hexokinase step that costs 1 ATP.
cards.why: One of glycolysis’s two ATP investments is already paid, so the net gain rises by one.

cards.front: What does the liver make new glucose from, and what can it not use?
cards.back: Lactate, amino acids (mainly alanine) and glycerol. Not fatty acids.
cards.why: Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, and acetyl CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate.

cards.front: Why is making glucose not just glycolysis run backward, and what does it cost?
cards.back: Three steps of glycolysis release so much energy that gluconeogenesis must go around them with different enzymes. One glucose from two pyruvate costs 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH.
cards.why: The liver pays with ATP from breaking down fatty acids, which are plentiful when glucose is scarce.

cards.front: What is the Cori cycle, and what does one round trip cost the body?
cards.back: Muscle turns glucose into lactate; the liver makes glucose from the lactate and sends it back. Each turn costs 4 ATP (2 gained in muscle, 6 spent in the liver).
cards.why: It lets muscle keep working anaerobically while the liver, with its own aerobic ATP, pays to recycle the carbon.

cards.front: How do glucagon and epinephrine switch glycogen breakdown on?
cards.back: Through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A, they switch glycogen phosphorylase on and glycogen synthase off. Insulin does the reverse.
cards.why: Switching both enzymes at once keeps the cell from building and breaking glycogen at the same time.

cards.front: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency vs McArdle disease (no muscle glycogen phosphorylase): what happens to fasting blood glucose in each?
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency: blood glucose falls sharply a few hours after a meal, and glycogen piles up in an enlarged liver. McArdle disease: blood glucose stays normal, but exercise causes early fatigue and cramps.
cards.why: The liver needs glucose-6-phosphatase to release glucose into the blood; muscle phosphorylase serves only the muscle’s own glycogen.

cards.front: LDL vs HDL: which way does each carry cholesterol?
cards.back: LDL carries it out to body cells; HDL collects it from cells, including cells in artery walls, and returns it to the liver.
cards.why: Both carry the same cholesterol molecule; what differs is the particle’s proteins, which decide where it goes.

cards.front: LDL vs HDL: where does each come from, and what takes it up?
cards.back: LDL is made in the blood from VLDL after it gives up its triglycerides, and is taken up by LDL receptor proteins, mostly in the liver. HDL starts as small particles from the liver and intestine and returns to the liver.
cards.why: Lipoprotein lipase strips triglyceride from VLDL, and the smaller, cholesterol-rich particle left behind is LDL.

cards.front: LDL vs HDL: which is a cause of heart disease, and which is mainly a marker?
cards.back: LDL is a cause: lowering it prevents heart attacks. A high HDL goes with lower risk, but raising HDL with drugs has not lowered risk, so HDL is best seen as a sign of health, not a cause of it.
cards.why: People born with very high LDL develop heart disease early, and more LDL entering artery walls drives plaque growth; no such causal evidence exists for HDL.

cards.front: How does a statin lower blood LDL?
cards.back: It blocks HMG CoA reductase, so liver cells make less cholesterol; they respond by making more LDL receptor proteins and pull more LDL out of the blood.
cards.why: A cell with too little cholesterol makes more LDL receptor proteins; the liver’s extra uptake lowers LDL, often by a third to a half.

cards.front: Why is a chylomicron the least dense lipoprotein and HDL the most dense?
cards.back: Lipid is less dense than protein. Chylomicrons are mostly triglyceride; HDL carries the most protein for its size.
cards.why: Lipoproteins are named by density, so the more triglyceride a particle carries, the lower its density and the larger it is.

cards.front: What does lipoprotein lipase do, and how does insulin change it?
cards.back: On the capillary lining of muscle, heart and fat, it breaks down the triglycerides in passing chylomicrons and VLDL so the fatty acids enter the nearby cells. Insulin raises it in adipose tissue after a meal.
cards.why: More lipoprotein lipase in fat capillaries after a meal steers dietary fat into storage.

cards.front: What switches lipolysis on, and what switches it off?
cards.back: On: epinephrine and norepinephrine (fast), cortisol and growth hormone (slower); exercise, stress and fasting. Off: insulin, even at low levels.
cards.why: The insulin brake is why fat breakdown runs out of control when insulin is almost absent, as in untreated type 1 diabetes.

cards.front: What does one turn of beta oxidation make, and why does fat need oxygen to be burned?
cards.back: 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl CoA; the chain is two carbons shorter. Every step after activation depends on the electron transport chain to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD.
cards.why: There is no anaerobic route for fat, so fat can supply ATP only when oxygen reaches the mitochondria.

cards.front: How much ATP does one 16-carbon palmitic acid yield, and why more per carbon than glucose?
cards.back: About 106 ATP (about 6.6 per carbon, against about 5.3 for glucose).
cards.why: Its carbons are less oxidized to start with, so each has more electrons to hand to the chain: 7 FADH<sub>2</sub> + 7 NADH + 8 acetyl CoA, minus 2 ATP to activate it.

cards.front: Why does the brain rely on glucose rather than fatty acids?
cards.back: Fatty acids do reach the brain, but its neurons carry out very little beta oxidation, so they burn little fatty acid.
cards.why: That is why, when food is scarce, the liver must make glucose for the brain, and later ketone bodies that the brain can burn.

cards.front: Why does the liver make ketone bodies when fat breakdown is fast?
cards.back: Beta oxidation makes acetyl CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can take it, and the liver is drawing oxaloacetate off to make glucose, so acetyl CoA builds up and is turned into ketone bodies.
cards.why: Less oxaloacetate means fewer acetyl groups can enter the cycle, so the extra goes to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.

cards.front: The liver makes ketone bodies. Why can it not burn them?
cards.back: It lacks the enzyme that turns acetoacetate back into acetyl CoA, so it exports them to the heart, muscle, kidneys and, after a few days of fasting, the brain.
cards.why: Ketone bodies are a water-soluble fuel the liver makes for other tissues, sparing glucose and the muscle protein that would be broken down to make it.

cards.front: Ketosis vs ketoacidosis: typical blood ketone levels and blood pH?
cards.back: Ketosis: about 0.5 to 3 mmol/L on a low-carbohydrate diet, about 5 to 7 after weeks without food; pH normal. Ketoacidosis: above 3 mmol/L, often 5 to 10 or more; pH below 7.35.
cards.why: In ketosis some insulin is still present and limits fat release, and buffers take up the H<sup>+</sup>; in ketoacidosis insulin is nearly absent and bicarbonate is used up.

cards.front: Ketosis vs ketoacidosis: usual cause and insulin level?
cards.back: Ketosis: a day or more without food or a very low-carbohydrate diet; insulin low but present. Ketoacidosis: almost no insulin, as in untreated type 1 diabetes (less often heavy alcohol use with no food).
cards.why: The deciding factor is the insulin brake on lipolysis: with a little insulin, fat release and ketone production stay limited.

cards.front: Why can the glycerol of a triglyceride become glucose, but its fatty acids cannot?
cards.back: Glycerol enters gluconeogenesis as a three-carbon sugar phosphate. Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, and the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA cannot run backward.
cards.why: So when glycogen runs out, fat can fuel most tissues but can supply only a little of the brain’s glucose; the rest must come from amino acids.

cards.front: When and where is fat built, and what is the committed step?
cards.back: Mainly in the liver and adipose tissue when fuel is plentiful and insulin is high. The committed step adds CO<sub>2</sub> to acetyl CoA (an enzyme that needs biotin), and insulin switches it on.
cards.why: Acetyl CoA leaves the mitochondrion as citrate and is split back in the cytosol, where fatty acid synthase builds a 16-carbon chain two carbons at a time.

cards.front: Transamination vs deamination: what does each do?
cards.back: Transamination moves an amino group from an amino acid onto alpha-ketoglutarate, making glutamate (needs vitamin B6). Deamination strips the amino group off glutamate as ammonia, in liver mitochondria.
cards.why: Glutamate collects the amino groups from many amino acids, so the liver has one route to release them as ammonia and make urea.

cards.front: Why are blood ALT and AST used as a test for liver injury?
cards.back: They are transaminases abundant inside liver cells; when the cells are damaged they leak into the blood.
cards.why: A rise in these enzymes in the blood shows liver cells are breaking open, as in hepatitis.

cards.front: Glucogenic vs ketogenic amino acids: what can each become?
cards.back: Glucogenic amino acids (such as alanine) give pyruvate or citric acid cycle molecules, which can become glucose. Ketogenic ones give acetyl CoA or acetoacetate, never glucose; leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic ones.
cards.why: Most amino acids are glucogenic, which is why muscle protein is broken down to supply glucose once glycogen is gone.

cards.front: Where do urea’s two nitrogens come from, and what does each urea cost?
cards.back: One from ammonia and one from the amino acid aspartate. Each urea costs the liver 3 ATP (4 high-energy phosphate bonds).
cards.why: The urea cycle, partly in mitochondria and partly in the cytosol, turns toxic ammonia into small, water-soluble urea that the kidneys excrete.

cards.front: Failing liver vs failing kidneys: what happens to blood ammonia and blood urea in each?
cards.back: Failing liver: ammonia rises and urea is often low, because little urea is made. Failing kidneys: urea rises, because it is made but not excreted.
cards.why: The liver makes urea and the kidneys excrete it, so which value rises tells you which organ is failing; high ammonia causes confusion and a flapping tremor.

cards.front: Does the liver make most of your cholesterol?
cards.back: Current estimates suggest most is made outside the liver (perhaps only about a tenth in the liver), but the liver dominates uptake and excretion.
cards.why: Nearly every cell can make cholesterol; the liver takes up most cholesterol-carrying particles and sends cholesterol out in bile. For your exam: many courses expect "the liver" (often "about 80%").

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: timing and hormone balance?
cards.back: Absorptive (fed): about 4 hours after a meal; insulin high, glucagon low. Postabsorptive (fasting): between meals and overnight; insulin low, glucagon high.
cards.why: Rising glucose and amino acids after a meal make beta cells release insulin; falling glucose lowers insulin and raises glucagon.

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: where does blood glucose come from?
cards.back: Absorptive: the gut. Postabsorptive: the liver, by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (roughly equal shares after an overnight fast).
cards.why: Only the liver (and kidneys) can release glucose into the blood, because only they have glucose-6-phosphatase.

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: what does the liver do in each?
cards.back: Absorptive: takes up glucose, builds glycogen, makes fat from extra glucose and exports it in VLDL. Postabsorptive: releases glucose by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and in a long fast makes ketone bodies.
cards.why: Insulin and glucagon set the direction of the liver’s enzymes, so the same cells store in one state and release in the other.

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: what does skeletal muscle do in each?
cards.back: Absorptive: takes up glucose through GLUT4, builds glycogen and protein. Postabsorptive: burns mostly fatty acids, keeps its glycogen, releases lactate and alanine.
cards.why: Insulin moves GLUT4 carriers into the membrane; with insulin low, muscle takes up little glucose and switches to fat.

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: what does adipose tissue do in each?
cards.back: Absorptive: stores triglyceride (lipoprotein lipase on, lipolysis off). Postabsorptive: lipolysis releases fatty acids and glycerol.
cards.why: Insulin switches on lipoprotein lipase in adipose capillaries and brakes lipolysis; when insulin falls, the brake comes off.

cards.front: After a meal, what happens to gluconeogenesis in the liver?
cards.back: It slows, and much of the glucose it still makes goes into glycogen instead of into the blood.
cards.why: Insulin and less glucagon slow it, and liver glucose release stops, so the new glucose is stored rather than exported.

cards.front: Absorptive vs postabsorptive state: what does the brain burn?
cards.back: Glucose in both; after a few days without food, ketone bodies as well.
cards.why: Brain glucose uptake does not depend on insulin, and the brain burns little fatty acid, so glucose is kept for it between meals.

cards.front: What is glucose sparing, and why does it matter between meals?
cards.back: Most tissues switch from glucose to fatty acids, leaving glucose mostly for the brain and red blood cells.
cards.why: It lets a limited supply, about 100 g of liver glycogen plus gluconeogenesis, keep the brain supplied until the next meal.

cards.front: Anabolic vs catabolic hormones: examples of each?
cards.back: Anabolic (build and store): insulin, and for protein growth hormone (through IGF-1) and testosterone. Catabolic (release fuel): glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol.
cards.why: The catabolic hormones raise blood glucose against insulin, so they are also called counterregulatory hormones.

cards.front: Why does growth hormone fit both the anabolic and the catabolic group?
cards.back: It builds protein (through IGF-1) but breaks down fat and opposes insulin’s effect on glucose.
cards.why: During a fast its release rises: its fat-releasing effect shifts fuel use to fat while its protein-building effect limits muscle loss.

cards.front: Put in order what supplies the brain’s fuel over a long fast.
cards.back: Liver glycogen (about the first day), then glucose made mostly from muscle amino acids (days 1 to 3), then ketone bodies, rising from day 2 or 3 and supplying about two thirds of the brain’s energy by a few weeks.
cards.why: Glycogen stores are small; protein is a costly glucose source, so the rise in ketone bodies is what lets the fast go on.

cards.front: Why does muscle protein breakdown fall from about 75 g a day early in a fast to about 20 g a day after several weeks?
cards.back: As the brain takes up ketone bodies, its glucose need falls from about 120 g to about 40 g a day, so less amino acid is needed to make glucose.
cards.why: Without that switch, making 120 g of glucose a day from protein would use up vital muscle, including heart and breathing muscle, within a few weeks.

cards.front: Why is untreated type 1 diabetes called "starvation in the midst of plenty"?
cards.back: With no insulin, the body acts as if it were fasting even though blood glucose is very high: the liver keeps releasing glucose, muscle and fat stop taking it up, lipolysis runs unchecked and ketone bodies are made.
cards.why: The signal of plenty, insulin, is missing, so the tissues follow glucagon and the other catabolic hormones.

cards.front: In starvation, what happens once fat stores are nearly used up?
cards.back: Protein breakdown rises sharply again: muscle, including heart and diaphragm, wastes, plasma proteins fall and the immune system weakens.
cards.why: With no other fuel left, the body burns its own proteins; death usually follows once a third to a half of body protein is lost.

cards.front: Why must a starved person be refed slowly?
cards.back: The insulin surge from the first meals drives phosphate and potassium into cells, and the low blood levels that follow can stop the heart.
cards.why: Insulin moves these ions into cells along with glucose, and a starved body has little of them to spare.

cards.front: Marasmus vs kwashiorkor: how does each look?
cards.back: Marasmus: too little food of every kind; a thin child with loose skin. Kwashiorkor: edema and a swollen belly that can hide the wasting.
cards.why: In kwashiorkor, low plasma albumin lowers colloid osmotic pressure so fluid collects in the tissues; infection and other factors also seem to matter.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: Radiation: how does it move heat, and about what share of heat loss does it carry at rest in a cool room?
cards.back: As infrared rays between surfaces that are not touching; about 60%.
cards.why: It needs surroundings cooler than your skin; from the sun or a fire it adds heat instead.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: Conduction: how does it move heat, and about what share of heat loss does it carry at rest?
cards.back: Directly to an object your skin touches; about 3%.
cards.why: It needs contact with a cooler object, such as cold stone; a hot surface adds heat instead.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: Convection: how does it move heat, and about what share of heat loss does it carry at rest?
cards.back: Carried off by air or water flowing past your skin; about 15%.
cards.why: Moving air or water keeps replacing the warmed layer next to the skin; in air hotter than skin it adds heat.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: Evaporation: how does it move heat, and what does it need?
cards.back: Water on your skin or in your airways turns to vapor, taking about 580 kcal per liter; it needs air that is not saturated with water vapor.
cards.why: It only ever removes heat; about 20% of heat loss at rest in a cool room, and nearly all of it in hot weather.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: The air is hotter than your skin. Which ways of losing heat still work?
cards.back: Only evaporation. Radiation, conduction and convection now add heat.
cards.why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler, so once the surroundings pass about 35 °C the first three routes run backward.

cards.compare: Radiation vs conduction vs convection vs evaporation
cards.front: Why is hard exercise more dangerous in hot, humid air than in hot, dry air?
cards.back: In humid air sweat evaporates slowly and drips off, and dripping sweat removes almost no heat.
cards.why: Evaporation depends on a water vapor gradient from skin to air; humid air shrinks it, removing the only route left for heat loss.

cards.front: What is basal metabolic rate, and how is it measured?
cards.back: The energy use of a person awake but lying at rest, 12 hours after eating, in a comfortably warm room: about 1,200 to 1,800 kcal a day for most adults.
cards.why: It is measured most often by oxygen use: each liter of oxygen consumed releases about 4.8 kcal from fuel on a mixed diet.

cards.front: What are the three parts of total metabolic rate, and which varies most?
cards.back: BMR (about 60 to 70%), the energy used to digest, absorb and store food (about 10%), and physical activity, which varies most.
cards.why: Hard exercise can raise the rate of energy use ten- to twentyfold for a while.

cards.front: Why do men average higher BMRs than women of the same weight, and why does BMR fall with age?
cards.back: Both follow lean mass: men carry more muscle, and muscle is lost with age.
cards.why: Lean tissue such as muscle, liver and brain uses far more energy than fat.

cards.front: Does a 3,500 kcal deficit always mean 1 pound (about 7,700 kcal per kilogram) lost?
cards.back: It is a fair estimate for a few weeks, but the first week’s loss is larger and over months it overestimates the loss.
cards.why: The first week also loses glycogen and the water stored with it; later, spending falls and appetite rises as weight falls. Use the rule if your exam asks for it.

cards.front: How is BMI calculated, and what are the adult categories?
cards.back: Weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Below 18.5 underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 healthy; 25 to 29.9 overweight; 30 or more obesity.
cards.why: BMI does not measure fat: a muscular athlete can score over 30, so it is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.

cards.front: Ghrelin vs leptin: source, effect on hunger and time scale?
cards.back: Ghrelin: from the empty stomach; raises hunger; meal to meal. Leptin: from fat cells in proportion to stored fat; lowers hunger; days to months.
cards.why: After weight loss ghrelin tends to rise and leptin falls, which together push appetite up and help explain why lost weight tends to return.

cards.front: What is normal core temperature in healthy adults?
cards.back: About 36.6 to 37 °C, lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon.
cards.why: Large modern studies find oral averages near 36.6 °C. For your exam: 37 °C (98.6 °F) is the traditional figure, from the 1800s.

cards.front: In the heat, what widens the vessels of most of your skin?
cards.back: Mainly active dilation by sympathetic cholinergic nerves; in the palms, soles and lips, withdrawal of sympathetic constrictor tone.
cards.why: Human studies show active dilation causes most of the rise in hairy skin. For your exam: many texts give only the loss of constrictor tone.

cards.front: During heat stress, what happens to blood flow to the gut and kidneys, and why?
cards.back: It falls: their vessels narrow, shifting blood toward the skin.
cards.why: Skin blood flow can rise to 6 to 8 L/min, a large share of cardiac output, so flow is taken from organs that can spare it for a while.

cards.front: How does brown adipose tissue make heat without shivering?
cards.back: Norepinephrine makes brown fat cells break down fat and run their mitochondria with a channel protein that lets H<sup>+</sup> leak back across the inner membrane, so the energy leaves as heat instead of ATP.
cards.why: The leak keeps the gradient low, so the electron transport chain runs flat out. Adults keep small deposits in the neck, above the collarbones and along the spine; how much heat they add in adults is still being studied.

cards.front: Why does shivering warm you?
cards.back: Skeletal muscles contract rapidly and out of step, doing no outside work, so almost all their energy becomes heat.
cards.why: Shivering can raise heat production three- to fivefold for a time.

cards.front: Heat exhaustion vs heat stroke: core temperature and brain function?
cards.back: Heat exhaustion: normal to about 40 °C, brain works normally (may faint briefly). Heat stroke: above about 40 °C, with confusion, seizures or coma.
cards.why: Heat exhaustion is a problem of water and salt loss and blood pooled in the skin; heat stroke is cell damage from heat itself.

cards.front: Heat exhaustion vs heat stroke: treatment?
cards.back: Heat exhaustion: rest in the cool, legs raised, fluids with salt. Heat stroke: rapid cooling, ideally cold-water immersion, and emergency care.
cards.why: Fever-reducing drugs do not help heat stroke, because the set point is normal; the loop is overwhelmed, not reset.

cards.front: In heat stroke, why can core temperature run away once heat gain has outrun heat loss?
cards.back: Heat speeds chemical reactions in every cell, so they make still more heat: a harmful positive feedback loop.
cards.why: Once heat loss has been outrun, each rise in temperature raises heat production, until proteins unfold above about 41 to 42 °C.

cards.front: What changes over one to two weeks of exercise in the heat?
cards.back: Sweating starts sooner and is heavier, each liter of sweat carries less salt, and plasma volume expands.
cards.why: So core temperature and heart rate rise less at the same workload. The salt saving comes through aldosterone.

cards.front: Hypothermia: core temperature ranges for mild, moderate and severe, and what happens to shivering?
cards.back: Mild 35 to 32 °C: intense shivering. Moderate 32 to 28 °C: shivering fades and stops. Severe below 28 °C: unconscious, risk of ventricular fibrillation.
cards.why: When shivering stops, heat production falls with it, so cooling speeds up.

cards.front: Why is falling into cold water so much more dangerous than standing in air at the same temperature?
cards.back: Water removes heat about 25 times faster than air, by conduction and convection.
cards.why: Heat loss depends on how fast the surroundings carry heat away, not only on their temperature.

cards.front: Do you lose most of your body heat through your head?
cards.back: No. You lose heat from any uncovered surface roughly in proportion to its area, and the head is about a tenth of the body surface.
cards.why: The face and scalp narrow their vessels less than the limbs in the cold, so an uncovered head matters more when the rest of you is well wrapped.

cards.front: Between which vertebrae do the kidneys lie, and which one sits lower?
cards.back: About T12 to L3; the right kidney sits 1 to 2 cm lower.
cards.why: The liver takes up the space above the right kidney. The 11th and 12th ribs cover the upper parts, so a blow to the lower ribs from behind can injure a kidney.

cards.front: Name the kidney’s three coverings from the outside in.
cards.back: Renal fascia, adipose capsule (renal fat pad), renal capsule.
cards.why: No bone protects the kidney. The fascia anchors it, the fat cushions it and holds it in place, and the tough capsule keeps its soft tissue in shape.

cards.front: Why can a surgeon reach a kidney from the back without opening the peritoneal cavity?
cards.back: The kidneys are retroperitoneal: peritoneum covers only their front surfaces.
cards.why: They lie against the muscles of the back wall of the abdomen, behind the peritoneum.

cards.front: Renal cortex vs renal medulla: shape and appearance?
cards.back: Cortex: a continuous grainy shell about 1 cm thick, plus the renal columns. Medulla: 8 to 18 striped, cone-shaped pyramids.
cards.why: The pyramids look striped because they are packed with parallel tubes and vessels running toward the papillae.

cards.front: Which gets most of the kidney’s blood flow, cortex or medulla?
cards.back: The cortex, about 90%; the medulla gets about 10%, slowly.
cards.why: The filtering units start in the cortex, where the blood is processed; slow medullary flow matters later for concentrating urine.

cards.front: Put in order: major calyx, renal papilla, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter.
cards.back: Renal papilla, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter.
cards.why: Each papilla drips into its own minor calyx; minor calyces join into major calyces, which join into the funnel-shaped pelvis that narrows into the ureter.

cards.front: From front to back, what passes through the renal hilum?
cards.back: Renal vein in front, renal artery in the middle, renal pelvis behind.
cards.why: The pelvis lies deepest because it leaves from inside the renal sinus, behind the vessels.

cards.front: What share of resting cardiac output goes to the kidneys?
cards.back: About 20 to 25%, roughly 1.1 to 1.2 L of blood a minute.
cards.why: The kidneys are under half a percent of body weight. The flow is far more than their cells need; it is the raw material for urine.

cards.front: Why does a clot in one segmental artery kill a wedge of kidney?
cards.back: Segmental arteries are end arteries: they do not connect with each other, so no neighbor can take over.
cards.why: The segment it supplies loses its blood, leaving a wedge of dead tissue with its broad side at the surface.

cards.front: Which named arteries of the kidney have no matching veins?
cards.back: The segmental arteries: interlobar veins join the renal vein directly.
cards.why: Otherwise the veins run back along the arteries’ paths with the same names.

cards.front: What stops urine being forced back up the ureters when the bladder contracts?
cards.back: Each ureter crosses the bladder wall at a slant for about 2 cm; bladder pressure squeezes that tunnel flat.
cards.why: The slanted tunnel acts as a one-way valve: peristalsis pushes urine in, but pressure in the bladder closes it.

cards.front: At which three points is a ureter narrowest?
cards.back: Where it leaves the renal pelvis, where it crosses the edge of the pelvis, and where it passes through the bladder wall.
cards.why: A small solid object in the urine is most likely to lodge at one of these points.

cards.front: What lets the bladder stretch as it fills?
cards.back: Transitional epithelium folded into rugae, and a detrusor whose bundles run in several directions.
cards.why: The folds flatten and the surface cells stretch thin; the interwoven detrusor squeezes from all sides when it contracts.

cards.front: What are the three corners of the trigone?
cards.back: The two ureter openings at the back and the urethral opening at the front.
cards.why: The trigone has no rugae and is very sensitive to stretch and irritation, which causes a strong urge.

cards.front: Internal vs external urethral sphincter: tissue and control?
cards.back: Internal: smooth muscle, involuntary. External: skeletal muscle, voluntary.
cards.why: The internal sphincter sits at the bladder neck; the external one where the urethra crosses the pelvic floor.

cards.front: Which nerves keep each urethral sphincter closed?
cards.back: Internal: sympathetic fibers acting on alpha-1 receptor proteins. External: the pudendal nerve (somatic, acetylcholine).
cards.why: Emptying needs both signals withdrawn: sympathetic output falls, and pudendal firing falls.

cards.front: Is there a distinct internal urethral sphincter in females?
cards.back: No distinct ring: smooth muscle of the bladder neck and upper urethra acts as a functional sphincter.
cards.why: In females the external sphincter and the pelvic floor do more of the holding.

cards.front: Female vs male urethra: length, and one consequence?
cards.back: Female about 3 to 4 cm; male about 18 to 20 cm. Bacteria reach a woman’s bladder far more easily.
cards.why: Skin bacteria near the opening have only a few centimeters to travel in women. The male urethra’s length and bends make a catheter harder to pass.

cards.front: Which nerve fibers make the detrusor contract, and from which segments?
cards.back: Parasympathetic fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves, from S2 to S4, acting on muscarinic receptor proteins.
cards.why: Sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2 do the opposite: they relax the detrusor during storage.

cards.front: When you start to void, what happens first: the external sphincter relaxes or the detrusor contracts?
cards.back: The external sphincter relaxes first; the detrusor contracts a few seconds later.
cards.why: Pudendal output falls and urethral pressure drops, then sacral parasympathetic fibers fire. Contracting against a closed outlet would only raise pressure.

cards.front: Which center throws the switch from storing to emptying, and which carries it out?
cards.back: The pontine micturition center throws the switch; the sacral micturition center (S2 to S4) carries it out.
cards.why: For your exam: if asked where the micturition reflex is integrated, the expected answer is the sacral spinal cord, S2 to S4. In healthy adults the loop runs up to the pons and back.

cards.front: At about what bladder volume do you first notice it, and what does it comfortably hold?
cards.back: First awareness at about 150 to 250 mL; a strong urge at about 300 to 500 mL.
cards.why: Stretch signals grow as the bladder fills, and the urge becomes harder to ignore.

cards.front: About how many nephrons does each kidney have, and can lost ones be replaced?
cards.back: About a million, varying from about 200,000 to over 2 million; lost nephrons are not replaced.
cards.why: You are born with all you will ever have, and after about age 40 you lose some every year.

cards.front: What three things does every nephron do to plasma, in order?
cards.back: Filters it, takes back most of it (reabsorption), and adds substances to it (secretion).
cards.why: What is left at the end is urine.

cards.front: What two parts make a renal corpuscle?
cards.back: The glomerulus (a tuft of fenestrated capillaries) and the glomerular capsule around it.
cards.why: Filtered fluid collects in the capsular space between the capsule’s parietal and visceral layers.

cards.front: What are podocytes?
cards.back: The cells of the capsule’s visceral layer, whose interlocking branches wrap the glomerular capillaries.
cards.why: The narrow gaps between their smallest branches are part of the filter.

cards.front: How is the proximal convoluted tubule built for reabsorbing the most?
cards.back: Cuboidal cells with a dense brush border of microvilli and many mitochondria.
cards.why: Microvilli multiply the surface for transport; mitochondria make the ATP the pumps use.

cards.front: How do the cells of the thin limbs and the thick ascending limb differ?
cards.back: Thin parts: simple squamous cells. Thick ascending limb: cuboidal cells full of mitochondria that pump salt.
cards.why: Thin cells suit passive movement; salt pumping needs ATP.

cards.front: Why is the collecting duct strictly not part of one nephron?
cards.back: Many nephrons drain into each collecting duct, and it grows from a different part of the embryo.
cards.why: Most courses still count it as the last part of the renal tubule, because the fluid in it is still being changed.

cards.front: Cortical vs juxtamedullary nephrons: share and loop length?
cards.back: Cortical: about 85%, short loops. Juxtamedullary: about 15%, long loops deep into the medulla.
cards.why: Where the corpuscle sits decides how long the loop is.

cards.front: Which nephrons let you make urine more concentrated than blood, and which vessels do only they have?
cards.back: Juxtamedullary nephrons, whose long loops are served by the vasa recta as well as peritubular capillaries.
cards.why: Their long loops build the salty medulla; desert rodents with very long loops concentrate urine far more than you.

cards.front: What is unusual about a nephron’s blood supply?
cards.back: Two capillary beds in a row, the glomerulus and the peritubular capillaries, with an arteriole between them.
cards.why: An arteriole on each side lets the kidney set glomerular pressure; after two resistances, pressure in the second bed is low, so it takes fluid in.

cards.front: Afferent vs efferent arteriole: which is narrower in most nephrons?
cards.back: The efferent arteriole.
cards.why: The narrow efferent arteriole resists outflow and backs pressure up into the glomerulus, which drives filtration. In juxtamedullary nephrons it is about as wide or wider, but still resists flow.

cards.front: Which glomerular arteriole contains the juxtaglomerular cells?
cards.back: The afferent arteriole.
cards.why: These modified smooth muscle cells store and release renin.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
cards.back: Macula densa, juxtaglomerular (granular) cells, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.
cards.why: It forms where the tubule, at the end of the thick ascending limb, touches its own afferent and efferent arterioles.

cards.front: Name three triggers for renin release by juxtaglomerular cells.
cards.back: Less stretch of the afferent arteriole, sympathetic stimulation through beta-1 receptor proteins, and a macula densa signal of low NaCl.
cards.why: All three mean blood pressure or volume may be low.

cards.front: What does the macula densa sense?
cards.back: How much sodium chloride is in the tubular fluid flowing past it.
cards.why: That lets each nephron signal its own arterioles and its renin-releasing cells.

cards.front: How much do the kidneys filter a day, and how much urine results?
cards.back: About 180 L of filtrate; 1 to 2 L of urine. More than 99% is reabsorbed.
cards.why: Your whole plasma volume is filtered about 60 times a day, so anything not specifically taken back is cleared quickly.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the filtration membrane from the blood side, and what each mainly holds back.
cards.back: Fenestrated endothelium (blood cells), glomerular basement membrane (large proteins), filtration slits with slit diaphragms (the finest sieve).
cards.why: The fenestrations are far too large to hold back any dissolved molecule.

cards.compare: What passes vs what is held back
cards.front: What passes the filter freely, and what is held back?
cards.back: Water, ions, glucose, amino acids, urea and many drugs pass; blood cells, platelets, albumin and larger proteins are held back.
cards.why: The filter sorts mainly by size; albumin sits at the edge of the size limit, and its negative charge adds a little resistance.

cards.compare: What passes vs what is held back
cards.front: How does the concentration of glucose in the filtrate compare with plasma?
cards.back: About the same.
cards.why: Small solutes pass freely, so the filtrate carries them at plasma concentration; only proteins are held back.

cards.front: Why is glomerular capillary pressure (about 55 mm Hg) so much higher than in other capillaries?
cards.back: The glomerulus drains into a resistance vessel, the efferent arteriole, and the afferent arteriole is short and wide.
cards.why: A downstream arteriole instead of a venule backs pressure up along the whole capillary.

cards.front: Why does BCOP rise from about 25 to 35 mm Hg along a glomerular capillary?
cards.back: Protein-free fluid leaves, so the proteins left behind become more concentrated.
cards.why: In a typical systemic capillary so little fluid leaves that the oncotic pull stays near 25 mm Hg.

cards.front: Using GBHP 55, CHP 15 and BCOP 30 mm Hg, what is the glomerular NFP?
cards.why: The small net push drives all 180 L a day; because the pressures nearly balance, a small change in one changes filtration a lot.

cards.front: What two factors set GFR?
cards.back: GFR = Kf × NFP: the filtration coefficient (filtering area and permeability) times the net filtration pressure.
cards.why: Kf falls when glomeruli are scarred or lost, so GFR can fall with normal pressures.

cards.front: What is the normal filtration fraction?
cards.back: About 20%: GFR ÷ renal plasma flow ≈ 125 ÷ 630.
cards.why: The other four fifths of the plasma leave in the efferent arteriole, richer in protein.

cards.front: Over what range of mean arterial pressure does autoregulation hold GFR nearly steady?
cards.back: About 80 to 180 mm Hg.
cards.why: Some courses quote 60 to 150 mm Hg, a round figure for organs in general; the kidney’s own plateau starts a little higher and extends further.

cards.front: Name the two mechanisms of GFR autoregulation and the vessel both act on.
cards.back: The myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback; both act on the afferent arteriole.
cards.why: The myogenic mechanism acts within seconds; tubuloglomerular feedback takes a few seconds more.

cards.front: In tubuloglomerular feedback, what signal constricts the afferent arteriole when more NaCl reaches the macula densa?
cards.back: ATP released by the macula densa, broken down to adenosine outside the cells.
cards.why: When less NaCl arrives, less adenosine and more nitric oxide widen the arteriole, and renin release rises.

cards.front: Afferent vs efferent constriction: effect on glomerular pressure?
cards.back: Afferent constriction lowers GBHP; moderate efferent constriction raises it.
cards.why: Narrowing before the glomerulus loses pressure on the way in; narrowing after it backs pressure up.

cards.front: Which arteriole’s constriction raises the filtration fraction?
cards.back: The efferent arteriole’s.
cards.why: GFR rises (or holds) while renal plasma flow falls. Afferent constriction lowers both by about the same share.

cards.front: Why can severe efferent constriction lower GFR?
cards.back: Flow slows so much that BCOP climbs steeply along the capillary until NFP reaches zero before the efferent end.
cards.why: The last part of the capillary stops filtering, so total filtration falls.

cards.front: How does moderate angiotensin II protect GFR when pressure falls?
cards.back: It constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, backing pressure up in the glomerulus.
cards.why: That is why an ACE inhibitor can drop GFR sharply in someone with narrowed renal arteries.

cards.front: Why can ibuprofen lower GFR in someone who is low on fluid?
cards.back: It blocks prostaglandin synthesis, and prostaglandins keep the afferent arterioles open when sympathetic activity and angiotensin II are high.
cards.why: In a healthy person the effect is small; when the afferent arterioles depend on those dilators, GFR falls.

cards.front: What is proteinuria, and what does heavy protein loss do?
cards.back: Protein in urine above the normal trace (under about 150 mg a day). Heavy loss lowers plasma albumin, so BCOP falls and edema appears.
cards.why: With less oncotic pull, fluid filters out of systemic capillaries faster than it drains.

cards.front: How can you tell glomerular hematuria from bleeding lower in the urinary tract?
cards.back: Glomerular red cells are misshapen, may be packed into casts, and usually come with proteinuria; lower-tract red cells look normal, usually without protein.
cards.why: Red cells squeezing through an inflamed filter are deformed and molded by the tubules.

cards.front: Write the bookkeeping for any substance the kidney handles.
cards.back: Excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.
cards.why: Glucose: filtered, fully reabsorbed. Potassium: mostly reabsorbed, then partly secreted. Some drugs: filtered and heavily secreted.

cards.front: Why does a 1% change in sodium reabsorption matter so much?
cards.back: About 25,200 mmol of sodium is filtered a day, so 1% is about 252 mmol, more than a day’s intake.
cards.why: Small changes in how much the tubule reabsorbs make large changes in what you excrete.

cards.front: Transcellular vs paracellular route: path and energy?
cards.back: Transcellular: through the cell, across two membranes, can be active. Paracellular: between cells through tight junctions, passive only.
cards.why: Only the transcellular route has carriers that hormones can add or remove.

cards.front: Why does stopping the basolateral sodium–potassium pump stop glucose reabsorption?
cards.back: The glucose symporter runs on the sodium gradient the pump builds; without the pump the gradient runs down.
cards.why: Secondary active transport: the pump spends ATP, the carriers spend the gradient.

cards.compare: Proximal tubule vs nephron loop vs distal tubule vs collecting duct
cards.front: What share of filtered sodium and water does the proximal tubule reabsorb, and what nutrients?
cards.back: About 65% of sodium and water, and nearly all glucose and amino acids.
cards.why: It also returns about 80% of bicarbonate and phosphate and about half the urea.

cards.compare: Proximal tubule vs nephron loop vs distal tubule vs collecting duct
cards.front: Why does fluid leave the proximal tubule at 300 mOsm/L though two thirds of it has gone?
cards.back: Water follows solute through aquaporins and leaky tight junctions, so solute and water leave in proportion.
cards.why: Removing solute leaves the lumen slightly dilute, and water follows by osmosis.

cards.front: What are the glucose transport maximum and renal threshold?
cards.back: Tm about 375 mg/min for both kidneys; renal threshold about 180 mg/dL of plasma glucose.
cards.why: The threshold is below Tm ÷ GFR (300 mg/dL) because some nephrons saturate early: the splay.

cards.front: Why does untreated diabetes mellitus cause polyuria?
cards.back: Glucose above the renal threshold stays in the tubule and holds water with it by osmosis.
cards.why: The carriers are saturated, so the extra filtered glucose is excreted along with water.

cards.compare: Descending limb vs thick ascending limb
cards.front: Descending limb vs thick ascending limb: water and salt?
cards.back: Descending: permeable to water, little salt transport. Thick ascending: nearly waterproof, pumps salt out on NKCC2.
cards.why: So the descending fluid grows more concentrated and the ascending fluid more dilute.

cards.compare: Descending limb vs thick ascending limb
cards.front: What does NKCC2 carry, and where is it?
cards.back: 1 Na+, 1 K+ and 2 Cl− into the cell together, on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb.
cards.why: Potassium leaks back into the lumen, making it positive and driving calcium and magnesium out between the cells.

cards.compare: Proximal tubule vs nephron loop vs distal tubule vs collecting duct
cards.front: Why is the thick ascending limb called the diluting segment?
cards.back: It removes salt but not water, so its fluid falls to about 100 mOsm/L.
