cards.why: It reabsorbs about 25% of filtered sodium with almost no aquaporins.

cards.compare: Proximal tubule vs nephron loop vs distal tubule vs collecting duct
cards.front: What does the distal convoluted tubule reabsorb, and which hormone acts there?
cards.back: About 5% of filtered sodium on a sodium–chloride symporter, and calcium, which PTH increases.
cards.why: It has little water permeability, so its fluid gets more dilute still.

cards.front: Principal vs intercalated cells: main job?
cards.back: Principal: sodium, potassium and water balance under aldosterone, ADH and ANP. Intercalated: acid–base balance, secreting H+ or bicarbonate.
cards.why: Intercalated cells can also reabsorb potassium when the body is short of it.

cards.front: Why do principal cells secrete more potassium when they reabsorb more sodium?
cards.back: Sodium entering through apical channels makes the lumen more negative and the pump brings more K+ into the cell, so more K+ leaves through apical potassium channels.
cards.why: Aldosterone raises both, by adding sodium channels, potassium channels and pumps.

cards.front: Why can tubular secretion clear a drug faster than filtration alone?
cards.back: Secretion reaches the four fifths of plasma that was not filtered, and protein-bound drug that filtration misses.
cards.why: Broad carriers in the proximal tubule secrete penicillin, uric acid and toxins.

cards.front: Obligatory vs facultative water reabsorption: where and how much?
cards.back: Obligatory: proximal tubule and descending limb, about 80 to 85%, whatever you need. Facultative: late distal tubule and collecting duct, the remaining 15 to 20%, only with ADH.
cards.why: For your exam: some textbooks round the split to 90% and 10%. Facultative reabsorption sets your urine volume.

cards.front: Why must the collecting duct pass through salty tissue for urine to reach 1,200 mOsm/L?
cards.back: No part of the tubule pumps water; water leaves only by osmosis, so fluid can never be more concentrated than the tissue around it.
cards.why: The inner medulla, at about 1,200 mOsm/L, sets the ceiling.

cards.front: Which two solutes build the medullary gradient?
cards.back: NaCl, mostly in the outer medulla, and urea, about half of it in the inner medulla.
cards.why: NaCl is pumped out by the thick ascending limbs; urea diffuses out of the inner medullary collecting ducts.

cards.front: Countercurrent multiplier vs exchanger: structure and job?
cards.back: Multiplier: the nephron loop, uses energy, builds the gradient. Exchanger: the vasa recta, passive, keeps blood flow from washing it out.
cards.why: The vasa recta also carry away the water reabsorbed from the loops and collecting ducts.

cards.front: How does a 200 mOsm/L single-level difference become a 900 mOsm/L gradient?
cards.back: Countercurrent flow: each round, fluid arriving at the bend is more concentrated, and pumping adds another step on top.
cards.why: The longer the loop, the more multiplication, which is why desert rodents concentrate urine above 5,000 mOsm/L.

cards.front: Why would ordinary straight capillaries destroy the medullary gradient?
cards.back: Blood entering at 300 mOsm/L would soak up salt and urea and carry them away.
cards.why: Hairpin vasa recta give solutes back on the way up, and their slow flow lets blood equilibrate at each level.

cards.front: Where does urea leave the collecting duct, and what increases it?
cards.back: In the inner medullary collecting duct, through urea carriers that ADH increases.
cards.why: Upstream segments keep urea in while water leaves, so it arrives concentrated. A very low-protein diet weakens concentrating.

cards.front: How does ADH put aquaporins into principal cells?
cards.back: It binds a receptor protein on the basolateral membrane, a G protein raises cAMP, protein kinase A makes aquaporin vesicles fuse with the apical membrane.
cards.why: When ADH falls, the aquaporins are pulled back in by endocytosis.

cards.front: High ADH vs no ADH: urine osmolarity and volume?
cards.back: High ADH: up to about 1,200 mOsm/L, as little as 0.5 L a day. No ADH: down to about 50 mOsm/L, many liters a day.
cards.why: Everything up to the end of the distal tubule is the same either way; the paths split in the collecting duct.

cards.front: What is the least urine that can carry 600 mOsm of daily waste?
cards.back: 600 mOsm ÷ 1,200 mOsm/L = 0.5 L a day.
cards.why: Pass less and waste solute builds up, however high ADH is.

cards.front: In diabetes insipidus, what is wrong and what is intact?
cards.back: ADH is lacking, or principal cells cannot respond to it; the medullary gradient is intact but unused.
cards.why: The person passes large volumes of dilute urine.

cards.compare: Loop vs thiazide vs osmotic diuretics
cards.front: Loop vs thiazide vs osmotic diuretic: where does each act?
cards.back: Loop (furosemide): NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Thiazide: sodium–chloride symporter in the DCT. Osmotic (mannitol): mainly proximal tubule and descending limb.
cards.why: Most diuretics block sodium reabsorption at one segment, and water stays with the sodium.

cards.compare: Loop vs thiazide vs osmotic diuretics
cards.front: Why are loop diuretics the strongest, and what do they do to concentrating ability?
cards.back: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 25% of filtered sodium; blocking NKCC2 also stops the multiplier, so the gradient fades.
cards.why: Thiazides act on only about 5% and leave the gradient intact.

cards.compare: Loop vs thiazide vs osmotic diuretics
cards.front: Loop vs thiazide diuretic: effect on urine calcium?
cards.back: Loop: urine calcium rises. Thiazide: urine calcium falls.
cards.why: Loop diuretics remove the positive lumen that drives calcium out between cells; thiazides make the distal tubule reabsorb more calcium.

cards.compare: Loop vs thiazide vs osmotic diuretics
cards.front: Why do loop and thiazide diuretics cause potassium loss?
cards.back: They send more sodium and faster flow to the principal cells, so potassium secretion rises.
cards.why: Potassium-sparing diuretics block aldosterone’s receptor protein or the sodium channels instead, so potassium secretion falls.

cards.front: Name the three main nitrogen wastes in urine and where each comes from.
cards.back: Urea (liver, from amino acids), creatinine (muscle creatine phosphate), uric acid (purine breakdown).
cards.why: Urea is the largest single solute, about 20 to 30 g a day.

cards.front: What should normal urine not contain?
cards.back: Glucose, more than a trace of protein, blood, or bacteria.
cards.why: Its pH ranges from about 4.5 to 8, usually near 6, and its osmolarity from about 50 to 1,200 mOsm/L.

cards.front: What is urine specific gravity, and its usual range?
cards.back: Its density relative to water (1.000); usually about 1.005 to 1.030.
cards.why: Every solute adds weight, so it is a quick index of concentration; heavy solutes like glucose raise it more than osmolarity shows.

cards.front: Why is 400 mL of urine a day (oliguria) too little?
cards.back: Even at the maximum 1,200 mOsm/L, 0.4 L carries only about 480 mOsm, less than the usual 600 mOsm of daily waste.
cards.why: The rest of the solute stays in the blood, so wastes build up.

cards.front: What is renal clearance, and its formula?
cards.back: The volume of plasma the kidneys completely clear of a substance per minute: C = (U × V) ÷ P.
cards.why: U × V is the amount excreted each minute; dividing by P turns it into the plasma volume that held it.

cards.front: Why does inulin clearance equal GFR?
cards.back: Inulin is filtered freely and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so all of it in urine got there by filtration.
cards.why: The plasma cleared of inulin each minute is exactly the plasma filtered each minute.

cards.front: Why does creatinine clearance run 10 to 20% above true GFR?
cards.back: The proximal tubule secretes a little creatinine as well as filtering it.
cards.why: It is still used to estimate GFR because creatinine is made steadily and is not reabsorbed.

cards.front: A drug’s clearance is 600 mL/min with a GFR of 120. What does the tubule do with it?
cards.back: Secretes it heavily: filtration alone could clear at most about 120 mL/min.
cards.why: Clearance above GFR means net secretion; below GFR means net reabsorption, as with urea or glucose.

cards.front: If GFR halves and stays low, what happens to plasma creatinine, and why can that mislead?
cards.back: It doubles, for example from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/dL.
cards.why: Half the filtering capacity still gives a small-looking number, so labs report an estimated GFR from creatinine, age and sex.

cards.front: What happens to sodium excretion when the arterial pressure reaching a kidney rises, with hormones held constant?
cards.back: It rises, steeply: pressure natriuresis, with pressure diuresis.
cards.why: GFR barely changes, but higher pressure around the tubules makes the proximal tubule reabsorb less sodium.

cards.compare: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH at the kidney
cards.front: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH: main trigger?
cards.back: ADH: rising plasma osmolarity or a large fall in volume. Aldosterone: angiotensin II or rising potassium. ANP: stretched atria. PTH: falling blood calcium.
cards.why: Each is released by a change the kidney can correct.

cards.compare: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH at the kidney
cards.front: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH: effect on urine?
cards.back: ADH: smaller, more concentrated. Aldosterone: less sodium, more potassium. ANP: more sodium and water. PTH: less calcium at first, more phosphate.
cards.why: PTH makes the distal tubule keep calcium and removes phosphate carriers from the proximal tubule.

cards.compare: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH at the kidney
cards.front: ADH vs aldosterone vs ANP vs PTH: main target in the kidney?
cards.back: ADH: principal cells of the collecting duct. Aldosterone: principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. ANP: collecting duct and glomerulus. PTH: proximal and distal tubules and the cells that make calcitriol.
cards.why: Each acts where its transport proteins are.

cards.front: Which three hormones does the kidney itself make?
cards.back: Renin (juxtaglomerular cells), erythropoietin (cells between the tubules), calcitriol (tubule cells, switched on by PTH).
cards.why: Dialysis replaces filtration but not these, so people on dialysis also need EPO and active vitamin D.

cards.compare: Acute kidney injury vs chronic kidney disease
cards.front: Acute kidney injury vs chronic kidney disease: speed and reversibility?
cards.back: AKI: hours to days, often reversible if the cause is fixed quickly. CKD: over 3 months, usually not reversible.
cards.why: CKD’s leading causes are diabetes mellitus and high blood pressure.

cards.compare: Acute kidney injury vs chronic kidney disease
cards.front: Sort the causes of AKI by where the problem is.
cards.back: Prerenal: too little blood reaches the kidney. Intrinsic: tubule cells or glomeruli damaged. Postrenal: urine cannot drain.
cards.why: Prerenal AKI after a hemorrhage reverses when perfusion is restored.

cards.front: Why is potassium often what makes kidney failure an emergency?
cards.back: Failing kidneys cannot secrete potassium, so plasma potassium rises (hyperkalemia), which can cause dangerous arrhythmias.
cards.why: Water, salt, acid and phosphate are retained too, and EPO and calcitriol fall.

cards.front: What is the biggest risk factor for kidney stones, and the main prevention?
cards.back: A small volume of concentrated urine; drinking enough to pass more than about 2.5 L a day.
cards.why: Solutes crystallize when they become too concentrated; a thiazide lowers urine calcium.

cards.front: Why are urinary tract infections far more common in women?
cards.back: The female urethra is 3 to 4 cm long and opens near the anus.
cards.why: Gut bacteria, most often E. coli, have a short path to the bladder.

cards.front: Stress vs urge incontinence: what fails?
cards.back: Stress: the pelvic floor and external sphincter cannot resist a jump in abdominal pressure. Urge: the detrusor contracts when it should not.
cards.why: Stress incontinence is treated first with pelvic floor training; urge incontinence with bladder training and drugs that relax the detrusor.

cards.front: ICF vs ECF: share of total body water, and volume in a 70 kg adult?
cards.back: ICF: about two thirds, about 28 L. ECF: about one third, about 14 L (10.5 L interstitial fluid, 3.5 L plasma).
cards.why: Total body water is about 60% of a young man’s mass (42 L); the 60–40–20 rule splits it into ICF at 40% of mass and ECF at 20%.

cards.front: ICF vs ECF: main cation and main anions?
cards.back: ICF: potassium (about 140 mmol/L), with phosphates and negatively charged proteins. ECF: sodium (about 140 mmol/L), with chloride, then bicarbonate.
cards.why: The sodium–potassium pump keeps moving sodium out and potassium in, and proteins made inside cells cannot leave, so the two fluids hold very different ions.

cards.front: ICF vs ECF: which has the higher osmolality?
cards.back: Neither: both are about 290 mOsm/kg.
cards.why: Water crosses plasma membranes so easily that it moves until the total particle count inside every cell equals the count outside, whatever the solutes are.

cards.front: Plasma vs interstitial fluid: how do they differ?
cards.back: They hold almost the same ions, but plasma holds far more protein.
cards.why: Capillary walls let water and small solutes cross freely through the gaps between endothelial cells, but they hold back most plasma proteins.

cards.front: Which solute sets the volume of the ECF, and which the volume of the ICF?
cards.back: Sodium, held outside cells, sets ECF volume. Potassium and the other solutes trapped inside cells set ICF volume.
cards.why: Water follows the solutes that a barrier holds back, so each compartment’s volume follows the solute that cannot leave it.

cards.front: Hypovolemia: what is lost, and what happens to plasma osmolality and cell size?
cards.back: Salt and water lost together; plasma osmolality stays normal; cells are unchanged. Only the ECF shrinks.
cards.why: An isotonic loss (bleeding, most diarrhea, burns, diuretics) leaves no osmotic gradient across plasma membranes, so no water leaves cells. The danger is low blood pressure and shock.

cards.front: Dehydration, strictly: what is lost, and what happens to plasma osmolality and cell size?
cards.back: More water lost than solute; plasma osmolality rises; water leaves cells, so both the ICF and the ECF shrink.
cards.why: The concentrated ECF draws water out of cells by osmosis. Shrinking brain cells explain the confusion of severe dehydration.

cards.front: Overhydration: what is gained, and what happens to plasma osmolality and cell size?
cards.back: More water gained than solute; plasma osmolality falls; water enters cells and all compartments swell. The danger is brain swelling: seizures.
cards.why: The dilute ECF drives water into cells. Inside the rigid skull, swelling brain cells raise the pressure quickly, which is water intoxication.

cards.front: Hypervolemia: what is gained, and what happens to plasma osmolality and cell size?
cards.back: Salt and water kept together; osmolality normal; cells unchanged. The extra ECF causes edema, including in the lungs.
cards.why: With osmolality unchanged no water enters cells, but the extra ECF raises capillary pressure, so fluid filters into the tissues faster than lymphatics drain it.

cards.front: For your exam: how do many nursing texts use the word “dehydration”?
cards.back: For any loss of body fluid, sometimes split into “isotonic dehydration” and “hypertonic dehydration”. Read how the question uses it.
cards.why: The distinction that matters is whether plasma osmolality changes, because only a change in osmolality moves water out of cells; an isotonic loss is hypovolemia in the strict sense.

cards.front: Typical daily water intake and output for an adult?
cards.back: In: drinks 1.5, food 0.75, metabolic water 0.25 = 2.5 L. Out: urine 1.5, insensible loss 0.7, sweat 0.1, feces 0.2 = 2.5 L.
cards.why: Body water stays steady because intake matches output: mass balance applied to water.

cards.front: Which water routes are adjusted to keep water in balance?
cards.back: Only two: drinking, through thirst, and urine volume, through ADH.
cards.why: Insensible loss follows fever, breathing and dry air; sweat follows body temperature; metabolic water follows fuel use. None of them responds to how much water you have.

cards.front: Why do you lose water every day even when you drink nothing?
cards.back: Urine has a floor of about 0.5 L a day, and insensible loss, feces and sweat add more: over a liter a day.
cards.why: You must excrete about 600 mOsm of waste solute, and urine cannot be more concentrated than about 1,200 mOsm/L, so the kidneys can slow water loss but never stop it.

cards.front: ADH vs thirst: which switches on at the lower plasma osmolality?
cards.back: ADH, which starts rising at about 280 to 285 mOsm/kg; thirst switches on a little higher.
cards.why: Small everyday rises are corrected by the kidneys saving water before you feel thirsty. Larger rises bring in thirst, the only response that can replace water already lost.

cards.front: After a large bleed, is ADH high or low if plasma osmolality is normal or low?
cards.back: High. A fall in blood volume of roughly 5 to 10% overrides concentration.
cards.why: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria, large veins and arteries drive ADH steeply once volume falls past that threshold, so the kidneys keep water even as the plasma becomes dilute.

cards.front: Why does thirst switch off within minutes of drinking, before the water is absorbed?
cards.back: Sensory receptors in the mouth and throat report the swallowed water to the hypothalamus.
cards.why: That early signal stops you from drinking far more than you need while the first gulps are still in your stomach.

cards.front: 1 L of 0.9% saline vs 1 L of D5W: how much of each stays in the plasma?
cards.back: Saline: about 250 mL (all 1,000 mL stays in the ECF). D5W: about 83 mL (two thirds goes into cells).
cards.why: Saline’s sodium stays outside cells, so the liter stays in the ECF, a quarter of it in plasma. Cells use D5W’s glucose, leaving free water that spreads through total body water.

cards.front: Why can drinking 4 L in an hour cause water intoxication even though the ADH loop works?
cards.back: Healthy kidneys can excrete only about 0.7 to 1 L of water an hour, so the extra water stays in cells for hours.
cards.why: The loop switches ADH off and the urine becomes dilute, but the rate of drinking beats the kidneys’ top speed, and brain cells swell.

cards.front: How can a patient with a large burn be hypovolemic and swollen at the same time?
cards.back: Leaky capillaries move plasma fluid and protein into the tissues: a fluid shift. The fluid is still in the body but no longer in the blood.
cards.why: A fluid shift changes where fluid is without changing the total, so plasma volume falls while the interstitial fluid grows.

cards.front: Hypokalemia vs hyperkalemia: effect on the resting potential?
cards.back: Hypokalemia (below 3.5 mmol/L): more negative, hyperpolarized. Hyperkalemia (above 5.0 mmol/L): less negative, depolarized toward threshold.
cards.why: Potassium leaking out of cells sets the resting potential. Less potassium outside means more leaks out; more outside means less leaks out.

cards.front: Hypokalemia vs hyperkalemia: common causes?
cards.back: Hypo: vomiting, diarrhea, loop and thiazide diuretics, too much aldosterone, insulin treatment. Hyper: kidney failure, ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, cell damage, acidosis.
cards.why: Potassium falls when it is lost from the gut or kidneys or pushed into cells, and rises when the kidneys cannot secrete it or cells release it.

cards.front: Hypokalemia vs hyperkalemia: effect on skeletal muscle?
cards.back: Both cause weakness and, if severe, paralysis.
cards.why: In hypokalemia fibers rest further from threshold and are harder to excite. In a large, lasting hyperkalemia the partial depolarization inactivates voltage-gated sodium channels, so action potentials become smaller and cells harder to excite.

cards.front: If hypokalemia makes muscle harder to excite, how does it cause arrhythmias?
cards.back: Heart cells repolarize more slowly (flattened T wave, U wave) and can fire extra beats.
cards.why: Low potassium outside also lets less current through some of the heart cells’ potassium channels, which slows repolarization. The risk is worse in people taking digoxin.

cards.front: Hypokalemia vs hyperkalemia: ECG changes?
cards.back: Hypokalemia: flattened T waves and an extra U wave after the T wave. Hyperkalemia: tall, peaked T waves, and later a wide QRS complex.
cards.why: Low potassium slows repolarization. High potassium speeds it, peaking the T wave, and then holds cells partly depolarized, inactivating sodium channels and slowing conduction.

cards.front: Hypokalemia vs hyperkalemia: main treatment?
cards.back: Hypo: replace potassium, by mouth or slowly by vein. Hyper: calcium by vein to protect the heart, insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells, then remove it (diuretics, binders, dialysis).
cards.why: Hyperkalemia is treated in order of danger: protect the heart first, then move potassium out of the ECF, then get it out of the body.

cards.front: Does IV calcium lower plasma potassium in hyperkalemia?
cards.back: No. It raises the threshold of heart muscle cells, restoring the gap between rest and threshold for 30 to 60 minutes.
cards.why: Calcium buys time. Insulin and glucose shift potassium into cells, and the kidneys, binders or dialysis remove it.

cards.front: Where is the body’s potassium, and why do small shifts matter?
cards.back: About 98% is inside cells; the whole ECF holds only about 60 mmol. Moving 1% of cell potassium (35 mmol) into 14 L of ECF raises plasma potassium by about 2.5 mmol/L.
cards.why: Because the ECF holds so little, the plasma value reports only a sliver of the total and changes fast when potassium moves between cells and ECF.

cards.front: Name three things that move potassium into cells.
cards.back: Insulin, epinephrine (through beta-2 receptor proteins) and alkalosis.
cards.why: Insulin and epinephrine stimulate sodium–potassium pumps, which is why the insulin released after a meal keeps its potassium from raising plasma potassium sharply.

cards.front: Does every acidosis shift potassium out of cells equally?
cards.back: No. The shift is largest with a mineral acid, such as hydrochloric acid; lactic acid and ketone bodies shift much less.
cards.why: One reason: an organic acid’s anion can enter cells along with its H+, so less potassium has to leave in exchange. The high plasma potassium of untreated type 1 diabetes comes mainly from the lack of insulin and the high glucose drawing water, and potassium with it, out of cells.

cards.front: What three things raise potassium secretion by principal cells?
cards.back: A high plasma potassium (directly and through aldosterone), more sodium and fluid reaching the principal cells, and alkalosis.
cards.why: Aldosterone adds sodium channels, potassium channels and pumps; more sodium entering makes the lumen more negative and faster flow carries potassium away, which is why loop and thiazide diuretics cause potassium loss.

cards.front: Why can a lab report a high potassium in a well patient whose plasma potassium is normal?
cards.back: Red blood cells burst in the tube (a hemolyzed sample) and release their potassium.
cards.why: A sample drawn through a small needle, shaken or left standing can hemolyze, so a surprising result is repeated before it is treated.

cards.front: Amount of sodium vs concentration of sodium: what does each reflect?
cards.back: The amount sets ECF volume (RAAS, aldosterone, ANP, pressure natriuresis). The concentration reflects water balance (ADH and thirst).
cards.why: Sodium held outside cells holds water with it, so its amount sets volume; its concentration changes when water is added or removed. Heart failure can give too much total sodium with a low concentration.

cards.front: Hyponatremia vs hypernatremia: underlying problem and water movement?
cards.back: Hypo (below 135): too much water for the sodium; water enters cells and brain cells swell. Hyper (above 145): too little water for the sodium; water leaves cells and brain cells shrink.
cards.why: Plasma sodium concentration tracks plasma osmolality, and water moves across plasma membranes toward the more concentrated side.

cards.front: Hyponatremia vs hypernatremia: danger of correcting a chronic case too fast?
cards.back: Chronic hyponatremia: osmotic demyelination (raise by no more than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours). Chronic hypernatremia: brain swelling, shown mainly in children (lower by no more than about 10 mmol/L a day).
cards.why: Over about two days, brain cells adapt by losing or gaining solute. A fast correction then moves water out of or into the adapted cells.

cards.front: Hyponatremia vs hypernatremia: typical causes?
cards.back: Hypo: SIADH, thiazides, replacing losses with plain water, heart failure. Hyper: no access to water, diabetes insipidus, fever and sweating.
cards.why: Hyponatremia is almost always water kept; hypernatremia almost always water lost without being replaced.

cards.front: Who gets hypernatremia, and why is it rare in everyone else?
cards.back: People who cannot reach water or feel thirst: infants, frail older adults, people who are unconscious or sedated.
cards.why: Anyone who can feel thirst and reach water drinks long before the sodium climbs far.

cards.front: How do you estimate plasma osmolality from a blood panel?
cards.back: 2 × Na + glucose ÷ 18 + urea nitrogen ÷ 2.8, all in the units a US lab reports. Normally about 290 mOsm/kg.
cards.why: Each sodium ion is matched by an anion, so sodium counts twice; dividing converts glucose and urea nitrogen from mg/dL to mmol/L.

cards.front: Why does a very high blood glucose lower the measured sodium?
cards.back: Without insulin, glucose stays outside most cells and draws water out of them, and that water dilutes the plasma sodium.
cards.why: Only solutes that stay outside cells set tonicity. Urea crosses cell membranes, so a high urea raises osmolality without moving water.

cards.front: In what three forms is plasma calcium carried, and which one acts on cells?
cards.back: About half ionized (free), about 40% bound to proteins (mainly albumin), about 10% bound to small anions. Only ionized calcium acts, and it is what the parathyroid glands sense.
cards.why: Only free calcium crosses membranes and affects nerves and muscle, so a low albumin can lower total calcium without changing the active part.

cards.front: Why does a panic attack cause tingling around the mouth when total calcium is normal?
cards.back: Hyperventilation makes the blood alkaline; albumin gives up hydrogen ions and binds more calcium, so ionized calcium falls.
cards.why: Total calcium is unchanged; calcium only moves from the free form to the bound form, but low free calcium makes nerves fire too easily.

cards.front: Hypocalcemia vs hypercalcemia: nerve and muscle excitability and ECG?
cards.back: Hypo: overexcitable (tingling, cramps, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs), longer QT. Hyper: less excitable (tiredness, weakness, constipation, confusion), kidney stones, shorter QT.
cards.why: Low extracellular calcium lets voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily; high calcium does the reverse.

cards.front: Hypocalcemia vs hypercalcemia: common causes?
cards.back: Hypo: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, kidney failure, low magnesium. Hyper: hyperparathyroidism, cancer that spreads to bone or releases a PTH-like protein.
cards.why: PTH and calcitriol are the main regulators, so disorders of the parathyroid glands, vitamin D and the kidneys, which make calcitriol, move calcium most.

cards.front: Why does a high phosphate lower ionized calcium?
cards.back: Calcium and phosphate together can reach a level at which calcium phosphate forms, so when phosphate rises, free calcium falls.
cards.why: This is why kidney failure, which keeps phosphate in, causes tingling and tetany, and over months calcium phosphate deposits in vessels.

cards.front: What is refeeding hypophosphatemia, and why is it dangerous?
cards.back: When a starved person is fed, insulin drives glucose and phosphate into cells, and plasma phosphate can crash.
cards.why: Without phosphate, cells cannot make enough ATP: muscles including the diaphragm weaken, red blood cells stiffen and burst, and less 2,3-BPG makes hemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly.

cards.front: Why does prolonged vomiting cause a low chloride and a high bicarbonate?
cards.back: Vomit removes hydrochloric acid. Each H+ the stomach secreted left a bicarbonate in the blood (the alkaline tide), and with the acid vomited that bicarbonate is never used up; low volume and low chloride then make the kidneys keep it.
cards.why: Chloride and bicarbonate are the two main anions of plasma, so when one falls the other tends to rise, and the blood becomes alkaline.

cards.front: Why can large volumes of 0.9% saline make the blood mildly acidic?
cards.back: Saline holds 154 mmol/L of chloride, half again as much as plasma, so plasma chloride rises and bicarbonate falls.
cards.why: Plasma must keep its charges balanced; extra chloride takes bicarbonate’s place. Balanced fluids such as lactated Ringer’s have a chloride closer to plasma.

cards.front: Why does a low potassium not correct until magnesium is replaced?
cards.back: Without magnesium, principal cells’ potassium channels leak potassium into the urine, so potassium given by mouth is lost.
cards.why: Magnesium inside principal cells normally limits the flow of potassium through those channels.

cards.front: Why does a low magnesium cause a low calcium?
cards.back: The parathyroid glands need magnesium to release PTH, and target tissues need it to respond.
cards.why: Without PTH action, calcium falls, and it recovers only once magnesium is restored.

cards.front: Why do nurses check tendon reflexes during an IV magnesium infusion?
cards.back: Reflexes disappear first as magnesium climbs too high, before weakness, low blood pressure, slow breathing and cardiac arrest.
cards.why: High magnesium depresses nerves and muscles. IV calcium counters it.

cards.front: Why do loop diuretics cause magnesium loss?
cards.back: Most filtered magnesium is reabsorbed between the cells of the thick ascending limb, pushed by the positive lumen that NKCC2 creates; blocking NKCC2 removes that push.
cards.why: The same block that causes sodium, chloride and water loss removes the driving force for magnesium reabsorption.

cards.front: Volatile vs fixed acid: how much per day, and which organ removes each?
cards.back: Volatile (carbonic acid, from carbon dioxide): about 13,000 to 20,000 mmol a day, removed by the lungs in minutes. Fixed: about 50 to 100 mmol a day, removed by the kidneys over hours to days.
cards.why: Carbonic acid can turn back into a gas and be breathed out; a fixed acid cannot, so it stays until the kidneys excrete it or tissues burn it.

cards.front: What are the main sources of fixed acid, and what lowers the load?
cards.back: Sulfuric acid from sulfur-containing amino acids (the largest share), phosphoric acid and unburned organic acids. Fruits and vegetables lower it.
cards.why: Plant foods contain salts of organic acids, such as citrate; burning those anions takes up H+ and leaves bicarbonate behind.

cards.front: Why do lactic acid and ketone bodies not normally need the kidneys?
cards.back: Tissues burn them almost as fast as they are made, which takes the H+ back up and restores bicarbonate.
cards.why: Only when production far outruns use, as in shock or untreated type 1 diabetes, do they overwhelm the buffers.

cards.compare: Bicarbonate vs phosphate vs protein buffers
cards.front: Bicarbonate vs phosphate vs protein buffer: main site?
cards.back: Bicarbonate: plasma and interstitial fluid. Phosphate: inside cells and in urine. Protein: inside cells, and hemoglobin in red blood cells.
cards.why: Plasma holds only about 1 mmol/L of phosphate, so it buffers little there; it is concentrated inside cells and in urine.

cards.compare: Bicarbonate vs phosphate vs protein buffers
cards.front: Why does the bicarbonate buffer matter more than its chemistry suggests?
cards.back: Its partners can be adjusted: the lungs remove carbon dioxide and the kidneys adjust bicarbonate.
cards.why: A buffer whose ends can be topped up or drained keeps working long after a closed buffer would be used up.

cards.compare: Bicarbonate vs phosphate vs protein buffers
cards.front: What is the main buffer inside cells?
cards.back: Proteins and phosphates buffer together, and proteins supply the larger share. Many textbooks say phosphate: give your course textbook’s answer.
cards.why: Most of your protein is inside your cells, which makes intracellular proteins the largest buffer store in the body.

cards.front: Do chemical buffers remove acid from the body?
cards.back: No. They take up H+ within seconds but only hold it until the lungs or kidneys deal with it.
cards.why: A buffer blunts a change in pH by binding H+; once it is used up, it cannot bind more.

cards.front: Buffers vs lungs vs kidneys: how fast, and what does each change?
cards.back: Buffers: seconds, how many H+ are free. Lungs: minutes (full effect 12 to 24 hours), PCO2. Kidneys: hours (full effect 3 to 5 days), bicarbonate.
cards.why: Each works on a different timescale, and only the lungs and kidneys remove acid, each a different kind.

cards.front: Lungs vs kidneys: main limit of each in pH control?
cards.back: Lungs: cannot remove fixed acid, and slowing breathing lowers PO2. Kidneys: slow, and they need to be working.
cards.why: The lungs restore the ratio but not the bicarbonate; the kidneys cannot excrete carbon dioxide. Each covers for the other.

cards.front: According to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, what does blood pH depend on?
cards.back: The ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide: pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PCO2)). Normally 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20, so pH is 7.4.
cards.why: Because 6.1 never changes, pH follows the ratio, not the amount of either partner.

cards.front: How much does pH change if the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio halves or doubles?
cards.back: Halving lowers pH by 0.3; doubling raises it by 0.3.
cards.why: log 2 is about 0.3, the same “0.3 means twofold” rule as for any pH change.

cards.front: Why is respiratory control of pH incomplete?
cards.back: As PCO2 falls, the central chemoreceptors sense the change in the brain’s fluid and act as a brake, so pH moves toward normal but not all the way.
cards.why: The lungs also cannot remove fixed acid, and slowing breathing to correct alkalosis lets PO2 fall until the carotid bodies drive breathing back up.

cards.front: What are the three parts of renal control of pH?
cards.back: Reclaim filtered bicarbonate; excrete the day’s fixed acid as H+ on urinary buffers; make new bicarbonate to replace what the acid used.
cards.why: All three rely on hydrogen ion secretion: carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3− inside the tubule cell, and the H+ is sent into the lumen.

cards.front: Is the bicarbonate “reabsorbed” in the proximal tubule the same ion that was filtered?
cards.back: No. The filtered ion becomes carbon dioxide in the lumen; a new one is made in the cell and sent to the blood.
cards.why: The effect is the same as moving it across, and no acid is excreted: the secreted H+ ends up in a water molecule.

cards.front: What makes bicarbonate “new”?
cards.back: It is made in the tubule cell for each H+ that leaves in the urine, replacing bicarbonate a fixed acid used up, rather than reclaiming filtered bicarbonate.
cards.why: Every H+ excreted as titratable acid or ammonium adds one new bicarbonate to the blood.

cards.front: Titratable acid vs ammonium: how much acid does each carry, and which can the kidneys turn up?
cards.back: Titratable acid (on phosphate): about 20 to 30 mmol a day, limited by filtered phosphate. Ammonium: about 30 to 50 mmol a day, rising five- to tenfold over 3 to 5 days of acid load.
cards.why: Proximal tubule cells break down more glutamine when acid persists; the slow ramp-up of ammonium is the main reason the kidneys are slow.

cards.front: Why can the kidneys not excrete the day’s acid as free H+?
cards.back: At the lowest urine pH, about 4.5, a liter holds only about 0.03 mmol of free H+, so 70 mmol would need over 2,000 L of urine.
cards.why: Proton pumps cannot push urine pH below about 4.5, so almost all excreted H+ is carried on phosphate and ammonia.

cards.compare: Type A vs type B intercalated cells
cards.front: Type A vs type B intercalated cells: what does each secrete into the urine, and when is each more active?
cards.back: Type A: H+ (by proton pumps), sending new bicarbonate to the blood; more active when blood is too acidic. Type B: bicarbonate (in exchange for chloride), sending H+ to the blood; more active when blood is too alkaline.
cards.why: The two cells are mirror images: each sends its acid or base one way and the partner ion the other.

cards.front: What turns up H+ secretion by the kidneys?
cards.back: Acid in the tubule cells, a high PCO2, a low plasma potassium, and aldosterone (angiotensin II speeds the proximal tubule’s sodium–hydrogen exchanger).
cards.why: A high PCO2 diffuses into tubule cells and makes more H+ there, which is how the kidneys compensate when breathing is the problem.

cards.front: How does acetazolamide change blood and urine?
cards.back: It blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so filtered bicarbonate leaves in the urine: urine pH up, blood bicarbonate and pH down.
cards.why: Without the enzyme the tubule cell makes little H+ to secrete, and filtered bicarbonate is not turned into carbon dioxide in the lumen, so it cannot be reclaimed.

cards.front: Normal ABG values for pH, PaCO2 and HCO3−?
cards.back: pH 7.35 to 7.45; PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg; HCO3− 22 to 26 mmol/L.
cards.why: PaCO2 is the respiratory number, set by ventilation; HCO3− is the metabolic number, set by the kidneys and fixed acids.

cards.front: Respiratory acidosis: primary change, cause, compensation, common causes?
cards.back: PaCO2 up (above 45) from hypoventilation; the kidneys raise HCO3− over 3 to 5 days. Causes: opioid or sedative overdose, COPD, weak breathing muscles, airway obstruction.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide builds up when alveolar ventilation falls below its production; the lungs cannot fix a problem they are causing, so the kidneys compensate.

cards.front: Respiratory alkalosis: primary change, cause, compensation, common causes?
cards.back: PaCO2 down (below 35) from hyperventilation; the kidneys lower HCO3− over 3 to 5 days. Causes: anxiety, pain, fever, high altitude, early pneumonia or asthma.
cards.why: Breathing out carbon dioxide faster than it is made lowers PaCO2; the kidneys respond by secreting less H+ and letting type B cells excrete bicarbonate.

cards.front: Metabolic acidosis: primary change, cause, compensation, common causes?
cards.back: HCO3− down (below 22) from fixed acid gained or bicarbonate lost; the lungs lower PaCO2 within minutes to hours. Causes: diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acid in shock, kidney failure, severe diarrhea.
cards.why: Bicarbonate is used up buffering an added acid or lost in stool or urine; the carotid bodies sense the fall in pH and speed breathing.

cards.front: Metabolic alkalosis: primary change, cause, compensation, common causes?
cards.back: HCO3− up (above 26) from acid lost or bicarbonate gained; the lungs raise PaCO2 by slowing breathing. Causes: vomiting, stomach suction, diuretics, excess aldosterone.
cards.why: Compensation is limited because slower breathing lowers PaO2, so PaCO2 rarely climbs above about 55 mm Hg.

cards.front: Acidosis vs alkalosis: typical signs?
cards.back: Acidosis mainly depresses the nervous system: drowsiness, confusion, coma (with deep, fast breathing in metabolic acidosis). Alkalosis makes nerves and muscles too excitable: tingling, cramps, spasms.
cards.why: In alkalemia albumin binds more calcium, so ionized calcium falls and nerves fire too easily.

cards.front: How do pH and the primary number move in respiratory vs metabolic disorders (“ROME”)?
cards.back: Respiratory opposite: PaCO2 up, pH down (or the reverse). Metabolic equal: HCO3− down, pH down (or both up).
cards.why: pH follows the ratio of bicarbonate (top) to carbon dioxide (bottom), so it moves with bicarbonate and against carbon dioxide.

cards.front: Which way does the compensating number move?
cards.back: In the same direction as the primary number: bicarbonate down, PaCO2 down; PaCO2 up, bicarbonate up.
cards.why: Moving both parts of the ratio the same way brings the ratio back toward 20, even though neither number is normal.

cards.front: Uncompensated vs partially vs fully compensated: how do you tell them apart?
cards.back: Uncompensated: the other number is still normal and pH is abnormal. Partially: both abnormal, same direction, pH still out of range. Fully: both abnormal, pH back in 7.35 to 7.45.
cards.why: For a fully compensated gas, the side of 7.40 points to the first disorder, because compensation seldom overshoots.

cards.front: Respiratory vs renal compensation: what compensates for what, and how fast?
cards.back: Respiratory (lungs change PaCO2): for metabolic disorders, starting in minutes, full in 12 to 24 hours. Renal (kidneys change HCO3−): for respiratory disorders, starting in hours, full in 3 to 5 days.
cards.why: Chemoreceptors change ventilation fast; tubule cells need days to raise ammonium production and bicarbonate output.

cards.front: For your exam: how do nursing and paramedic exams label a gas with both numbers abnormal and a pH of 7.35 to 7.45?
cards.back: “Fully compensated.” In practice compensation rarely brings pH all the way back, except in respiratory alkalosis that has lasted days to weeks.
cards.why: When pH is normal and both numbers are well out of range, clinicians also consider two disorders at once. Use the exam label when asked.

cards.front: Acute vs chronic respiratory acidosis: how do they look on an ABG?
cards.back: Acute: PaCO2 high, bicarbonate barely changed, pH low (for example 7.26, 60, 26). Chronic: PaCO2 high, bicarbonate high, pH low-normal or a little low (7.34, 60, 31).
cards.why: Renal compensation needs 3 to 5 days, so the bicarbonate tells you how long the carbon dioxide has been high.

cards.front: What pattern on an ABG means two primary disorders at once?
cards.back: PaCO2 and bicarbonate moving in opposite directions (for example PaCO2 up and bicarbonate down), or one moving far more or less than compensation explains.
cards.why: Compensation always moves the second number in the same direction as the first. In cardiac arrest, poor breathing and lactic acid push pH down together.

cards.front: What is the anion gap, and its normal value?
cards.back: Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8 to 12 mmol/L with modern analyzers (8 to 16 in older texts).
cards.why: It stands for the anions the panel does not measure, mostly albumin, plus phosphate, sulfate and organic anions; it is not a real gap in charge.

cards.front: High vs normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: what does each mean?
cards.back: High gap: acid gained, its unmeasured anion replacing bicarbonate (ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, poisons). Normal gap: bicarbonate lost, with chloride rising in its place (diarrhea).
cards.why: Whether bicarbonate is replaced by an unmeasured anion or by chloride decides whether the gap rises.

cards.front: Why can a normal anion gap hide an added acid in a very ill patient?
cards.back: Albumin is the largest unmeasured anion; each 1 g/dL fall lowers the normal gap by about 2.5 mmol/L.
cards.why: A low albumin shrinks the baseline, so an acid’s anion can raise the gap back into the “normal” range.

cards.front: What three findings diagnose diabetic ketoacidosis?
cards.back: Blood glucose of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more, or known diabetes; beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 mmol/L or more; and a metabolic acidosis, with pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L.
cards.why: Known diabetes counts because DKA can occur at near-normal glucose; the ketone and acidosis criteria show that ketone acids have overwhelmed the buffers.

cards.front: In DKA, why is plasma potassium often normal or high although the body has lost a lot of it?
cards.back: Lack of insulin lets potassium leave cells, and the high glucose draws water, and potassium with it, out of cells, while glucose in the urine carries potassium out of the body.
cards.why: When insulin treatment starts, potassium moves back into cells and plasma potassium can fall dangerously, so fluids, insulin and potassium are given together.

cards.front: What is Kussmaul breathing, and why does it happen?
cards.back: Deep, sighing, fast breathing in severe metabolic acidosis, such as DKA.
cards.why: The carotid bodies sense the low arterial pH and drive breathing, lowering PaCO2 to move the ratio back toward 20; its expected PaCO2 is about 1.5 × HCO3− + 8.

cards.front: Healthy kidneys excrete extra bicarbonate fast. Why does the alkalosis of vomiting last, and what fixes it?
cards.back: Volume loss (angiotensin II and aldosterone), chloride loss and potassium loss make the kidneys keep bicarbonate. Saline and potassium chloride fix it.
cards.why: Angiotensin II speeds bicarbonate reclaim, type B cells need chloride to excrete bicarbonate, and low potassium speeds H+ secretion. Once all three are replaced the excess leaves within a day or two.

cards.front: After days of vomiting, why can the urine be acidic while the blood is alkaline?
cards.back: The kidneys hold on to sodium at almost any cost, trading H+ and K+ for it in the collecting duct: paradoxical aciduria.
cards.why: Protecting blood volume takes priority over pH; it ends when saline restores the volume.

cards.front: What PaCO2 should you expect in a metabolic acidosis (Winter’s formula)?
cards.back: 1.5 × HCO3− + 8, ± 2. A value far outside that range means a second, respiratory disorder.
cards.why: The formula is a rule of thumb from studies of patients; lower than expected suggests a respiratory alkalosis too (as in aspirin poisoning), higher a respiratory acidosis.

cards.front: Why is the respiratory alkalosis of a panic attack uncompensated?
cards.back: Renal compensation takes days, and the attack is over in minutes.
cards.why: Buffers release a little H+ within minutes, so bicarbonate can dip slightly, but the kidneys have not acted.

cards.front: Is breathing into a paper bag recommended for anxiety hyperventilation?
cards.back: No. Calm coaching toward slower breathing is used, once other causes have been considered.
cards.why: The bag can lower the oxygen breathed, and the same fast breathing can come from a lung clot, a heart attack or diabetic ketoacidosis, where it would be dangerous.

cards.front: What does severe acidemia do to the body?
cards.back: It depresses the nervous system (confusion, drowsiness, coma), weakens heart contractions, dilates arterioles and makes the heart prone to abnormal rhythms.
cards.why: It can also shift potassium out of cells, most of all when the acid is a mineral acid, raising plasma potassium.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: how many rounds of DNA copying, and how many divisions?
cards.back: Both copy DNA once. Mitosis divides once; meiosis divides twice (meiosis I and II).
cards.why: Meiosis has no S phase between its two divisions, which is why the chromosome number halves.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: how many cells are made, and with how many chromosomes each (human)?
cards.back: Mitosis: two cells with 46 (diploid). Meiosis: four cells with 23 (haploid).
cards.why: Meiosis I separates the homologs, halving the number; meiosis II then splits each cell again without copying.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: are the new cells identical to the parent?
cards.back: Mitosis: genetically identical. Meiosis: different from the parent and from each other.
cards.why: Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis I mix the mother’s and father’s chromosomes; mitosis only copies.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: do homologs pair up and cross over?
cards.back: Mitosis: no. Meiosis: yes, in prophase I.
cards.why: Homologs must pair before they can swap pieces and then be separated as partners in anaphase I.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: what lines up at metaphase?
cards.back: Mitosis: single chromosomes. Meiosis I: homologous pairs. Meiosis II: single chromosomes.
cards.why: In metaphase I each pair faces the two ends, so partners go to opposite cells; in metaphase II and mitosis each chromatid faces a different end.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: what separates at anaphase?
cards.back: Mitosis: sister chromatids. Anaphase I: homologs. Anaphase II: sister chromatids.
cards.why: In anaphase I the proteins holding sisters together are kept at the centromere, so each homolog moves as a double chromosome.

cards.front: Mitosis vs meiosis: what is each for in the body?
cards.back: Mitosis: growth, repair and replacing cells. Meiosis: making sperm and eggs.
cards.why: Only cells in the gonads that are becoming gametes undergo meiosis; every other dividing cell uses mitosis.

cards.front: Homologous chromosomes vs sister chromatids: what are they?
cards.back: Homologs: two separate chromosomes, one from each parent. Sister chromatids: two identical copies of one chromosome, made in S phase.
cards.why: Homologs carry the same genes but can carry different alleles; sisters are copies, identical apart from crossing over.

cards.front: When are homologs separated, and when are sister chromatids separated?
cards.back: Homologs: meiosis I. Sister chromatids: mitosis and meiosis II.
cards.why: Homologs pair only in meiosis I; sisters are held together at the centromere until mitosis or meiosis II releases them.

cards.front: Diploid vs haploid: what do 2n and n mean in humans?
cards.back: Diploid (2n = 46): both members of all 23 pairs. Haploid (n = 23): one member of each pair.
cards.why: Two haploid gametes join to restore 46, so the number stays the same from one generation to the next.

cards.front: A human cell in anaphase holds 46 chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids. Which division is it in?
cards.back: Anaphase I of meiosis.
cards.why: Whole double chromosomes moving apart means homologs are separating while sisters stay joined. Mitosis would show 92 single chromosomes, and anaphase II 46 single ones.

cards.front: How do you count chromosomes in a cell that has copied its DNA?
cards.back: Count centromeres: a chromosome of two sister chromatids is one chromosome.
cards.why: When sister chromatids separate, each becomes a chromosome in its own right, so the count doubles at that moment.

cards.front: How many different gametes can independent assortment alone make in a human?
cards.back: 2²³, about 8.4 million.
cards.why: Each of the 23 pairs lines up either way at random, independently: 2 choices per pair, multiplied 23 times. Crossing over raises the real number far higher.

cards.front: What is crossing over, and where can you see where it happened?
cards.back: A chromatid of each homolog breaks at the same point and swaps pieces in prophase I; a chiasma marks the joint.
cards.why: The swap makes new chromosomes that are part mother’s and part father’s, so no two gametes are alike.

cards.front: What gametes does nondisjunction make, and what cell forms if one joins a normal gamete?
cards.back: Gametes with 24 or 22 chromosomes; the new cell has 47 or 45.
cards.why: A pair of homologs (or sister chromatids) goes to the same end instead of opposite ends, so one cell gets both and the other none.

cards.front: Why does nondisjunction become more common as a mother ages?
cards.back: The proteins that hold her oocytes’ chromosomes together were laid down before birth and weaken over decades.
cards.why: Oocytes pause in meiosis I for years; weak links let pairs come apart early or wrongly, mostly in meiosis I.

cards.front: What makes the early gonad of an XY embryo become a testis?
cards.back: SRY, a gene on the Y chromosome.
cards.why: SRY protein switches on testis genes in the gonad’s supporting cells; the testis’s hormones then drive male development of the ducts and genitals.

cards.front: Why does the father’s sperm, not the egg, decide a baby’s sex?
cards.back: Every egg carries an X; half of sperm carry an X and half a Y.
cards.why: A man’s X and Y separate in meiosis I like any other pair; a woman has only X chromosomes to give.

cards.front: An XXY person develops as male and an X-only person as female. What does that show?
cards.back: That SRY on the Y, not the number of X chromosomes, is the switch for testis development.
cards.why: One Y is enough whatever the number of X chromosomes, and without a Y there is no SRY. For your exam, SRY is the answer to what makes the gonad a testis; the ovary’s own genes are also actively switched on.

cards.front: Seminiferous tubules vs interstitial cells: what does each make?
cards.back: Tubules: sperm. Interstitial (Leydig) cells: testosterone.
cards.why: One organ, two jobs in two places: sperm inside the tubules, the hormone in the tissue between them.

cards.front: Seminiferous tubules vs interstitial cells: exocrine or endocrine, and which pituitary hormone drives each?
cards.back: Tubules: exocrine-like, cells leave by ducts; driven mainly by FSH with testosterone. Interstitial cells: endocrine, into the blood; driven by LH.
cards.why: The tubules release a product into a duct system; the interstitial cells release a hormone into the capillaries.

cards.front: How much cooler than the body are the testes, and why does it matter?
cards.back: About 2 to 3 °C cooler; 37 °C is too warm for making sperm.
cards.why: The scrotum holds the testes outside the body cavity, and the dartos, cremaster and pampiniform plexus fine-tune their temperature.

cards.front: How does the pampiniform plexus cool the testis?
cards.back: By countercurrent heat exchange: warm arterial blood gives up heat to cooler venous blood flowing back beside it.
cards.why: The mesh of veins wraps the testicular artery, so blood is already cooled when it reaches the testis.

cards.front: Dartos vs cremaster: muscle type and what each does in cold?
cards.back: Dartos: smooth muscle under the skin; wrinkles the skin. Cremaster: skeletal muscle around the cord; pulls the testis up.
cards.why: Both reduce heat loss from the testes; the cremasteric reflex also lifts the testis when the inner thigh is stroked.

cards.front: What happens to sperm in the epididymis, and how long does it take?
cards.back: They gain the ability to swim forward and are stored in its tail; transit takes several days, about 2 days to 2 weeks.
cards.why: Sperm leave the testis unable to swim; they mature as they pass along the 6 m coiled tube.

cards.front: List the route of sperm from testis to urethra.
cards.back: Seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.
cards.why: The ductus deferens climbs in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal and joins a seminal vesicle’s duct to form the ejaculatory duct inside the prostate.

cards.front: Why are inguinal hernias far more common in males?
cards.back: The inguinal canal, the path the testis took down before birth, leaves a weak spot in the abdominal wall.
cards.why: A loop of intestine can push into the canal alongside the spermatic cord.

cards.front: Seminal vesicles vs prostate: share of semen volume and pH of their fluid?
cards.back: Seminal vesicles: about 60–70%, alkaline. Prostate: about 20–30%, slightly acidic.
cards.why: The larger alkaline share outweighs the prostate’s acid, so semen is slightly alkaline, about pH 7.2 to 8.0.

cards.front: Seminal vesicles vs prostate: key contents?
cards.back: Seminal vesicles: fructose, prostaglandins and a clotting protein. Prostate: citrate, zinc and PSA.
cards.why: Fructose fuels the sperm’s ATP; the clotting protein gels the semen, and PSA dissolves the gel within 15 to 30 minutes.

cards.front: Seminal vesicles vs prostate: which is commonly diseased, and why does its growth cause urinary symptoms?
cards.back: The prostate: benign enlargement and cancer are both common. It wraps around the urethra, so its growth squeezes urine outflow.
cards.why: Benign prostatic hyperplasia gives a weak stream, trouble starting and getting up at night; the seminal vesicles are rarely diseased.

cards.front: What do the bulbourethral glands add, and when?
cards.back: A little clear, slippery mucus during arousal, before ejaculation.
cards.why: It lubricates the tip of the penis and neutralizes traces of acidic urine in the urethra.

cards.front: Corpora cavernosa vs corpus spongiosum: number, position and which holds the urethra?
cards.back: Cavernosa: two, on the upper side. Spongiosum: one, on the underside, around the spongy urethra; it forms the glans.
cards.why: The spongiosum carries the urethra from the pelvic floor to the tip.

cards.front: Corpora cavernosa vs corpus spongiosum: why does one fill hard and the other stay softer?
cards.back: The cavernosa have a thick tunica albuginea; the spongiosum’s is thin, so it fills but stays softer.
cards.why: A softer spongiosum keeps the urethra open for ejaculation.

cards.front: Erection vs emission vs expulsion: which nerves run each?
cards.back: Erection: parasympathetic (S2–S4). Emission: sympathetic (about T10–L2). Expulsion: somatic pudendal nerve (S2–S4).
cards.why: “Point and shoot”: parasympathetic for erection, sympathetic then somatic for ejaculation.

cards.front: Erection vs emission vs expulsion: messenger and muscle?
cards.back: Erection: nitric oxide and cGMP relax smooth muscle. Emission: norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins contracts smooth muscle. Expulsion: acetylcholine contracts skeletal muscle.
cards.why: Relaxing erectile smooth muscle lets blood in; contracting duct smooth muscle moves semen; skeletal muscle at the root of the penis forces it out.

cards.front: Why does blood stay in the penis during an erection?
cards.back: The swelling tissue squeezes the draining veins flat against the tunica albuginea.
cards.why: Inflow rises while outflow falls, so pressure in the corpora cavernosa climbs close to arterial pressure.

cards.front: Exam question: is erection a sympathetic or parasympathetic effect, and what relaxes the smooth muscle?
cards.back: Parasympathetic; the relaxing chemical is nitric oxide, released by those nerves and the endothelium.
cards.why: Acetylcholine plays a smaller part, mainly by making the endothelium release nitric oxide.

cards.front: Why does sildenafil need sexual stimulation to work, and why is it dangerous with nitrate drugs?
cards.back: It only slows PDE5’s breakdown of cGMP, so nitric oxide must first make cGMP. Nitrates also raise cGMP, and together they can drop blood pressure dangerously.
cards.why: Blocking breakdown adds nothing if no cGMP is being made; with nitrates, cGMP rises in blood vessels everywhere.

cards.front: Why can an alpha-1 blocker for an enlarged prostate leave little or no semen at ejaculation?
cards.back: It weakens emission: the ducts, seminal vesicles and prostate contract less.
cards.why: Emission runs on norepinephrine at alpha-1 receptor proteins. Retrograde flow into the bladder is more typical after prostate surgery or diabetic nerve damage.

cards.front: After a vasectomy, what happens to semen volume and testosterone?
cards.back: Both barely change; only sperm are missing from the semen.
cards.why: The glands that make most of the volume join the route below the cut, and testosterone goes straight into the blood.

cards.front: Why is testicular torsion a surgical emergency?
cards.back: The twisted cord shuts off the testicular artery and veins; a testis untwisted within about six hours can usually be saved.
cards.why: Without blood flow the testis dies, so the twist must be undone quickly.

cards.front: Order the cells of spermatogenesis.
cards.back: Spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, sperm.
cards.why: Mitosis renews the spermatogonia; meiosis I and II give spermatids; spermiogenesis reshapes them into sperm.

cards.front: Why does a high fever show up in a semen sample only two to three months later?
cards.back: Spermatogenesis takes about 64 to 74 days, plus several days in the epididymis.
cards.why: Cells harmed early in the process are released as sperm weeks later, and recovery is just as slow.

cards.front: How many sperm come from 16 primary spermatocytes?
cards.why: Each primary spermatocyte gives 2 secondary spermatocytes and then 4 spermatids, and each spermatid becomes one sperm without dividing.

cards.front: What happens in spermiogenesis?
cards.back: A round spermatid reshapes into a sperm without dividing: DNA packs tightly, an acrosome forms, a tail grows and cytoplasm is shed.
cards.why: The divisions are finished; the Sertoli cell eats the shed cytoplasm.

cards.front: Sertoli vs Leydig cells: where are they, and which hormone drives each?
cards.back: Sertoli: inside the tubule wall, basement membrane to lumen; FSH with testosterone. Leydig: between the tubules near capillaries; LH.
cards.why: The Sertoli cells wrap the germ cells; the Leydig cells sit by the blood they release testosterone into.

cards.front: Sertoli vs Leydig cells: main product and the feedback it sends?
cards.back: Sertoli: support for spermatogenesis and inhibin, which lowers FSH. Leydig: testosterone, which lowers LH and GnRH.
cards.why: Each cell type brakes the pituitary hormone that drives it, giving two separate negative feedback loops.

cards.front: Sertoli vs Leydig cells: which forms the blood-testis barrier, and how?
cards.back: Sertoli cells, joined near their bases by tight junctions.
cards.why: The seal splits the tubule wall into a basal compartment open to blood and an adluminal compartment reached only through Sertoli cells.

cards.front: Why do developing sperm need a blood-testis barrier?
cards.back: They make new surface proteins after the immune system learned to ignore your own proteins, so they look foreign.
cards.why: The barrier keeps antibodies and lymphocytes away; if injury breaks it, a man can make antibodies against his own sperm.

cards.front: What does androgen-binding protein do?
cards.back: It holds testosterone inside the tubule, keeping it 50 to 100 times the blood level.
cards.why: Spermatogenesis needs that high local level, which only the neighboring Leydig cells can supply.

cards.front: Name the three parts of a sperm and what each does.
cards.back: Head: nucleus and acrosome of enzymes. Midpiece: mitochondria making ATP. Tail: a flagellum that drives it forward.
cards.why: The acrosome’s enzymes digest a path to the egg; the midpiece burns fructose and other fuels to power the tail.

cards.front: Why does your mitochondrial DNA come from your mother?
cards.back: The sperm’s mitochondria are destroyed soon after it enters the egg.
cards.why: The oocyte supplies nearly all the cytoplasm and organelles of the new cell.

cards.front: Why must GnRH come in pulses?
cards.back: The pituitary responds to rising and falling GnRH but stops responding to steady GnRH.
cards.why: That is why a long-acting GnRH-like drug first raises LH and then shuts it down, lowering testosterone in prostate cancer.

cards.front: Low testosterone with high LH and FSH points to what?
cards.back: The testes themselves have failed (for example, Klinefelter syndrome).
cards.why: With no testosterone or inhibin brake, a healthy pituitary works harder.

cards.front: Low testosterone with low LH and FSH points to what?
cards.back: Pituitary or hypothalamic failure.
cards.why: Nothing drives the testes, so all three are low together.

cards.front: Normal testosterone and LH but high FSH points to what?
cards.back: Loss of germ cells with Leydig cells intact, as after some chemotherapy.
cards.why: Sertoli cells without germ cells release less inhibin, so only the FSH brake weakens.

cards.front: Why do anabolic steroids shrink the testes and cut sperm counts?
cards.back: The drug brakes GnRH and LH, so the Leydig cells stop supplying the high local testosterone the tubules need.
cards.why: Blood androgen is high, but the tubules lose their local supply; the axis takes months to restart after stopping.

cards.front: What do 5-alpha reductase and aromatase turn testosterone into?
cards.back: 5-alpha reductase: DHT, a stronger androgen. Aromatase: estradiol.
cards.why: DHT acts in the prostate, genital skin and hair follicles; estradiol closes growth plates and keeps bone dense in both sexes.

cards.front: Before birth, testosterone vs DHT: what does each shape?
cards.back: Testosterone: the internal ducts (epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles). DHT: the penis, scrotum and prostate.
cards.why: 5-alpha reductase deficiency shows the split: ducts form, but the external genitals may look female or in between at birth.

cards.front: Name four secondary sex characteristics testosterone produces in males.
cards.back: Male-pattern hair, a deeper voice, more muscle mass, heavier bones and broader shoulders (also larger sebaceous glands).
cards.why: Testosterone acts through androgen receptor proteins that change gene expression; faster protein synthesis builds muscle.

cards.front: Why do men’s hematocrits run higher than women’s?
cards.back: Testosterone raises erythropoietin release and marrow activity.
cards.why: More red blood cell production raises the hematocrit.

cards.front: Exam question: do androgens drive sex drive? What does the evidence say?
cards.back: Exam answer: androgens help drive sex drive in both sexes. Evidence: clear in men; in women less clear, since a woman’s own level predicts desire poorly.
cards.why: Testosterone given to older women with low desire raises it modestly, so a role is possible but weaker than in men.

cards.front: Why can a vaginal infection spread to the peritoneum in females?
cards.back: The tract is open at both ends: the uterine tube opens into the pelvic cavity next to the ovary.
cards.why: Bacteria climbing from the vagina can reach the peritoneum; scarring from pelvic inflammatory disease can block the tubes.

cards.front: Ovarian ligament vs suspensory ligament of the ovary: what does each connect?
cards.back: Ovarian ligament: ovary to the uterus. Suspensory ligament: ovary to the pelvic wall, carrying its artery, vein and nerves.
cards.why: The suspensory ligament is the ovary’s lifeline, because its blood supply runs inside it.

cards.front: Name the parts of the uterine tube from the ovary inward.
cards.back: Fimbriae at the open funnel, ampulla, isthmus, then a short part through the uterine wall.
cards.why: The ampulla, the longest and widest part, is where sperm usually meet the oocyte.

cards.front: How does an oocyte get into and along the uterine tube?
cards.back: Fimbriae sweep the ovary and their cilia set up a current that draws it in; cilia and waves of smooth muscle move it to the uterus over three to four days.
cards.why: The ovary is not attached to the tube, so the oocyte must be caught.

cards.front: Name the three regions of the uterus.
cards.back: Fundus (rounded top), body (main part) and cervix (narrow lower end in the vagina).
cards.why: The uterine tubes enter below the fundus; the cervical canal links the cavity to the vagina.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the uterine wall from outside in.
cards.back: Perimetrium (serosa), myometrium (smooth muscle), endometrium (mucosa).
cards.why: The myometrium is most of the wall’s bulk and contracts in childbirth and during periods.

cards.front: Functional vs basal layer of the endometrium: which is shed at menstruation?
cards.back: The functional layer is shed; the basal layer stays and regrows it.
cards.why: “The lining is shed” is only half right: the basal layer supplies the cells that rebuild the functional layer.

cards.front: Functional vs basal layer: how does each get its blood?
cards.back: Functional: coiled arteries that constrict before shedding. Basal: short straight arteries that keep it alive.
cards.why: Because the basal layer has its own steady supply, it survives when the functional layer breaks down.

cards.front: Why is the vagina acidic?
cards.back: Estrogen makes its cells store glycogen; the glycogen is broken into sugars that lactobacilli ferment to lactic acid.
cards.why: A pH of about 3.8 to 4.5 holds back many harmful microbes.

cards.front: What lines the vagina, and where does lubrication come from?
cards.back: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with no glands; fluid seeps through the wall from blood vessels, plus mucus from the cervix and glands at the opening.
cards.why: The layered epithelium resists wear, and its folds flatten as the vagina stretches.

cards.front: Where do most cervical cancers start, and what drives them?
cards.back: Where the vaginal side’s stratified squamous epithelium meets the canal’s columnar epithelium; persistent HPV infection.
cards.why: Screening samples cells from that junction, and HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

cards.front: Follow milk from where it is made to the nipple.
cards.back: Alveoli (clustered in lobules), smaller ducts, lactiferous duct, duct opening on the nipple.
cards.why: Myoepithelial cells around the alveoli squeeze milk into the ducts.

cards.front: Exam question: where does milk collect before leaving the nipple? What does ultrasound show?
cards.back: Exam answer: the lactiferous sinuses. Ultrasound shows no storage sacs; the ducts widen only briefly while milk flows, with about 9 duct openings.
cards.why: The sinus is the older textbook description; the ducts also branch close to the nipple.

cards.front: Give the male counterparts of the labia majora, the glans of the clitoris and the greater vestibular glands.
cards.back: Scrotum, glans penis and bulbourethral glands.
cards.why: Both sets of organs grow from the same early tissues, so each female structure has a male counterpart.

cards.front: Give the male counterparts of the body of the clitoris and the vestibular bulbs.
cards.back: Corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum.
cards.why: The paired erectile bodies match; the bulbs beside the vaginal opening match the spongy tissue around the male urethra.

cards.front: Can the appearance of the hymen show whether someone has had intercourse?
cards.back: No.
cards.why: Its shape varies widely and changes with age and estrogen; it is usually a ring or crescent with an opening.

cards.front: Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis: when does meiosis start?
cards.back: Spermatogenesis: at puberty, then continuously. Oogenesis: before birth.
cards.why: Primary oocytes enter meiosis I in the fetal ovary and pause there for years or decades.

cards.front: Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis: do the stem cells last?
cards.back: Spermatogonia divide throughout adult life. Oogonia divide only before birth; none remain after.
cards.why: That is why men keep making sperm into old age while the follicle supply runs out in midlife.

cards.front: Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis: where does each pause?
cards.back: Spermatogenesis: no pauses, about 64 to 74 days. Oogenesis: prophase I (for years) and metaphase II.
cards.why: The second pause ends only if a sperm enters the secondary oocyte.

cards.front: Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis: how is the cytoplasm divided, and how many gametes per cell entering meiosis?
cards.back: Sperm: equal division, four gametes. Oocytes: unequal division, one gamete plus polar bodies.
cards.why: The spindle sits at the oocyte’s edge, so one large cell keeps the nutrients and organelles an early embryo will run on.

cards.front: Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis: how many gametes?
cards.back: About 400 oocytes released in a lifetime vs on the order of 100 million sperm made a day.
cards.why: Oocytes are lost mainly by atresia, not ovulation; sperm are made continuously from renewing stem cells.

cards.front: How many oocytes are there at mid-gestation, at birth and at puberty?
cards.back: About 6 to 7 million, 1 to 2 million, and 300,000 to 400,000.
cards.why: No new oocytes are made after birth, and they die off steadily by atresia.

cards.front: Which cell is released at ovulation, and at what stage is it paused?
cards.back: A secondary oocyte, paused at metaphase II.
cards.why: Meiosis I finishes just before ovulation; meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters.

cards.front: What is a polar body?
cards.back: A tiny cell from an unequal meiotic division that gets a set of chromosomes and little else, and later breaks down.
cards.why: It lets the oocyte discard half its chromosomes while keeping almost all the cytoplasm.

cards.front: Order the follicle stages.
cards.back: Primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary (vesicular), mature vesicular (Graafian).
cards.why: Flat cells become cube-shaped granulosa cells, then several layers with a theca, then an antrum forms and grows.

cards.front: From which stage does a follicle need FSH to keep growing?
cards.back: The tertiary stage, once it has an antrum.
cards.why: Early stages run on signals inside the ovary; each month the tertiary follicles ready when FSH is high are rescued.

cards.front: Why does usually only one follicle mature each month?
cards.back: As FSH falls, only the follicle with the most FSH receptor proteins keeps growing; the others lose their support and undergo atresia.
cards.why: Estradiol and inhibin from the growing group are what lower FSH.

cards.front: Theca vs granulosa cells: what does each contribute to estradiol, and which hormone drives each?
cards.back: Theca: androgens from cholesterol, driven by LH. Granulosa: aromatase converts those androgens to estradiol, driven by FSH.
cards.why: Theca cells lack aromatase and granulosa cells lack the androgen-making enzymes, so a follicle needs both hormones.

cards.front: How long after LH starts to rise does ovulation occur, and how long can the oocyte be joined by a sperm?
cards.back: About 34 to 36 hours; about 12 to 24 hours.
cards.why: LH finishes meiosis I, loosens the oocyte, and triggers enzymes that weaken the follicle wall.

cards.front: Why can high doses of prostaglandin-blocking drugs delay ovulation?
cards.back: Prostaglandins are needed for the enzymes that break down the follicle wall at its thin spot.
cards.why: Without them the wall does not give way on time, even if LH rises normally.

cards.front: What does the corpus luteum make, how long does it last, and what does it need?
cards.back: Progesterone, plus estradiol and inhibin; about 12 to 14 days without pregnancy; steady LH.
cards.why: It forms from the emptied follicle’s cells under LH and becomes the corpus albicans when it dies.

cards.front: What empties the ovary over a lifetime?
cards.back: Atresia, the degeneration of follicles that never open.
cards.why: More than 99% of follicles die this way; only about 400 are ovulated.

cards.front: Do the two ovaries take turns ovulating?
cards.back: No: which ovary ovulates is close to random, and a woman with one ovary usually ovulates from it every month.
cards.why: Each month’s dominant follicle can be in either ovary.

cards.compare: FSH vs LH in males and females
cards.front: FSH vs LH: target cells in the testis and the ovary?
cards.back: FSH: Sertoli cells; granulosa cells. LH: Leydig cells; theca cells, and later the granulosa cells too.
cards.why: The parallel jobs follow from the same pituitary hormones acting on the matching cells of each gonad.

cards.compare: FSH vs LH in males and females
cards.front: FSH vs LH: main effect in females?
cards.back: FSH: follicle growth and aromatase. LH: theca androgens; the surge triggers ovulation; forms and sustains the corpus luteum.
cards.why: Estradiol needs both: LH for the androgen starting material, FSH for converting it.

cards.compare: FSH vs LH in males and females
cards.front: FSH vs LH: what holds each back selectively, and which GnRH pulse speed favors each?
cards.back: FSH: inhibin (and estradiol); slower pulses. LH: testosterone in males, progesterone and estradiol in females; faster pulses.
cards.why: In polycystic ovary syndrome, fast GnRH pulses favor LH, and theca cells overproduce androgens.

cards.front: Estrogen vs progesterone: main source in a nonpregnant woman?
cards.back: Estrogen: granulosa cells of growing follicles, also the corpus luteum. Progesterone: the corpus luteum.
cards.why: That is why progesterone stays near zero until ovulation and peaks about a week after it.

cards.front: Estrogen vs progesterone: effect on the endometrium?
cards.back: Estrogen: makes the functional layer grow and adds progesterone receptor proteins. Progesterone: turns it secretory, coiling glands and arteries.
cards.why: Progesterone can act only on tissue estrogen has first primed with its receptor proteins.

cards.front: Estrogen vs progesterone: effect on cervical mucus?
cards.back: Estrogen: thin, watery and stretchy, so sperm pass easily. Progesterone: thick and sticky, forming a plug.
cards.why: Thin mucus around ovulation eases sperm entry; the progestin in the pill keeps it thick as a backup barrier.

cards.front: Estrogen vs progesterone: effect on resting body temperature, and what does a morning rise tell you?
cards.back: Estrogen: little. Progesterone: raises it about 0.3 to 0.5 °C. A rise shows ovulation has already happened.
cards.why: Progesterone is high only after ovulation, so the rise cannot predict ovulation in advance.

cards.front: Estrogen vs progesterone: feedback on GnRH, FSH and LH?
cards.back: Estrogen: negative at low to moderate levels, positive when high and sustained. Progesterone: negative, slowing GnRH pulses.
cards.why: That switch in estradiol’s effect is what produces the LH surge.

cards.front: Name three effects of estrogen outside the reproductive tract.
cards.back: Keeps bone mass by limiting osteoclasts; closes growth plates; raises HDL (also raises clotting factors from the liver).
cards.why: Losing estrogen at menopause speeds bone loss and lets LDL climb.

cards.front: Estradiol’s negative vs positive feedback: when and at what level?
cards.back: Negative: most of the cycle, at low to moderate levels. Positive: about two days before ovulation, when high (about 200 pg/mL or more) and sustained.
cards.why: Dose and time switch its effect in the hypothalamus and pituitary.

cards.front: How does high, sustained estradiol drive the LH surge?
cards.back: It excites the kisspeptin neurons that drive GnRH neurons, and adds GnRH receptor proteins to pituitary cells so each pulse releases far more LH.
cards.why: Before the surge, rising LH and FSH make the follicle release still more estradiol: positive feedback.

cards.front: What ends the positive feedback of the LH surge?
cards.back: The surge sets up its own ending: it turns the follicle’s cells toward making progesterone, so estradiol falls and the stimulus disappears.
cards.why: Estradiol peaks as the surge begins and then falls; ovulation follows, and progesterone begins to hold GnRH down.

cards.front: On the cycle graph, does estradiol peak before, with, or after LH?
