cards.back: Just before: estradiol peaks as the LH surge begins, then falls while LH is still rising.
cards.why: The LH is already switching the follicle toward progesterone.

cards.front: Cycles are 32 days long. On about which day is ovulation?
cards.back: Day 18: ovulation day ≈ cycle length − 14.
cards.why: The luteal phase is steady, set by the corpus luteum’s lifespan, so the extra days fall before ovulation.

cards.front: Can a follicle ovulate during the luteal phase?
cards.back: No. Follicles may start to grow, but none can go on to ovulate while the corpus luteum is working.
cards.why: Progesterone with estradiol and inhibin holds FSH and LH at their lowest, so no follicle gets the support to dominate and no surge can occur.

cards.front: Exam question: what causes menstruation?
cards.back: Falling progesterone when the corpus luteum dies makes the functional layer break down and be shed.
cards.why: Current evidence gives the leading role to progesterone withdrawal setting off inflammation and enzyme breakdown, with coiled artery spasm contributing.

cards.front: Name the phases of the uterine cycle, their days in a 28-day cycle, and the hormone driving each.
cards.back: Menstrual (1–5): falling progesterone. Proliferative (6–14): rising estradiol. Secretory (15–28): progesterone.
cards.why: The ovary’s hormones drive the uterus, so the two cycles stay in step.

cards.front: Why does FSH rise in the last days of one cycle and the first days of the next?
cards.back: The dying corpus luteum’s estradiol, progesterone and inhibin fall, lifting their brake on FSH.
cards.why: The rise rescues the next group of follicles from atresia.

cards.front: Exam question: why do hormone levels rise at puberty? What is the better-supported cause?
cards.back: Exam answer: decreased sensitivity of the hypothalamus to negative feedback. Better supported: the GnRH pulse generator reawakens inside the brain, with kisspeptin neurons central.
cards.why: Children without working gonads still show the rise in FSH and LH at the usual age.

cards.front: What is the usual order of puberty in girls?
cards.back: Breast budding (about 10), pubic and underarm hair, growth spurt, then menarche at about 12 to 13.
cards.why: Early cycles often release no oocyte, because the positive-feedback LH surge takes a year or more to mature.

cards.front: Why is a high FSH the laboratory sign of menopause?
cards.back: With few follicles left, inhibin and estradiol fall, and FSH loses both of its brakes.
cards.why: LH rises too, but FSH rises first and most.

cards.front: Name four effects of low estrogen after menopause.
cards.back: Hot flashes and night sweats, a thinner and less acidic vaginal lining, faster bone loss, and a rising LDL.
cards.why: A woman with a uterus on hormone therapy needs a progestin too, because estrogen alone overstimulates the endometrium.

cards.front: How does the combined pill prevent ovulation?
cards.back: Steady estrogen and progestin keep negative feedback on, so FSH and LH stay low, no follicle dominates, and estradiol never triggers an LH surge.
cards.why: Thick cervical mucus and a thin endometrium from the progestin act as backups.

cards.front: Is the bleed in the pill’s hormone-free days a true period?
cards.back: No: it is a withdrawal bleed, since no ovulation came before it.
cards.why: The drop in hormones sheds the thin lining the pill kept in place.

cards.front: Levonorgestrel vs ulipristal emergency pills: when does each stop working?
cards.back: Levonorgestrel works poorly once the LH surge has begun. Ulipristal can still delay ovulation early in the surge, but not once LH has peaked.
cards.why: Both work mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation; neither ends an established pregnancy.

cards.front: Why do periods stop in endurance athletes who eat too little, and in breastfeeding?
cards.back: Low energy and high prolactin both slow the GnRH pulse generator.
cards.why: Low GnRH means low FSH, LH and estrogen; months of low estrogen thin the bones.

cards.front: Where does fertilization normally happen?
cards.back: In the ampulla, the wide outer part of the uterine tube.
cards.why: The fimbriae sweep the oocyte into the tube and it moves inward, while sperm swim up from the uterus; the two meet in the ampulla.

cards.front: How long is the fertile window, and why?
cards.back: About six days: the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation.
cards.why: Sperm can survive in the female tract for up to about five days, but an oocyte can be fertilized for only 12 to 24 hours after release.

cards.front: Capacitation vs acrosomal reaction: what is each?
cards.back: Capacitation: slow changes that make a sperm able to fertilize. Acrosomal reaction: exocytosis of the acrosome’s enzymes.
cards.why: Capacitation readies the membrane and the tail; the acrosomal reaction is the fast release event that it makes possible.

cards.front: Capacitation vs acrosomal reaction: where and how long?
cards.back: Capacitation: in the uterus and tube, over several hours. Acrosomal reaction: near or at the zona pellucida, in seconds to minutes.
cards.why: Capacitation depends on hours in the fluids of the female tract; the acrosomal reaction is triggered by a sharp calcium rise near the oocyte.

cards.front: Capacitation vs acrosomal reaction: main events?
cards.back: Capacitation: cholesterol removed, calcium and bicarbonate enter, hyperactivated motility. Acrosomal reaction: acrosome membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and acrosin is released.
cards.why: Albumin strips cholesterol and the entering calcium changes the beat; later, a calcium rise in the head fuses the acrosome with the plasma membrane.

cards.front: Which comes first, capacitation or the acrosomal reaction, and why must it?
cards.back: Capacitation first; only a capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosomal reaction.
cards.why: Capacitation destabilizes the membrane so the acrosome can later fuse with it and release its enzymes.

cards.front: How does a sperm pass the corona radiata?
cards.back: Its hyperactivated beat forces it between the cells, and hyaluronidase on its head digests the hyaluronic acid gluing them.
cards.why: The corona radiata is granulosa cells held together by hyaluronic acid, so an enzyme that cuts that glue opens a way through.

cards.front: For your exam: what is often said to trigger the acrosomal reaction, and what does newer evidence show?
cards.back: Exam answer: binding a zona pellucida glycoprotein (often named ZP3). Newer evidence: in mice most sperm have already reacted before reaching the zona; where it starts in humans is debated.
cards.why: Filming of fertilization in mice showed early reactions among the cells around the oocyte; either way, a sperm that cannot release its enzymes cannot cross the zona.

cards.front: What is the cortical reaction, and how does it block polyspermy?
cards.back: Exocytosis of cortical granules under the zona; an enzyme they release cuts ZP2 and the zona stiffens.
cards.why: Sperm bind the zona through ZP2, so cutting it stops new sperm attaching, and a stiffer zona stops those already inside.

cards.front: Do human oocytes use a fast electrical block to polyspermy?
cards.back: No, they do not appear to. The zona block (cortical reaction) and the membrane shedding its sperm-binding protein keep extra sperm out.
cards.why: The fast depolarizing block is real in sea urchins and frogs; exams may still ask for it as the “fast block”.

cards.front: What starts the calcium waves in the oocyte, and what two things do they trigger?
cards.back: An enzyme (a phospholipase) delivered by the sperm; the waves trigger the cortical reaction and the completion of meiosis II.
cards.why: The enzyme releases calcium from the oocyte’s endoplasmic reticulum, and calcium is the signal that activates the oocyte.

cards.front: Why do your mitochondria come from your mother?
cards.back: The sperm’s midpiece mitochondria enter the oocyte but are marked and destroyed within days.
cards.why: Only the oocyte’s own mitochondria survive, so their DNA is inherited from the mother.

cards.front: When and by what is genetic sex set?
cards.back: At fertilization, by whether the sperm carries an X or a Y.
cards.why: Every oocyte carries an X, and half of sperm carry X and half Y.

cards.front: Do the male and female pronuclei fuse into one nucleus?
cards.back: No. Each copies its DNA, their envelopes break down, and the two chromosome sets line up together on the first mitotic spindle.
cards.why: This happens about a day after sperm entry; the combined set is the diploid zygote.

cards.front: An embryo is 3 weeks old counted from fertilization. What week of pregnancy is that on the clinical count?
cards.back: About week 5.
cards.why: Clinicians count from the first day of the last menstrual period, about two weeks before fertilization.

cards.front: Why does the embryo not grow during cleavage?
cards.back: The cells skip most of the growth phase and divide again, cutting the same cytoplasm into smaller blastomeres inside the zona pellucida.
cards.why: Early divisions run largely on the proteins and RNA stored in the oocyte, so the embryo stays about the oocyte’s size.

cards.front: Morula, blastocyst, hatching, implantation: roughly which days after fertilization?
cards.back: Morula reaches the uterus about day 4; blastocyst about day 5; hatching day 5 to 6; implantation begins day 6 to 7.
cards.why: The embryo divides while drifting down the tube, becomes hollow once it is in the uterus, and must hatch before it can attach.

cards.front: How does the blastocoel fill with fluid?
cards.back: Outer cells pump sodium into the center, and water follows the solute in.
cards.why: Sodium–potassium pumps on the inner surfaces of the sealed outer layer build up solute inside.

cards.front: Trophoblast vs inner cell mass: what does each become?
cards.back: Trophoblast: the chorion and the embryo’s side of the exchange organ. Inner cell mass: the embryo, amnion and yolk sac.
cards.why: The trophoblast forms none of the embryo’s body; everything of the body comes from the inner cell mass.

cards.front: Trophoblast vs inner cell mass: position and potency?
cards.back: Trophoblast: the outer layer, committed to supporting tissues. Inner cell mass: a cluster inside at one end, pluripotent.
cards.why: Cells on the outside, facing the fluid, switch on trophoblast genes; cells enclosed by others become the inner cell mass.

cards.front: Trophoblast vs inner cell mass: which makes hCG?
cards.back: The trophoblast, as syncytiotrophoblast, once it is implanting. The inner cell mass makes none of note.
cards.why: The invading syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG into the mother’s blood.

cards.front: Cytotrophoblast vs syncytiotrophoblast?
cards.back: Cytotrophoblast: separate, dividing cells on the inside. Syncytiotrophoblast: fused cells with many nuclei and no boundaries, which invades.
cards.why: The syncytiotrophoblast forms as cytotrophoblast cells fuse; it digests the endometrium and reaches maternal blood.

cards.front: What does hCG do in early pregnancy?
cards.back: It binds LH receptor proteins on the corpus luteum and keeps it alive, so it keeps secreting progesterone.
cards.why: Without hCG the corpus luteum dies at 12 to 14 days, progesterone falls and the endometrium, with the embryo, is shed.

cards.front: Why do pregnancy tests not react with LH?
cards.back: They use antibodies against the part of hCG that is unique to hCG.
cards.why: hCG is built so much like LH that it binds the same receptor proteins, so a test must target the part that differs.

cards.front: How does hCG change in a healthy early pregnancy?
cards.back: It roughly doubles every two to three days, peaks about 7 to 8 weeks after fertilization, then falls to a lower level for the rest of pregnancy.
cards.why: By the time it falls, the tissues grown from the trophoblast make enough progesterone, so the corpus luteum is no longer needed.

cards.front: What is gastrulation, and when does it happen?
cards.back: Week 3: epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm.
cards.why: All three germ layers come from the epiblast; the first cells through replace the hypoblast as endoderm.

cards.front: Germ layers: what does ectoderm form?
cards.back: The epidermis, hair, nails, skin glands, the nervous system (neural tube and neural crest), tooth enamel, the lens and the adrenal medulla.
cards.why: Rule of thumb: ectoderm makes the outer covering and the nervous system.

cards.front: Germ layers: what does mesoderm form?
cards.back: Muscle of all three kinds, bone, cartilage, blood, the dermis, most connective tissue, the heart, kidneys, gonads and adrenal cortex, and vessel endothelium.
cards.why: Rule of thumb: mesoderm makes almost everything between the outer covering and the gut lining.

cards.front: Germ layers: what does endoderm form?
cards.back: The lining of the digestive tract, airways and urinary bladder, and the liver, pancreas, thyroid, parathyroids and thymus lining.
cards.why: Rule of thumb: endoderm lines the gut and airways and forms the glands that bud from them.

cards.front: Which germ layer does epithelium come from?
cards.back: All three: epidermis from ectoderm, gut lining from endoderm, vessel endothelium from mesoderm.
cards.why: Epithelium is a tissue type, not a germ layer; most organs are also built from more than one layer.

cards.front: What do the three parts of a somite form?
cards.back: Sclerotome: vertebrae and ribs. Myotome: skeletal muscle of the back and body wall (and limb muscle cells). Dermatome: dermis of the back.
cards.why: Each somite is supplied by its own spinal nerve, which is why skin and muscles are supplied in segments.

cards.front: What does the notochord do, and what is left of it in an adult?
cards.back: It signals the ectoderm above it to form the neural plate; its remnant is the nucleus pulposus of each intervertebral disc.
cards.why: The notochord is the embryo’s first body axis and patterns the tissues around it, but it does not become the vertebrae.

cards.front: When does the neural tube close, and why does folic acid timing matter?
cards.back: From about day 22 to day 28 after fertilization, often before a pregnancy is known.
cards.why: A lack of folic acid while the tube closes can leave it open, so folic acid must be taken before pregnancy is recognized.

cards.front: Amnion vs chorion: what does each form from?
cards.back: Amnion: epiblast. Chorion: trophoblast lined with mesoderm.
cards.why: The amnion comes from the embryo’s own disc; the chorion is the outer layer of the blastocyst.

cards.front: Amnion vs chorion: position and later role?
cards.back: Amnion: inner, around the fluid, next to the embryo. Chorion: outermost, next to the endometrium, and forms the embryo’s side of the exchange organ.
cards.why: By about the third month the growing amnion presses against the chorion and they fuse into the sac that breaks when the waters break.

cards.front: What does a human yolk sac do, since it holds no yolk?
cards.back: Makes the first blood cells and vessels, gives rise to the cells that become gametes, and forms part of the gut lining.
cards.why: Its wall is the first site of blood formation in week 3, and part of it is pinched into the body when the embryo folds.

cards.front: Where does amniotic fluid come from late in pregnancy?
cards.back: Mostly fetal urine. The kidneys start adding urine at about week 9 after fertilization, and it becomes the main source in the second half of pregnancy; the fetus also swallows the fluid.
cards.why: Early on it is water from maternal plasma; once the kidneys work, their urine becomes the main source.

cards.front: When is an embryo most easily harmed, and why?
cards.back: Weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization, while the organs are forming.
cards.why: An exposure can disrupt an organ as it forms and leave a major structural defect.

cards.front: What does the apical ectodermal ridge do?
cards.back: Releases growth factors that keep the mesoderm under it dividing, so the limb grows from its tip, body end first.
cards.why: Removing the ridge early leaves only the upper limb; removing it later leaves out only the fingers.

cards.front: How are fingers and toes freed from the paddle-shaped limb?
cards.back: The tissue between them dies by apoptosis in weeks 6 to 8.
cards.why: If those cells do not die, the digits stay joined.

cards.front: What two tissues make the placenta?
cards.back: The chorion with its villi (fetal part) and the remodeled endometrium (maternal part).
cards.why: The villi grow into the endometrium at the implantation site; the two tissues grow together into one organ.

cards.front: Why does blood flow to the placenta rise so much during pregnancy?
cards.back: Cytotrophoblast cells replace the smooth muscle of the spiral arteries, turning them into wide tubes that cannot constrict.
cards.why: Wider, floppy arteries have far lower resistance, so flow into the intervillous space can rise many times over.

cards.front: Do fetal and maternal blood mix in the placenta?
cards.back: Normally no: fetal blood stays in villus capillaries, and maternal blood bathes the villi from outside.
cards.why: The placental barrier separates them, although small numbers of fetal red cells leak across, especially at delivery.

cards.front: What are the layers of the placental barrier?
cards.back: Syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast (patchy later), villus connective tissue, and fetal capillary endothelium.
cards.why: These layers lie between maternal blood in the intervillous space and fetal blood in the villus capillary.

cards.front: Why does the placental barrier get better at diffusion as pregnancy goes on?
cards.back: It gets thinner (down to 2 to 4 micrometers) and larger (about 12 square meters).
cards.why: Diffusion rate rises with area and falls with distance, so a larger, thinner barrier moves gases faster.

cards.front: Crossing the placenta by simple diffusion: examples?
cards.back: Oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, alcohol, nicotine, steroid hormones and many drugs.
cards.why: Small or fat-soluble molecules pass through the lipid of the membranes, down their own gradients.

cards.front: How does glucose cross the placenta?
cards.back: By facilitated diffusion on carrier proteins, down its gradient from mother to fetus.
cards.why: No ATP is used, so fetal glucose follows maternal glucose.

cards.front: Which substances are actively transported to the fetus?
cards.back: Amino acids, calcium and iron.
cards.why: They are pumped to the fetus against their gradients by carrier proteins driven by ATP or the sodium gradient.

cards.front: How does IgG reach the fetus, and why does IgM not?
cards.back: IgG is carried across in vesicles by receptor proteins on the syncytiotrophoblast; IgM is too large and has no such carrier.
cards.why: Receptor-mediated endocytosis moves IgG, mostly in the last three months, giving the newborn passive immunity.

cards.front: Name substances that do not cross the placenta in useful amounts.
cards.back: Most proteins, including insulin and IgM; heparin; blood cells.
cards.why: They are too large or too charged to pass the barrier, and they have no carrier.

cards.front: Why is heparin, not warfarin, used as a blood thinner in pregnancy?
cards.back: Heparin is large and highly charged and does not cross the placenta; warfarin is small and does.
cards.why: The barrier sorts by size, charge and lipid solubility, not by safety.

cards.front: Fetal blood leaves the placenta with a PO2 of only about 30 mm Hg. How does it still carry plenty of oxygen?
cards.back: Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly (about 80% saturated at 30 mm Hg), the double Bohr effect, and a high hemoglobin concentration.
cards.why: Each feature raises the oxygen fetal blood holds at a low partial pressure.

cards.front: What is the double Bohr effect?
cards.back: As fetal blood loses carbon dioxide its curve shifts left and it loads more oxygen; as maternal blood gains it, its curve shifts right and it unloads more.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide moving from fetus to mother helps oxygen move the other way.

cards.front: Umbilical arteries vs umbilical vein: how many, and what does each carry?
cards.back: Two arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta; one vein carries oxygen-rich blood to the fetus.
cards.why: Arteries and veins are named for direction relative to the heart, not for oxygen content.

cards.front: When does hCG peak on the clinical count, and why does its fall do no harm?
cards.back: Around week 10; by then the placenta makes enough progesterone itself.
cards.why: The placenta takes over progesterone production from about weeks 7 to 9, so the corpus luteum is no longer needed.

cards.front: Why can the placenta not make estrogens on its own?
cards.back: It lacks enzymes to build them from cholesterol, so it converts an androgen made by the fetal adrenal cortex.
cards.why: The fetus and placenta make estrogens together; the main one is the weak estrogen estriol.

cards.front: What does hPL do in the mother?
cards.back: Together with placental growth hormone, progesterone and cortisol, it makes her cells less responsive to insulin, leaving more glucose for the fetus.
cards.why: hPL is made in proportion to the syncytiotrophoblast’s mass, so it climbs as the placenta grows.

cards.front: Where does relaxin come from in human pregnancy, and what does it mainly do?
cards.back: Mostly the corpus luteum, peaking in the first 12 weeks; it relaxes blood vessels and helps raise kidney blood flow.
cards.why: The pelvic-loosening role comes mainly from other mammals. For your exam: “relaxin from the placenta loosens the pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix.”

cards.front: What is the classic result of placental insufficiency?
cards.back: A small baby with too little amniotic fluid.
cards.why: Less oxygen and glucose slow growth, and blood redirected away from the fetal kidneys means less urine.

cards.front: Embryonic vs fetal period: when?
cards.back: Embryonic: weeks 1 to 8 after fertilization (to about week 10 on the clinical count). Fetal: week 9 after fertilization to birth.
cards.why: The two counts differ by about two weeks, because clinicians start at the last menstrual period.

cards.front: Embryonic vs fetal period: main process?
cards.back: Embryonic: forming the organs from the germ layers. Fetal: growth and maturation of organs already formed.
cards.why: Every organ system is present by the end of week 8 after fertilization; the fetus then gains about a thousandfold in weight.

cards.front: Embryonic vs fetal period: size at the end of each?
cards.back: Embryonic: about 3 cm and a few grams. Fetal: about 50 cm and about 3.4 kg at term.
cards.why: The fetal period is mostly growth, so the change in size is huge.

cards.front: Embryonic vs fetal period: effect of a harmful exposure?
cards.back: Embryonic: major structural defects most likely. Fetal: poor growth, loss of function or smaller defects; the brain stays vulnerable.
cards.why: Organs are formed in the embryonic period; later exposures act on organs that already exist.

cards.front: Where are the trimester boundaries?
cards.back: First: to the end of week 13. Second: weeks 14 to 27. Third: week 28 to birth.
cards.why: Clinicians divide the roughly 40 weeks into three parts of about three months each.

cards.front: What is quickening, and when does it happen?
cards.back: The mother first feeling the fetus move, around weeks 16 to 20.
cards.why: The fetus moves from weeks 10 to 13, but the mother cannot feel it until it is larger; later pregnancies notice it a little earlier.

cards.front: What sets the edge of viability at about weeks 22 to 24?
cards.back: The lungs reach the stage where gas exchange first becomes possible.
cards.why: Respiratory bronchioles and close capillaries form in the canalicular stage; before that, no gas exchange is possible.

cards.front: What counts as term?
cards.back: Week 37 to just under week 42 of pregnancy.
cards.why: A full-term pregnancy is about 40 weeks on the clinical count; birth before 37 weeks is preterm.

cards.compare: Regions of the embryonic heart tube
cards.front: Heart tube: what do the truncus arteriosus and bulbus cordis become?
cards.back: Truncus arteriosus: the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Bulbus cordis: most of the right ventricle and the outflow parts of both ventricles.
cards.why: They are the outflow end of the tube, at the head end, so they form the exits of the heart.

cards.compare: Regions of the embryonic heart tube
cards.front: Heart tube: what do the primitive ventricle and primitive atrium become?
cards.back: Primitive ventricle: most of the left ventricle. Primitive atrium: the front parts of both atria, including the auricles.
cards.why: They lie in the middle of the tube, between the outflow and inflow ends.

cards.compare: Regions of the embryonic heart tube
cards.front: Heart tube: what does the sinus venosus become?
cards.back: The smooth back wall of the right atrium, the coronary sinus and the region of the SA node.
cards.why: The sinus venosus is the inflow end, where the veins drain, so it forms the receiving parts of the right atrium.

cards.front: Why is the foramen ovale a one-way valve?
cards.back: The thin septum primum lies against the opening in the stiff septum secundum from the left side, so it can swing only toward the left atrium.
cards.why: Higher right pressure pushes it open; higher left pressure presses it shut against the septum secundum.

cards.front: Why does blood cross the foramen ovale from right to left before birth?
cards.back: Little blood returns from the lungs, so the left atrium fills at low pressure, while the right atrium receives venous return from the body and placenta.
cards.why: Blood flows down the pressure gradient, from the higher-pressure right atrium to the left.

cards.front: Name the three fetal shunts and what each bypasses.
cards.back: Ductus venosus: the liver. Foramen ovale: the right ventricle and lungs. Ductus arteriosus: the lungs.
cards.why: Before birth the placenta, not the lungs, exchanges gases, so blood is routed around organs not yet working.

cards.front: What keeps the ductus arteriosus open before birth?
cards.back: Low oxygen in fetal blood and prostaglandins from the placenta and the ductus wall.
cards.why: Both keep its smooth muscle relaxed; this is why prostaglandin blockers are avoided late in pregnancy.

cards.front: Which fetal organs get the best-oxygenated blood, and why?
cards.back: The heart and brain: the oxygen-rich stream crosses to the left heart and enters the first branches of the aorta.
cards.why: The ductus arteriosus joins the aorta after the arteries to the head and arms, so oxygen-poor blood enters downstream.

cards.front: Vasculogenesis vs angiogenesis?
cards.back: Vasculogenesis: new vessels from scratch, from mesoderm in blood islands. Angiogenesis: new vessels sprouting from existing ones.
cards.why: The first network forms by vasculogenesis; after that, most new vessels form by angiogenesis.

cards.front: Where are blood cells made before birth, in order?
cards.back: Yolk sac, then liver (with the spleen) from about week 6 after fertilization, then bone marrow from about the fifth month.
cards.why: Blood formation follows the growing body; by birth the marrow is the main site.

cards.front: Lung stages: pseudoglandular and canalicular?
cards.back: Pseudoglandular (to about week 17): all conducting airways form. Canalicular (weeks 16 to 26): respiratory bronchioles, close capillaries, type II cells.
cards.why: Conducting airways branch first; gas-exchange parts grow at their ends later.

cards.front: Lung stages: saccular and alveolar?
cards.back: Saccular (weeks 24 to 36): thin air sacs and rising surfactant. Alveolar (week 36 into childhood): true alveoli, mostly after birth.
cards.why: Surfactant is usually enough only by weeks 34 to 36, and most alveoli are made in the first years of life.

cards.front: Why does the right lung have three lobes and the left two?
cards.back: The right lung bud divides into three and the left into two.
cards.why: The lobes are set by how the two lung buds first divide at the end of week 4.

cards.front: Why do the fetal lungs need fluid and breathing movements?
cards.back: The stretch they give is needed for the lungs to grow.
cards.why: With too little amniotic fluid, or pressure on the chest, the lungs stay small.

cards.front: Anti-Müllerian hormone vs testosterone in the male embryo?
cards.back: Anti-Müllerian hormone (Sertoli cells) removes the paramesonephric ducts. Testosterone (Leydig cells) keeps the mesonephric ducts.
cards.why: Two hormones from the testis decide the two pairs of ducts separately.

cards.front: What happens to the ducts in an embryo with ovaries?
cards.back: The paramesonephric ducts survive as uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina; the mesonephric ducts break down.
cards.why: There is no anti-Müllerian hormone to remove the first pair and almost no testosterone to keep the second.

cards.front: Is the ovary simply the “default” when there is no Y chromosome?
cards.back: No. The ducts and external genitalia develop as female without gonadal hormones, but forming and keeping an ovary needs its own active genes.
cards.why: Switching some of those genes off in adult female mice turns ovary cells toward testis cells. For your exam, “female is the default” may still be expected.

cards.front: Name the male and female structures that grow from the same starting tissue.
cards.back: Penis and clitoris; scrotum and labia majora; testes and ovaries.
cards.why: With DHT the bump grows into a penis and the swellings fuse into a scrotum; without it they become the clitoris and labia majora.

cards.front: Atrial vs ventricular septal defect: which chambers are overloaded?
cards.back: Atrial: the right atrium, right ventricle and lungs. Ventricular: the lungs and, as that blood returns, the left atrium and left ventricle.
cards.why: After birth left pressures are higher, so blood crosses left to right and recirculates through the lungs.

cards.front: Why is a patent foramen ovale usually harmless, and when is it not?
cards.back: Higher left atrial pressure keeps the flap shut; but when right pressure briefly rises, as in straining, a clot from a vein can cross and cause a stroke.
cards.why: The flap never sealed but is still pressed closed by the usual pressure difference.

cards.front: What three things decide whether an exposure harms development?
cards.back: Timing, dose and genes.
cards.why: Weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization are the most sensitive, more exposure usually harms more, and pregnancies differ in how they handle an agent.

cards.front: Rubella, alcohol and folic acid lack: main effects on development?
cards.back: Rubella: cataracts, deafness, heart defects. Alcohol: fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. Folic acid lack: neural tube defects.
cards.why: Each acts on the tissues forming at the time of exposure.

cards.front: What three drivers explain most maternal changes in pregnancy?
cards.back: Placental hormones, the growing uterus, and the demands of the fetus and placenta.
cards.why: Hormones relax smooth muscle and change metabolism; the uterus presses on nearby organs; the fetus draws on her blood.

cards.front: Where is the fundus at 12, 20 and 36 weeks?
cards.back: Just above the pubic symphysis at 12, near the navel at 20, near the bottom of the sternum at 36.
cards.why: Between weeks 20 and 36, the distance from the pubic symphysis to the fundus in centimeters roughly equals the weeks.

cards.front: Why does hemoglobin concentration fall in a healthy pregnancy?
cards.back: Plasma rises 40 to 50% but red cell mass only 20 to 30%: dilutional anemia.
cards.why: The body has more red cells than before, but each liter holds fewer of them.

cards.front: How much does cardiac output rise in pregnancy, and what rises first?
cards.back: About 30 to 50%, mostly by weeks 20 to 24; heart rate rises first, stroke volume a few weeks later.
cards.why: Stroke volume waits for the growing blood volume to raise venous return and preload.

cards.front: Why does blood pressure dip in mid-pregnancy despite a higher cardiac output?
cards.back: Total peripheral resistance falls by about a quarter to a third. Pressure is output times resistance, and 1.4 × 0.7 ≈ 0.98, so the fall in resistance slightly outweighs the rise in output.
cards.why: Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times resistance, so the two changes nearly cancel.

cards.front: Why is a pregnant patient tilted to the left?
cards.back: From about week 20 the uterus can press on the inferior vena cava when she lies on her back.
cards.why: Less venous return lowers stroke volume, cardiac output and blood pressure; tilting left lifts the uterus off the vein.

cards.front: Why does PaCO2 fall to about 30 mm Hg in pregnancy?
cards.back: Progesterone makes the brainstem’s chemoreceptors more sensitive to carbon dioxide, so ventilation rises more than metabolism needs.
cards.why: Minute ventilation rises 40 to 50% while oxygen use rises only 20 to 30%; the kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate.

cards.front: What happens to functional residual capacity in pregnancy, and why does it matter?
cards.back: It falls by about 20%, so she has less oxygen in reserve.
cards.why: The raised diaphragm lowers expiratory reserve and residual volume; her blood oxygen falls faster if she stops breathing.

cards.front: Why can a “normal” serum creatinine be worrying in pregnancy?
cards.back: GFR rises about 50%, so creatinine normally falls; a value normal outside pregnancy may mean kidney trouble.
cards.why: Faster filtration clears creatinine faster, lowering the expected level.

cards.front: Why are urinary infections treated promptly in pregnancy?
cards.back: Progesterone relaxes the ureters and the uterus presses on them, so urine flows slowly and bacteria climb to the kidney more easily.
cards.why: Slower flow gives bacteria in the bladder more chance to ascend.

cards.front: Why are heartburn and constipation common in pregnancy?
cards.back: Progesterone relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter and slows movement through the gut.
cards.why: The uterus also pushes up on the stomach, and slower gut contents lose more water.

cards.front: Why is the mother insulin resistant in the second half of pregnancy?
cards.back: hPL, placental growth hormone, progesterone and cortisol make her cells less responsive to insulin.
cards.why: Her glucose stays higher after meals, leaving more to cross to the fetus; her beta cells secrete two to three times more insulin.

cards.front: Why is fasting glucose lower in pregnancy even though after-meal glucose is higher?
cards.back: The fetus draws glucose from her blood constantly, between meals as well.
cards.why: After an overnight fast she also starts making ketone bodies sooner.

cards.front: Placenta previa vs placental abruption: pain and bleeding?
cards.back: Previa: usually painless, bright red bleeding seen outside. Abruption: usually painful with a tender, hard uterus; dark bleeding that may be hidden.
cards.why: In previa the low placenta tears as the lower uterus stretches; in abruption a normally placed placenta separates, and blood can collect behind it.

cards.front: Placenta previa vs placental abruption: what is each, and common links?
cards.back: Previa: a placenta over or near the cervix; linked to earlier cesarean delivery and several pregnancies. Abruption: early separation; linked to high blood pressure, trauma, cocaine and smoking.
cards.why: Previa is about where the placenta implanted; abruption is about a normally placed placenta coming away.

cards.front: Why is a digital examination of the cervix avoided until the placenta’s position is known?
cards.back: If the placenta lies over the cervix, the examination can set off heavy bleeding.
cards.why: An ultrasound first shows where the placenta is.

cards.front: Why is an ectopic pregnancy in a uterine tube dangerous?
cards.back: The thin tube wall cannot stretch, so as the trophoblast invades and the embryo grows, the tube can rupture and bleed into the abdomen.
cards.why: Scarring from earlier infection is the most common cause, by slowing the embryo so it implants in the tube.

cards.front: Where does preeclampsia begin, and what is its only cure?
cards.back: In the placenta, with shallow spiral artery remodeling early in pregnancy; delivering the placenta.
cards.why: The stressed placenta releases factors that damage the mother’s endothelium everywhere, raising pressure and letting protein leak into the urine.

cards.front: Why can the newborn of a mother with gestational diabetes become hypoglycemic?
cards.back: Cutting the cord ends the mother’s glucose supply, but the baby’s pancreas is still secreting extra insulin.
cards.why: High glucose crossing the placenta, without the mother’s insulin, made the fetal pancreas secrete more insulin.

cards.front: False vs true labor: timing and strength?
cards.back: False: irregular, no steady pattern, stays the same or fades. True: regular, gaps shorten, grows stronger and longer.
cards.why: True labor contractions build on each other as the uterus contracts as one unit.

cards.front: False vs true labor: the deciding difference?
cards.back: Its effect on the cervix: true labor progressively thins and opens it; false labor does not.
cards.why: Pain is not the test; a clinician checks the cervix to decide.

cards.front: False vs true labor: effect of walking or rest, and where it is felt?
cards.back: False: often eases or stops, felt mostly at the front. True: continues whatever she does, often starts in the back and wraps around.
cards.why: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular tightenings; true labor has its own momentum.

cards.front: Name three changes that ready the myometrium in the last weeks.
cards.back: More gap junctions, about a hundredfold more oxytocin receptor proteins, and more prostaglandins.
cards.why: Gap junctions spread each action potential so the uterus contracts as one unit, and more receptor proteins magnify the response to oxytocin.

cards.front: What is thought to set labor off in humans, and what is the exam answer?
cards.back: Functional progesterone withdrawal (the uterus stops responding to progesterone) and rising placental CRH. For your exam: a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio.
cards.why: In women, blood progesterone does not fall before labor; the falling-progesterone story comes from sheep and some other mammals.

cards.front: What is the Ferguson reflex?
cards.back: Stretch of the cervix triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary through a nerve-to-pituitary reflex.
cards.why: It is the stretch-to-oxytocin half of the labor positive feedback loop; oxytocin then strengthens the contractions that stretch the cervix more.

cards.front: What ends the labor positive feedback loop?
cards.back: Birth: the stretch on the cervix stops, so the afferent signals stop.
cards.why: A positive feedback loop does not settle at a set point; only an outside event can break it.

cards.front: Is oxytocin needed for labor to start?
cards.back: No. It strengthens contractions through positive feedback, but labor can start and progress without it.
cards.why: Mice lacking oxytocin give birth normally, and women with very little oxytocin have had normal labors.

cards.front: Effacement vs dilation?
cards.back: Effacement: thinning and shortening of the cervix, in percent. Dilation: how wide the opening is, in centimeters (10 cm is full).
cards.why: In a first labor the cervix usually thins before it opens; in later labors the two often happen together.

cards.front: How does each contraction make lasting progress?
cards.back: Retraction: the upper uterine muscle relaxes without returning to full length, so the wall shortens and pulls the cervix up around the head.
cards.why: Contractions are strongest in the fundus, so the net push is downward, and the shortened wall keeps the fetus low.

cards.front: Stage 1 of labor: what defines it?
cards.back: The dilation stage: from the start of true labor to full dilation (10 cm), with a latent and an active phase.
cards.why: It is the longest stage, often 12 hours or more in a first labor.

cards.front: When does the active phase begin, and why did the number change?
cards.back: At about 6 cm; older texts used 3 to 4 cm.
cards.why: Studies of modern labors showed many women open slowly until about 6 cm.

cards.front: Stage 2 of labor: what defines it?
cards.back: The expulsion stage: from full dilation to the birth of the baby.
cards.why: Pushing adds voluntary force: she closes her glottis and contracts her abdominal muscles.

cards.front: Stage 3 of labor: what defines it?
cards.back: The placental stage: from the birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes, usually 5 to 30 minutes.
cards.why: The shrinking uterus shears the placenta off its wall, and further contractions push it out.

cards.front: What stops the bleeding from the placental site?
cards.back: Firm contraction of the crisscrossing myometrial fibers pinches the vessels shut; clotting then seals them.
cards.why: This is why a soft, relaxed uterus (atony) causes most postpartum hemorrhage.

cards.front: Why is oxytocin given at birth and the fundus rubbed if the uterus feels soft?
cards.back: Both make the myometrium contract and clamp the placental-bed vessels.
cards.why: Uterine atony leaves the vessels open; contraction is the main brake on bleeding.

cards.front: Why is episiotomy no longer routine?
cards.back: Trials showed routine cutting does not prevent severe tears or heal better than a natural tear.
cards.why: It is now used only for a specific reason, such as speeding the birth of a baby in distress.

cards.front: Why wait 30 to 60 seconds before clamping the cord?
cards.back: More blood moves from the placenta into the baby, improving its iron stores.
cards.why: The extra red cells are later broken down and their iron kept.

cards.front: How fast does the uterus involute?
cards.back: From about 1 kg after birth to under 100 g by six weeks; the fundus drops about 1 cm a day.
cards.why: Muscle cells shrink rather than disappear, breaking down their own proteins as estrogen and progesterone fall.

cards.front: How does lochia change after birth?
cards.back: Red for 3 or 4 days, pinkish-brown to about day 10, then yellowish-white, ending by four to six weeks.
cards.why: It is blood, mucus and shed lining as the placental site heals; heavy bright red bleeding after the first days is not normal.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: where does blood pick up oxygen?
cards.back: Fetal: the placenta. Newborn: the lungs.
cards.why: Before birth the lungs are fluid-filled; after the first breaths they take over gas exchange.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: pulmonary and systemic resistance?
cards.back: Fetal: pulmonary high, systemic low. Newborn: pulmonary low, systemic higher.
cards.why: Expanded, oxygenated lungs relax their vessels, and clamping the cord removes the low-resistance placenta.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: which atrium has the higher pressure, and what happens to the foramen ovale?
cards.back: Fetal: right; the foramen ovale is open, right to left. Newborn: left; it is pressed shut and later becomes the fossa ovalis.
cards.why: More blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium after birth, and none arrives from the umbilical vein.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: the ductus arteriosus?
cards.back: Fetal: open, pulmonary trunk to aorta. Newborn: constricts in 1 to 3 days and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
cards.why: Rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2 make its smooth muscle contract.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: the ductus venosus?
cards.back: Fetal: open, umbilical vein to inferior vena cava. Newborn: closes in 1 to 2 weeks and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
cards.why: Once the cord is clamped, no blood flows in the umbilical vein to keep it open.

cards.front: Fetal vs newborn circulation: how are the two circuits arranged?
cards.back: Fetal: partly side by side, sharing blood through the shunts. Newborn: in series, right heart to lungs, left heart to body.
cards.why: Closing the shunts forces all blood through both ventricles in turn.

cards.front: How do the lungs start to drain before birth, and why do babies born by planned cesarean breathe fast more often?
cards.back: Rising epinephrine and cortisol in labor switch the airway cells from secreting chloride to absorbing sodium, and water follows out of the airspaces.
cards.why: Without labor, much of this switch is missed and fluid is left in the lungs.

cards.front: Why is the first breath the hardest, and what makes later ones easier?
cards.back: Surface tension holds the collapsed, liquid-lined alveoli shut; once open, surfactant keeps them from collapsing completely.
cards.why: Some air stays after each breath, so the lungs’ resting volume builds and later breaths take far less work.

cards.front: Patent ductus arteriosus after birth: which way does blood flow, and what are the signs?
cards.back: Aorta to pulmonary trunk (left to right); bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure and a continuous “machinery” murmur.
cards.why: Blood running off into the lungs during diastole lowers diastolic pressure.

cards.front: Indomethacin vs a prostaglandin infusion for the ductus arteriosus?
cards.back: Indomethacin or ibuprofen closes it; a prostaglandin infusion keeps it open.
cards.why: Prostaglandin keeps the ductus relaxed, so blocking its synthesis closes it, and giving it holds the ductus open in babies who depend on it.

cards.front: What causes respiratory distress syndrome, and what are its three treatments?
cards.back: A shortage of surfactant; a glucocorticoid to the mother before birth, continuous positive airway pressure, and surfactant given into the trachea.
cards.why: Each treatment follows from the mechanism: speed surfactant production, hold alveoli open, or replace surfactant.

cards.front: Why does a baby with respiratory distress grunt?
cards.back: Breathing out against a partly closed glottis keeps some pressure in the airways at the end of each breath, holding alveoli open.
cards.why: Continuous positive airway pressure does the same thing, better.

cards.front: What are the five Apgar signs?
cards.back: Appearance (color), pulse, grimace (response), activity (tone) and respiration.
cards.why: Each is scored 0 to 2 at 1 and 5 minutes; 7 to 10 is reassuring.

cards.front: Why do most healthy babies score 8 or 9 at 1 minute, and what are the score’s limits?
cards.back: Their hands and feet are still blue. Resuscitation never waits for the score, and a low score alone does not prove oxygen starvation.
cards.why: Prematurity and drugs given to the mother can also lower the score.

cards.front: What is meconium, and when is it passed?
cards.back: A sticky, dark green-black paste of swallowed fluid, shed cells, mucus, bile and fine hair; nearly all term babies pass it within 48 hours.
cards.why: Failure to pass it can signal a blocked or poorly working intestine.

cards.front: Why are newborns given vitamin K at birth?
cards.back: Little vitamin K crosses the placenta and breast milk contains little, so stores are low and bleeding is a risk.
cards.why: Vitamin K is needed to make several clotting factors.

cards.front: How does a newborn make heat, and at what cost?
cards.back: Nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat, driven by norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves; it uses oxygen and glucose fast.
cards.why: A cold baby can become short of oxygen, low in glucose and acidotic, so newborns are dried and kept warm at once.

cards.front: Why do newborns lose heat so easily?
cards.back: A large surface for their size, wet skin, little insulating fat and weak shivering.
cards.why: They have about three times as much skin per kilogram as an adult.

cards.front: Prolactin vs oxytocin in lactation: what does each do?
cards.back: Prolactin makes milk for the next feed. Oxytocin ejects the milk already made, now.
cards.why: Prolactin acts on the alveolar cells; oxytocin on the myoepithelial cells around them.

cards.front: Prolactin vs oxytocin: where does each come from, and what controls its release?
cards.back: Prolactin: anterior pituitary, held back mainly by dopamine. Oxytocin: posterior pituitary, released by hypothalamic neurons.
cards.why: Suckling lowers dopamine, so prolactin surges, and activates the oxytocin neurons, so milk is ejected.

cards.front: How can a mother’s mind affect let-down?
cards.back: Hearing her baby cry can trigger it (conditioned); pain, fear and stress inhibit oxytocin release.
cards.why: The hypothalamus is part of the reflex, so the brain can start or stop it.

cards.front: How does this course classify the milk ejection reflex, and what may an exam say?
cards.back: A neuroendocrine reflex (nerve signal in, hormone out). For your exam: it is often called positive feedback.
cards.why: The response does not make the stimulus itself grow the way contractions grow cervical stretch; it ends when the baby stops feeding.

cards.front: Why does milk come in only 30 to 72 hours after birth?
cards.back: High progesterone blocks prolactin’s action until the placenta is delivered and progesterone falls.
cards.why: A piece of placenta left behind keeps progesterone up and delays the milk.

cards.front: What is the main way to raise milk supply?
cards.back: Frequent, effective feeding.
cards.why: Milk left in a full breast slows production locally, while emptying the breast often speeds it, breast by breast.

cards.front: Colostrum vs mature milk: protein, fat and lactose?
cards.back: Colostrum: high protein, much of it antibodies; lower fat and lactose. Mature milk: about 1% protein, 4% fat and 7% lactose.
cards.why: Colostrum is thick and yellowish; mature milk thin and bluish-white.

cards.front: Colostrum vs mature milk: when and how much?
cards.back: Colostrum: first 2 to 4 days, a few teaspoons per feed. Mature milk: from about 2 weeks, about 750 to 800 mL a day.
cards.why: Colostrum changes gradually into mature milk over about two weeks.

cards.front: Colostrum vs mature milk: secretory IgA, and what does it do?
cards.back: Very high in colostrum, lower but present throughout in mature milk; it coats the baby’s gut lining and blocks microbes from attaching.
cards.why: Plasma cells switched on in the mother’s gut and airways travel to the breast, so her milk’s IgA targets the family’s microbes.

cards.front: Foremilk vs hindmilk: why does milk get fattier through a feed?
cards.back: Fat droplets stick to the walls of the alveoli and small ducts and are carried out only as the breast empties.
cards.why: Foremilk and hindmilk are not two different milks; the fat content climbs through the feed.

cards.front: Genotype vs phenotype?
cards.back: Genotype: the alleles a person carries. Phenotype: what is expressed and can be observed or measured.
cards.why: The environment acts on phenotype too: a baby with the PKU genotype fed a low-phenylalanine diet develops normally.

cards.front: Homozygous vs heterozygous?
cards.back: Homozygous: two copies of the same allele (AA or aa). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Aa).
cards.why: You carry two copies of every autosomal gene, one from each parent.

cards.front: Why is the cystic fibrosis allele recessive?
cards.back: It makes no working chloride channel, and one working copy makes enough channel for normal function.
cards.why: Dominance is usually about protein amounts, not one allele overpowering another.

cards.front: Why is the Huntington disease allele dominant?
cards.back: Its abnormal protein slowly damages neurons, and one copy is enough to cause harm.
cards.why: A dominant allele shows its effect in the heterozygote as well as the homozygote.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, codominant, X-linked recessive: copies needed to show the phenotype?
cards.back: Dominant: one. Recessive: two. Codominant: each allele shows whenever present. X-linked recessive: one in males, two in females.
cards.why: A male has only one X, so nothing masks an X-linked allele in him.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked recessive: what is the heterozygote like?
cards.back: Dominant: affected. Recessive: healthy carrier. Codominant: shows both alleles. X-linked recessive: a female is usually a healthy carrier.
cards.why: Each pattern is defined by what happens when two different alleles meet.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: Typical parents of an affected child: dominant, recessive, X-linked recessive?
cards.back: Dominant: one affected parent. Recessive: two unaffected carriers. X-linked recessive: a carrier mother and an unaffected father.
cards.why: The parents’ phenotypes follow from how many copies each needs to show the trait.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: Risk for each child in the typical family: dominant, recessive, X-linked recessive?
cards.back: Dominant: 1 in 2. Recessive: 1 in 4. X-linked recessive: 1 in 2 sons affected, 1 in 2 daughters carriers.
cards.why: Each comes straight from the Punnett square for the typical cross.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: Which pattern never passes from father to son, and why?
cards.back: X-linked: a father gives his sons his Y, not his X.
cards.why: Every daughter of an affected father gets his X, so all are carriers of an X-linked recessive allele.

cards.compare: Dominant vs recessive vs codominant vs X-linked
cards.front: One example each: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, codominant, X-linked recessive?
cards.back: Huntington disease; cystic fibrosis; ABO type AB; hemophilia A.
cards.why: The examples show one copy causing disease, two copies needed, both alleles showing, and a male-affected pattern.

cards.front: What is the law of segregation, and what explains it?
cards.back: Each gamete carries only one allele of each gene, each with a 1 in 2 chance; homologs separate in anaphase I of meiosis.
cards.why: Mendel inferred it from counting pea plants; meiosis supplies the mechanism.

cards.front: Two carriers have a healthy child. What is the chance that child is a carrier?
cards.back: 2 in 3.
cards.why: Of the three healthy boxes (CC, Cc, Cc), two are carriers; the affected box is already ruled out.

cards.front: Two carriers already have one child with cystic fibrosis. What is the chance for the next child?
cards.back: Still 1 in 4.
cards.why: Gametes are drawn fresh for every pregnancy; one outcome does not change the next.

cards.front: Incomplete dominance vs codominance?
cards.back: Incomplete: the heterozygote is in between (familial hypercholesterolemia). Codominance: both alleles fully shown (ABO type AB).
cards.why: Which pattern you see can depend on the phenotype measured, as sickle cell shows.

cards.front: Sickle cell: codominant, incomplete or recessive?
cards.back: All three, depending on level: molecule (both hemoglobins, codominant), red cell (sickles only in severe oxygen shortage, in between), disease (recessive).
cards.why: Dominance describes a relationship for one phenotype, not a fixed property of an allele.

cards.front: How can two parents have a child with a blood type neither has?
cards.back: An AO parent and a BO parent can have an AB or an OO child.
cards.why: A and B are codominant with each other and both dominant over O, so hidden O alleles can pair up.

cards.front: A carrier mother and an unaffected father: risk for sons and daughters for hemophilia A?
cards.back: Half the sons affected; half the daughters carriers; no daughters affected.
cards.why: A son’s X comes from his mother; a daughter also gets her father’s normal X.

cards.front: Why does height form a bell curve instead of neat groups?
cards.back: It is polygenic: thousands of variants each add or subtract a little, plus the environment.
cards.why: Most people get a mix of “up” and “down” variants that roughly cancel; few get mostly one kind.

cards.front: What causes most trisomy 21, and why does it rise with the mother’s age?
cards.back: Nondisjunction, mostly in the mother’s meiosis I; the proteins holding her oocyte’s paired chromosomes weaken over decades.
cards.why: About 4% of cases are translocations, which do not depend on the mother’s age.

cards.front: Rough trisomy 21 risk at maternal ages 25, 35, 40 and 45?
cards.back: About 1 in 1,200, 1 in 350, 1 in 100 and 1 in 30.
cards.why: The risk climbs steeply after about 35 as the oocyte’s chromosome links fail.

cards.front: Why are extra or missing sex chromosomes tolerated better than extra autosomes?
cards.back: Every X beyond the first is mostly silenced, and the Y carries few genes.
cards.why: A few X genes escape silencing, so their dose still matters, as in the short stature of Turner syndrome.

cards.front: Klinefelter vs Turner syndrome: karyotype and main features?
cards.back: Klinefelter: 47,XXY; small testes, low testosterone, usually infertile. Turner: 45,X; short stature, ovaries that fail early.
cards.why: Turner syndrome is the only survivable monosomy, and even so nearly all 45,X pregnancies miscarry.

cards.front: What is the one idea behind most aging physiology?
cards.back: Resting values are usually kept in range, but reserve, the extra capacity for stress, shrinks (homeostenosis).
cards.why: A stress a young body absorbs can overwhelm an old one even though its resting values were normal.

cards.front: Are dementia, anemia and incontinence normal aging?
cards.back: No: they become common with age but are diseases with their own causes.
cards.why: Normal aging lowers reserve; a disease is a separate process that needs its own explanation and often its own treatment.

cards.front: What causes aging, and which “theories” do exams expect?
cards.back: Many interacting damage processes that outpace repair; for your exam, the free radical theory and telomere shortening.
cards.why: Oxidative damage contributes, but antioxidant supplements have not slowed aging, and beta-carotene raised lung cancer in smokers.

cards.front: Why do telomeres shorten with each division?
cards.back: The end-replication problem: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very tip of one new strand beyond its last primer.
cards.why: Each division loses about 50 to 100 base pairs; most body cells make almost no telomerase to replace them.

cards.front: What is the Hayflick limit, and what sets it?
cards.back: Normal human cells divide only about 40 to 60 times in a dish; it is set largely by telomeres.
cards.why: When a telomere becomes too short, its cap fails and the cell reads the end as damaged DNA.

cards.front: Which cells use telomerase?
cards.back: Germ cells, stem cells a little, and most cancer cells.
cards.why: Telomerase carries its own RNA template and adds repeats back, which is one reason cancer cells can divide without limit.

cards.front: Senescence: protective or harmful?
cards.back: Both: it stops damaged cells from dividing into tumors, but senescent cells release inflammatory cytokines and enzymes that harm the tissue around them.
cards.why: Senescent cells build up with age and feed “inflammaging”; removing them in mice delays many age-related problems.

cards.front: How does bone change with age, and why is loss faster after menopause?
cards.back: Bone mass peaks around 30 and then falls about 0.5 to 1% a year; estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts.
cards.why: Spongy bone, with its large surface, is lost first, so vertebrae and the ends of long bones weaken most.

cards.front: Why does strength fall faster than muscle mass with age?
cards.back: Motor neurons die and motor units become fewer and larger, and fast glycolytic fibers shrink most.
cards.why: Resistance training reverses much of the loss at any age.

cards.front: Why does systolic pressure rise with age while diastolic does not?
cards.back: The aorta stiffens and cannot stretch to absorb each stroke volume, and it stores less energy for recoil in diastole.
cards.why: Pulse pressure widens: isolated systolic hypertension, common in older adults.

cards.front: How does maximum heart rate change with age?
cards.back: It falls by roughly 0.7 to 1 beat per minute each year; one estimate is 208 − (0.7 × age).
cards.why: The SA node loses pacemaker cells and the heart responds less to sympathetic stimulation; resting cardiac output changes little.

cards.front: Why do vaccines work less well in older adults?
cards.back: The thymus shrinks, few new naive T cells are made, and B cell responses weaken.
cards.why: That is why high-dose or boosted influenza vaccines are given after 65.

cards.front: How can pneumonia show up in an older adult without a fever?
cards.back: Fever is often blunted, and the infection may show first as confusion, a fall or loss of appetite.
cards.why: A weaker immune response and less brain reserve change how infections present.

cards.front: Why can plasma creatinine stay normal while GFR falls with age?
cards.back: Less muscle makes less creatinine.
cards.why: GFR falls on average about 1 mL/min a year after 40, which is why eGFR, corrected for age and sex, is used.

cards.front: Why do older adults become dehydrated and hypernatremic quickly?
cards.back: Blunted thirst, less total body water, and kidneys that concentrate urine and conserve sodium less well.
cards.why: A small water loss moves sodium further in a smaller body water pool.

cards.front: Why do doctors “start low and go slow” with drugs in older adults?
cards.back: Lower GFR and liver blood flow clear drugs more slowly, less body water concentrates water-soluble drugs, and more fat stores fat-soluble ones.
cards.why: Many older adults also take several drugs at once.

cards.front: How do the lungs change with age?
cards.back: They lose elastic recoil and the chest wall stiffens; residual volume rises and vital capacity and FEV1 fall.
cards.why: Small airways close earlier in expiration, trapping more air.

cards.front: What slows much of the decline once blamed on age?
cards.back: Regular exercise: aerobic training for oxygen uptake, resistance training for muscle and bone, and balance training against falls.
cards.why: Much of the decline comes from inactivity, so activity preserves reserve at any age.

cards.front: Can a skeletal muscle push?
cards.back: No. A muscle can only shorten and pull; when it stops, it simply stops pulling.
cards.why: Cross-bridges pull thin filaments inward and cannot drive them apart, so reversing a movement takes a muscle on the other side of the joint, or gravity.

cards.front: Origin vs insertion: which one moves?
cards.back: The insertion, on the bone that moves. The origin stays still, usually the proximal attachment.
cards.why: A contracting muscle pulls its insertion toward its origin, because fixators and body weight hold the origin’s bone steady.

cards.front: In a pull-up, which attachment of the elbow-bending muscle moves?
cards.back: The origin: the upper arm and trunk rise toward the fixed forearm, a reverse action.
cards.why: When the usual insertion is held still (hands on a bar), the pull moves the other end. The names still follow the usual case.

cards.front: What is a prime mover (agonist)?
cards.back: The muscle most responsible for a movement.
cards.why: Other muscles may help, but the agonist supplies most of the force for that particular movement.

cards.front: What does the antagonist of a movement do?
cards.back: It produces the opposite movement, and relaxes or brakes while the prime mover works.
cards.why: It lies on the other side of the joint. It often contracts eccentrically at the end of a fast movement so the joint is not jammed.

cards.front: Synergist vs fixator?
cards.back: A synergist helps the prime mover make the movement. A fixator is a synergist that holds a bone still as a stable base.
cards.why: In lifting a glass, the muscles beside the main elbow flexor are synergists; the muscles steadying the scapula are fixators.

cards.front: Is the muscle on the back of the upper arm an agonist or an antagonist?
cards.back: Both: antagonist when you bend the elbow, prime mover when you straighten it.
cards.why: A role belongs to a movement, not to a muscle. Learn “antagonist for elbow flexion”, never just “antagonist”.

cards.front: You lower a heavy glass slowly. Which muscle controls it?
cards.back: The elbow-bending muscle on the front of the arm, lengthening while it works (an eccentric contraction).
cards.why: Gravity supplies the movement; the flexor pays out slowly to brake it. Its antagonist does not push the arm down.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: In a body lever, what are the bar, fulcrum, effort and load?
cards.back: Bar: a bone. Fulcrum: the joint. Effort: the muscle’s pull at its insertion. Load: the body part plus anything it holds.
cards.why: Mapping each part is the first step before naming the class or doing the arithmetic.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: What sits in the middle of a first-, second- and third-class lever?
cards.back: First: fulcrum. Second: load. Third: effort (“1-2-3, F-L-E”).
cards.why: The class is set only by which of the three lies between the other two.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: Give two body examples of a first-class lever.
cards.back: Tipping the head back at the atlanto-occipital joint; straightening the elbow.
cards.why: In both the joint lies between the muscle’s pull (behind it) and the load (in front of it), like a seesaw.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: What is the textbook body example of a second-class lever?
cards.back: Rising onto your toes: fulcrum at the ball of the foot, load through the ankle, effort from the calf at the heel.
cards.why: Some biomechanists treat the ankle as the pivot and call it first-class. For your exam, give second-class.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: Give two body examples of a third-class lever.
cards.back: Bending the elbow; closing the jaw.
cards.why: In both the muscle attaches between the joint and the load, so the effort is in the middle. Most body levers are this kind.

cards.compare: First vs second vs third class levers
cards.front: What does a third-class lever favor, and what does a second-class lever favor?
cards.back: Third: speed and range (the muscle pulls harder than the load). Second: force (a smaller pull moves a bigger load).
cards.why: In a third-class lever the effort arm is always shorter than the load arm; in a second-class lever it is always longer.

cards.front: What is mechanical advantage?
cards.back: Effort arm ÷ load arm.
cards.why: Above 1, the muscle can move more than it pulls; below 1, it must pull harder than the load but moves the load farther and faster.

cards.front: You hold 40 N in the hand, 32 cm from the elbow; the flexor inserts 4 cm from it. How hard must it pull?
cards.back: 320 N (mechanical advantage 0.125).
cards.why: Effort × 4 cm = 40 N × 32 cm = 1,280 N·cm, so effort = 320 N: eight times the weight. In return, the hand moves 8 cm for every 1 cm the insertion moves.

cards.front: Why are most body levers third-class, if they make muscles pull so hard?
cards.back: A fiber shortens only about a third of its length, and slowly; inserting near the joint turns that short pull into a long, fast sweep of the hand or foot.
cards.why: The cost is huge forces in muscles and tendons, one reason tendons tear under heavy lifting.

cards.front: Parallel vs pennate: which way do the fascicles run?
cards.back: Parallel: in line with the pull. Pennate: at an angle to a central tendon, like the barbs of a feather.
cards.why: That one difference in direction sets fiber length, how many fibers fit and the force–range trade-off.

cards.front: Parallel vs pennate: which is stronger for its size, and which shortens farther?
cards.back: Pennate is stronger for its size. Parallel shortens farther and faster.
cards.why: Short, angled fibers pack more fibers (more cross-bridges) into the same volume; long fibers have more sarcomeres in series, so they shorten farther.

cards.front: Unipennate vs bipennate vs multipennate?
cards.back: Fascicles on one side of the tendon; on both sides; converging on several tendons from many angles.
cards.why: The thick muscle that caps the shoulder is the notes’ multipennate example.

cards.front: Strap vs fusiform muscle?
cards.back: Both are parallel. A strap muscle is the same width all along; a fusiform muscle has a thick belly that tapers at each end.
cards.why: Fusus means spindle, the shape of a fusiform muscle.

cards.front: Convergent vs circular muscle?
cards.back: Convergent: fans out from one tendon over a broad origin. Circular: fascicles run in rings around an opening (a sphincter).
cards.why: A convergent muscle can pull in several directions depending on which fascicles fire; a circular one closes the opening it surrounds.

cards.front: Name the seven kinds of clue used in muscle names.
cards.back: Location, shape, size, direction of fascicles, number of origins (heads), attachments and action.
cards.why: Most names combine two or three clues; decode them as what it does, where, and any size or shape word.

cards.front: Decode “abductor digiti minimi”.
cards.back: The muscle that abducts the smallest digit: the little finger.
cards.why: Abductor = moves away from the midline; digiti = of the digit; minimi = of the smallest.

cards.front: Facial expression vs mastication muscles: where do they insert?
cards.back: Facial muscles: into the skin (or another muscle). Chewing muscles: on the mandible.
cards.why: That is why facial muscles move the skin of the face while chewing muscles move the jaw at the temporomandibular joint.

cards.front: Name the four muscles of mastication.
cards.back: Masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid.
cards.why: All start on the skull and insert on the mandible; the buccinator is not one of them.

cards.front: Is the buccinator a chewing muscle?
cards.back: No. It is a muscle of facial expression that presses the cheek against the teeth.
cards.why: It inserts into the orbicularis oris, not the mandible, so it cannot move the jaw; it keeps food on the teeth while the chewing muscles work.

cards.front: Which chewing muscles close the jaw, and which help open it?
cards.back: Close: masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid. Open: the lateral pterygoids, helped by the suprahyoids and gravity.
cards.why: Three of four chewing muscles close the jaw, which is why biting is far stronger than opening.

cards.front: Masseter: origin, insertion, action?
cards.back: Zygomatic arch → outer surface of the angle of the mandible. Elevates the mandible (prime mover of jaw closing).
cards.why: Clench your teeth and you feel it bulge at the angle of the jaw.

cards.front: Temporalis: origin, insertion, action?
cards.back: Temporal fossa → coronoid process of the mandible. Elevates the mandible; its back fibers retract it.
cards.why: It is convergent: a broad fan on the side of the skull narrowing to a tendon under the zygomatic arch.

cards.front: What does the lateral pterygoid do?
cards.back: Protracts the mandible, helps open the mouth, and moves the jaw side to side for grinding.
cards.why: It runs almost horizontally from the sphenoid to the condyle and the joint’s disc, so it pulls the condyle forward.

cards.front: Frontalis: what does it do, and what does it pull against?
cards.back: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead, pulling against the epicranial aponeurosis.
cards.why: The occipitalis anchors the aponeurosis from behind so the frontalis has something to pull on.

cards.front: Orbicularis oculi vs orbicularis oris?
cards.back: Oculi: ring around the eye that closes the eyelids. Oris: ring around the lips that closes and protrudes them.
cards.why: Both are circular muscles acting as sphincters around an opening.

cards.front: Which muscle pulls the corner of the mouth up and back in a smile?
cards.back: Zygomaticus major.
cards.why: It runs from the zygomatic bone (the cheekbone) to the corner of the mouth, so its pull lifts that corner.

cards.front: The right sternocleidomastoid contracts alone. Which way does your face turn?
cards.back: To the left (the opposite side), while the head tilts toward the right shoulder.
cards.why: It pulls the mastoid process behind the right ear down and forward toward the sternum, which swings the face to the left.

cards.front: What do both sternocleidomastoids do together?
cards.back: Flex the neck, bringing the chin toward the chest.
cards.why: As when you lift your head off a pillow.

cards.front: Scalenes: attachments and main action?
cards.back: Transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae → first two ribs. Elevate the upper ribs; with the ribs fixed, flex the neck.
cards.why: Recordings show they work in most breaths at rest and hardest in heavy breathing. For your exam, they are listed as accessory breathing muscles.

cards.front: Suprahyoid vs infrahyoid muscles: what do they do to the hyoid?
cards.back: Suprahyoids elevate it (in swallowing). Infrahyoids depress it (after swallowing) and hold it still.
cards.why: The hyoid forms no joint with another bone, so these opposing sets are what position it.

cards.front: How do the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles work together to open the mouth?
cards.back: The infrahyoids hold the hyoid still as fixators; the suprahyoids then pull the mandible down.
cards.why: With its lower end fixed, a suprahyoid muscle moves its upper attachment instead.

cards.front: Name two suprahyoid and two infrahyoid muscles.
cards.back: Suprahyoid: digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, stylohyoid. Infrahyoid: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid.
cards.why: Their names give their attachments: each includes the hyoid plus where it runs to.

cards.front: Name the three columns of the erector spinae, lateral to medial.
cards.back: Iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis (“I Love Spaghetti”).
cards.why: Together they are the prime mover for extending the vertebral column.

cards.front: What do the erector spinae do as you bend forward to touch your toes?
cards.back: They contract eccentrically, lengthening while they brake the forward bend.
cards.why: Gravity pulls you forward; the back extensors pay out slowly, then pull you back upright.

cards.front: Which two muscles turn your head to the right?
cards.back: The right splenius and the left sternocleidomastoid.
cards.why: One splenius turns the face to its own side; one sternocleidomastoid turns it to the opposite side.

cards.front: Rectus abdominis: origin, insertion, action?
cards.back: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis → xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5–7. Flexes the spine and compresses the abdomen.
cards.why: Its tendinous intersections make the “six-pack”; each strap lies in a rectus sheath meeting at the linea alba.

cards.front: External oblique vs internal oblique vs transversus abdominis: fascicle direction?
cards.back: External: down and toward the midline (“hands in pockets”). Internal: up and toward the midline. Transversus: horizontal, like a belt.
cards.why: Three layers in three directions make the wall strong in every direction, like plywood.

cards.front: Which obliques turn your trunk to the right?
cards.back: The left external oblique and the right internal oblique.
cards.why: One external oblique turns the trunk to the opposite side and one internal oblique to its own side; these two line up in one diagonal.

cards.front: Which abdominal muscle mainly compresses the abdomen without turning the trunk?
cards.back: Transversus abdominis.
cards.why: Its horizontal fibers squeeze the belly like a belt; they have no diagonal line of pull to rotate the trunk.

cards.front: What does the quadratus lumborum do?
cards.back: One side bends the trunk sideways or hikes the pelvis; both extend the lower spine; it anchors the twelfth rib for the diaphragm.
cards.why: It runs from the iliac crest to the twelfth rib and the lumbar transverse processes, in the back wall of the abdomen.

cards.front: Diaphragm: origin, insertion, and what contraction does.
cards.back: Lower rim of the rib cage, xiphoid and upper lumbar vertebrae → its own central tendon. Contracting flattens the dome and makes the chest taller.
cards.why: It has no bony insertion: its fibers pull their own tendon down.

cards.front: External vs internal intercostals: fiber direction and effect on the ribs?
cards.back: External: down and forward; lift the ribs up and out. Internal: down and back; pull them down and in (except beside the sternum).
cards.why: The externals run the same way as the external oblique, the internals at right angles to them.

cards.front: External vs internal intercostals: when do they work?
cards.back: External: breathing in. Internal: forceful breathing out.
cards.why: At rest, breathing out is passive recoil, so the internal intercostals join in only when you breathe out hard.

cards.front: Which muscles work in a breath in at rest?
cards.back: The diaphragm does most of the work; for your exam, the diaphragm and the external intercostals.
cards.why: Recordings show the scalenes and the internal intercostals beside the sternum are also active in most resting breaths.

cards.front: Which extra muscles join in hard breathing?
cards.back: In: the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids lift the top of the rib cage harder. Out: the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles squeeze air out.
cards.why: At rest breathing out is passive; hard breathing makes it active.

cards.front: What are the two muscles of the pelvic diaphragm, and what do they do?
cards.back: Levator ani and coccygeus. They support the pelvic organs, resist abdominal pressure and help keep the openings closed.
cards.why: The levator ani contracts at the same moment as the abdominal wall in a cough, sneeze or lift.

cards.front: How is the perineum divided?
cards.back: A line between the ischial tuberosities splits it into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.
cards.why: Its corners are the pubic symphysis, the coccyx and the two ischial tuberosities.

cards.front: What is the chain rule for limb muscles?
cards.back: A muscle moves the bone beyond the one it sits on.
cards.why: Trunk muscles position the scapula, trunk and scapular muscles move the humerus, arm muscles move the forearm, forearm muscles move the wrist and fingers.

cards.front: What do the three parts of the trapezius do?
cards.back: Upper fibers elevate the scapula, middle fibers retract it, lower fibers depress it; upper and lower together rotate it upward.
cards.why: Its fibers run in three directions from the skull and spine to the clavicle and scapula.

cards.front: Serratus anterior vs rhomboids: what is their relationship?
cards.back: Antagonists: the serratus anterior protracts the scapula; the rhomboids retract it.
cards.why: Paralysis of the serratus anterior gives a winged scapula when the person pushes on a wall.

cards.front: Pectoralis major vs latissimus dorsi at the shoulder?
cards.back: Pectoralis major flexes the arm; latissimus dorsi extends it. Both adduct and medially rotate it.
