cards.why: They are antagonists for flexion and extension but synergists for adduction and medial rotation.

cards.front: Deltoid: prime mover of what, and where does it insert?
cards.back: Abduction of the arm; it inserts on the deltoid tuberosity.
cards.why: Its front fibers also flex and medially rotate the arm, and its back fibers extend and laterally rotate it.

cards.front: Name the rotator cuff muscles (SITS).
cards.back: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.
cards.why: Their tendons blend with the joint capsule and hold the head of the humerus in the shallow glenoid cavity.

cards.front: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle?
cards.back: The subscapularis. The other three insert on the greater tubercle.
cards.why: The subscapularis lies on the front (rib side) of the scapula, so it reaches the front of the humerus.

cards.front: Which rotator cuff muscles rotate the arm laterally, and which medially?
cards.back: Laterally: infraspinatus and teres minor. Medially: subscapularis.
cards.why: The cuff rotates in both directions; its main job is holding the head of the humerus in place.

cards.front: Which muscle initiates abduction of the arm?
cards.back: For your exam: the supraspinatus. Recordings show the supraspinatus and deltoid are both active from the start and throughout.
cards.why: The supraspinatus also keeps the head of the humerus seated so the deltoid’s upward pull turns into rotation rather than sliding.

cards.front: Which rotator cuff tendon tears most often, and why?
cards.back: The supraspinatus. Most tears come from age-related wear of the tendon itself; repeated overhead work adds strain.
cards.why: Its tendon runs through the tight space between the head of the humerus and the acromion.

cards.front: What is the prime mover of elbow flexion, and what are its synergists?
cards.back: For your exam: the biceps brachii, with the brachialis and brachioradialis as synergists.
cards.why: Many anatomists call the brachialis the main flexor, since it inserts on the ulna and works in every forearm position.

cards.front: Elbow flexors vs extensor: where do they insert?
cards.back: Biceps brachii: radial tuberosity. Brachialis: coronoid process of the ulna. Triceps brachii: olecranon of the ulna.
cards.why: Flexors insert in front of the elbow, the extensor behind it.

cards.front: Elbow flexion vs extension: which lever classes?
cards.back: Flexion: third class. Extension by the triceps brachii: first class.
cards.why: The flexors insert between the elbow and the hand; the triceps pulls on the olecranon behind the joint, with the load in front.

cards.front: Why does the brachialis flex the elbow in every forearm position, but the biceps brachii does not?
cards.back: The brachialis inserts on the ulna, which does not rotate; the biceps inserts on the radius, which rolls.
cards.why: The biceps pulls hardest with the palm up; the brachioradialis is strongest with the thumb up.

cards.front: Which muscles supinate the forearm, and which pronate it?
cards.back: Supinate: supinator and biceps brachii (the strongest). Pronate: pronator quadratus (the main one) and pronator teres.
cards.why: Think of driving a screw in with your right hand: that is supination.

cards.compare: Wrist and finger flexors vs extensors
cards.front: Wrist and finger flexors vs extensors: common origin?
cards.back: Flexors: medial epicondyle. Extensors: lateral epicondyle.
cards.why: Each group starts from a shared tendon on one epicondyle of the humerus.

cards.compare: Wrist and finger flexors vs extensors
cards.front: Tennis elbow vs golfer’s elbow?
cards.back: Tennis elbow: strain of the extensors’ origin on the lateral epicondyle. Golfer’s elbow: strain of the flexors’ origin on the medial epicondyle.
cards.why: Repeated gripping and twisting strains the common tendon where it attaches.

cards.compare: Wrist and finger flexors vs extensors
cards.front: Flexor digitorum superficialis vs profundus: where do they insert?
cards.back: Superficialis: middle phalanges. Profundus: distal phalanges.
cards.why: The profundus tendons pass through splits in the superficialis tendons, so it is the only muscle that bends the fingertips.

cards.compare: Wrist and finger flexors vs extensors
cards.front: Which two muscles bend the wrist toward the thumb?
cards.back: Flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis (longus and brevis) together.
cards.why: The flexor and extensor on the same edge cancel each other’s flexion and extension and add their sideways pull.

cards.front: What passes through the carpal tunnel, and why do its symptoms appear in the thumb?
cards.back: The finger flexor tendons and a nerve. Swollen tendon sheaths squeeze the nerve, which supplies the thumb side of the hand and the thenar muscles.
cards.why: Late, severe cases show wasting of the thenar eminence.

cards.front: Extrinsic vs intrinsic muscles of the hand?
cards.back: Extrinsic: in the forearm, sending tendons to the hand; give grip strength. Intrinsic: start and end in the hand; make fine movements.
cards.why: Keeping the big muscles in the forearm keeps the hand slim.

cards.front: Which muscles fill the anterior and posterior compartments of the arm?
cards.back: Anterior: biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis (flex the elbow). Posterior: triceps brachii (extends it).
cards.why: Muscles in one compartment usually share a main action.

cards.front: Prime mover of hip flexion vs hip extension?
cards.back: Flexion: iliopsoas. Extension: gluteus maximus.
cards.why: The iliopsoas crosses in front of the hip to the lesser trochanter; the gluteus maximus lies behind it.

cards.front: When does the gluteus maximus work hardest?
cards.back: Climbing stairs, running or rising from a squat; it does little in easy level walking.
cards.why: Those movements need powerful hip extension against body weight.

cards.front: What does the gluteus medius do in every step?
cards.back: It holds the pelvis level over the standing leg.
cards.why: Weak, it lets the pelvis drop toward the lifted leg: a positive Trendelenburg sign.

cards.front: Which two muscles pull on the iliotibial tract?
cards.back: Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae.
cards.why: The tract is thickened deep fascia from the iliac crest to the lateral tibia; tightening it steadies the knee.

cards.front: Quadriceps femoris vs hamstrings: action at the knee and hip?
cards.back: Quadriceps: extend the knee; the rectus femoris also flexes the hip. Hamstrings: flex the knee and extend the hip.
cards.why: They are the antagonist pair of the knee.

cards.front: Name the four quadriceps and the three hamstrings.
cards.back: Quadriceps: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius. Hamstrings: biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus.
cards.why: The quadriceps share one tendon to the tibial tuberosity; the hamstrings share an origin on the ischial tuberosity.

cards.front: Quadriceps femoris vs hamstrings: origin and insertion?
cards.back: Quadriceps: ilium (rectus femoris) and femur (vasti) → tibial tuberosity via the patella and patellar ligament. Hamstrings: ischial tuberosity → head of the fibula and medial tibia.
cards.why: Only the rectus femoris and the hamstrings (except the short head of the biceps femoris) cross the hip.

cards.front: When are the hamstrings most at risk of a strain?
cards.back: When the hip is flexed and the knee straight at once, as at the end of a sprinter’s forward swing.
cards.why: They cross both joints, so that position stretches them most while they work to brake the leg.

cards.front: What does the sartorius do?
cards.back: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh and flexes the knee.
cards.why: The longest muscle in the body, it crosses the thigh diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia.

cards.front: What borders the femoral triangle?
cards.back: The inguinal ligament above, the sartorius laterally and the adductor longus medially.
cards.why: The thigh’s main artery, vein and a large nerve lie just under the skin there.

cards.front: Which muscles are the antagonists of the hip abductors?
cards.back: The medial thigh muscles: adductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis and pectineus.
cards.why: They start on the pubis and pull the thigh toward the midline; the gluteus medius and minimus pull it away.

cards.compare: The three muscle groups of the leg
cards.front: Front vs side vs back of the leg: main action at the ankle?
cards.back: Front: dorsiflexion. Side: eversion. Back: plantar flexion.
cards.why: Each group sits in its own fascial compartment and shares one main job.

cards.compare: The three muscle groups of the leg
cards.front: What does weakness of each leg group cause?
cards.back: Front: toes drag when the leg swings forward. Side: the ankle rolls inward easily. Back: cannot rise onto the toes.
cards.why: Each sign is the loss of that group’s main action.

cards.compare: The three muscle groups of the leg
cards.front: Gastrocnemius vs soleus?
cards.back: Both plantar flex through the calcaneal tendon. The gastrocnemius also crosses the knee and helps flex it; the soleus crosses only the ankle and works almost constantly when you stand.
cards.why: The gastrocnemius starts on the femoral condyles; the soleus on the fibula and tibia.

cards.front: Tibialis anterior vs tibialis posterior?
cards.back: Anterior: dorsiflexes and inverts the foot. Posterior: plantar flexes and inverts it and holds up the medial arch.
cards.why: Antagonists for up-and-down movement, synergists for inversion.

cards.front: What are the signs of a ruptured calcaneal (Achilles) tendon?
cards.back: The person cannot rise onto the toes of that foot, and squeezing the calf no longer points the foot.
cards.why: The tendon is the only link from the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus.

cards.front: What are the early signs of compartment syndrome?
cards.back: Pain far worse than the injury explains, and pain on passive stretch of the compartment’s muscles.
cards.why: Numbness and weakness come later, and a pulse can still be present, because the artery’s pressure is far higher than the compartment’s.

cards.front: Why does swelling inside a limb compartment become dangerous so fast?
cards.back: Deep fascia barely stretches, so added fluid raises the pressure, closes the veins, traps more fluid and stops capillary flow.
cards.why: The treatment is surgery to slit the fascia open along the compartment.

cards.front: Deltoid site: where, and what is it used for?
cards.back: About 2–3 finger widths below the acromion, on the side of the arm. The usual site for vaccines in adults; small volumes only.
cards.why: The muscle is small. Too low or far back risks a nerve winding around the humerus; too high, the subacromial bursa.

cards.front: Ventrogluteal site: landmarks and use?
cards.back: Heel of the hand on the greater trochanter, index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine, middle finger along the iliac crest; inject in the center of the V. Preferred for larger volumes in adults and children.
cards.why: The gluteus medius and minimus there are thick, with no large nerves or vessels.

cards.front: Vastus lateralis site: where, and who is it preferred for?
cards.back: The middle third of the outer front thigh. Preferred for infants.
cards.why: Infants’ gluteal muscles are still small, while the vastus lateralis is already thick.

cards.front: Why is the dorsogluteal site (upper outer buttock) avoided?
cards.back: A large nerve leaving the pelvis below the piriformis lies close by, and thick fat means the needle often misses the muscle.
cards.why: Vaccines go into the deltoid or, in infants, the vastus lateralis, not the buttock.
